courses.title: Critical and Cultural Theories
courses.overview: Critical theories offer different questions about how texts and cultural practices make meaning. Move from form and signs to readers, then power and identity, and finally the instability and social life of meaning. Use each approach as a justified interpretive lens.
journey: Notice form and signifying relations.
Ask what readers bring and how interpretation happens.
Examine institutions, material conditions, gender and colonial power.
Test fixed meanings and identities through texts and cultural practices.

topics.title: Defamiliarization
topics.core: Defamiliarization makes familiar things seem unfamiliar, renewing perception.
topics.explanation: Shklovsky associates art with slowing habitual perception through unusual perspective, description or form.
topics.example: Teaching illustration: Describe a lift as a small room that carries people through a building; the unfamiliar wording renews attention.
topics.confusion: It concerns an effect on perception, not simply using difficult vocabulary.

questions.prompt: Explain defamiliarization briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Defamiliarization makes familiar things seem unfamiliar, renewing perception.
questions.answer: Defamiliarization makes familiar things seem unfamiliar, renewing perception. Shklovsky associates art with slowing habitual perception through unusual perspective, description or form.
keyPoints: Defamiliarization makes familiar things seem unfamiliar, renewing perception.

questions.prompt: How could a familiar bus journey be defamiliarized?
questions.shortAnswer: Describe it through someone encountering buses for the first time, attending to its sounds and rituals.

questions.prompt: What is Formalism?
questions.shortAnswer: Formalism studies the devices and organisation that create literary effects.
questions.answer: Formalism studies the devices and organisation that create literary effects. It foregrounds how a work uses language and form, including literariness and defamiliarization.
keyPoints: Formalism studies the devices and organisation that create literary effects.

topics.title: Foregrounding
topics.core: Foregrounding makes features of language especially noticeable.
topics.explanation: Deviation or patterned repetition can draw attention to sound, syntax or wording. Mayakovsky illustrates startling poetic language; the concept is associated with Prague School work.
topics.example: Teaching illustration: Repeated initial sounds in a slogan make its wording prominent.
topics.confusion: Foregrounding can occur outside poetry and need not depend only on deviation.

questions.prompt: Explain foregrounding briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Foregrounding makes features of language especially noticeable.

questions.prompt: Does repeated alliteration count as foregrounding even without unusual grammar?
questions.shortAnswer: Yes.
questions.answer: Yes. Repetition can make a sound pattern salient. Foregrounding includes parallelism as well as departures from expected language.
keyPoints: Yes. Repetition can make a sound pattern salient. Foregrounding includes parallelism as well as departures from expected language.

topics.title: Practical criticism
topics.core: Practical criticism closely analyses a text with external identifying information withheld.
topics.explanation: Richards used anonymous poems to investigate readers' responses and misunderstandings. Attention falls on words, tone, imagery and their relations.
topics.example: Teaching illustration: Read a poem without knowing its author, then justify a reading from its wording.
topics.confusion: A reading exercise without biography does not establish that historical context never matters.

topics.title: New Criticism and close reading
topics.core: New Criticism studies the internal relations of literary language through close reading.
topics.explanation: It often seeks organic unity through tensions, paradoxes and irony. Form and meaning are understood as closely interdependent.
topics.example: Teaching illustration: Explain how a poem's opposing images contribute to an overall interpretation.
topics.confusion: Close reading is a method used by many approaches, not the exclusive property of New Criticism.

topics.title: Sign and signification
topics.core: A Saussurean sign links a signifier with a signified; signification is meaning production.
topics.explanation: The signifier is the form and the signified is the concept. Their association is conventional within a language system.
topics.example: Teaching illustration: The sound pattern of tree calls up a concept; another language uses a different form.
topics.confusion: The signified is a concept, not the physical object itself.

questions.shortAnswer: A Saussurean sign links a signifier with a signified; signification is meaning production.

questions.prompt: Why does another language's different word for tree support arbitrariness?
questions.shortAnswer: It shows that the sound–concept association is socially conventional rather than a necessary natural resemblance.
questions.answer: It shows that the sound–concept association is socially conventional rather than a necessary natural resemblance.
keyPoints: It shows that the sound–concept association is socially conventional rather than a necessary natural resemblance.

questions.prompt: What is structuralism?
questions.shortAnswer: Structuralism examines how elements acquire meaning through relations within a system.
questions.answer: Structuralism examines how elements acquire meaning through relations within a system. In literary study, it investigates sign systems, narrative conventions and contrasts rather than treating each element as self-contained.
keyPoints: Structuralism examines how elements acquire meaning through relations within a system.

topics.title: Paradigm and syntagm
topics.core: A paradigm concerns alternatives; a syntagm concerns combinations.
topics.explanation: A speaker selects among possible items and combines selected items into an organised sequence.
topics.example: Teaching illustration: In the dog sleeps, cat can replace dog paradigmatically; the whole sequence is syntagmatic.
topics.confusion: Selection and combination are related axes, not two separate kinds of language.

questions.prompt: Explain paradigm and syntagm briefly.

questions.prompt: Identify both axes in the phrase a bright student.
questions.shortAnswer: Bright could be replaced by quiet or talented on the selection axis.
questions.answer: Bright could be replaced by quiet or talented on the selection axis. The ordered combination of determiner, adjective and noun is the syntagmatic axis.

topics.title: Binary oppositions
topics.core: Binary oppositions organise meaning through paired contrasts.
topics.explanation: Structuralist analysis examines how contrasts such as nature/culture organise a text. Later critics ask whether one term is privileged and how the opposition is unsettled.
topics.example: Teaching illustration: A story opposes city and village, associating each with different values.
topics.confusion: A contrast need not be a simple or universal natural division.

topics.title: Mythoi and archetypal criticism
topics.core: Frye's mythoi are recurring narrative patterns used in archetypal criticism.
topics.explanation: His seasonal scheme associates comedy with spring, romance with summer, tragedy with autumn, and irony/satire with winter.
topics.example: Teaching illustration: A story of social renewal ending in celebration fits a comic pattern.
topics.confusion: A critical classification is an interpretive framework, not proof that every culture tells identical stories.

topics.title: Narratology and narrative order
topics.core: Narratology studies how narratives are structured and presented.
topics.explanation: Distinguish the chronological sequence of events from their artistic arrangement. Todorov's model describes equilibrium, disruption and a changed equilibrium.
topics.example: Teaching illustration: A novel starts with a death, then returns to the events that led to it.

topics.title: Barthes's myth
topics.core: For Barthes, myth makes historically constructed cultural values appear natural.
topics.explanation: A first-level sign can become the signifier of a second-level ideological message. Analyse what a representation encourages audiences to take for granted.
topics.example: Teaching illustration: An advert links a product with an idealised national lifestyle.

topics.title: Hermeneutics
topics.core: Hermeneutics concerns interpretation and understanding.
topics.explanation: Interpretation moves between parts and whole and is shaped by historical assumptions. Different hermeneutic traditions place different weight on author, history and reader.
topics.example: Teaching illustration: An ending changes your understanding of an earlier scene, prompting rereading.
topics.confusion: The hermeneutic circle is a productive movement of understanding, not merely circular proof.

topics.title: Phenomenology
topics.core: Phenomenology investigates how things appear in experience and consciousness.
topics.explanation: In literary study it can focus on the structures of reading experience. Husserl's intentionality means consciousness is directed toward something.

topics.title: Horizon of expectations
topics.core: A horizon of expectations is the historically shaped background readers bring to a work.
topics.explanation: Genre knowledge, earlier reading and cultural assumptions affect reception. A new work may confirm or challenge these expectations.
topics.example: Teaching illustration: Readers expecting a conventional detective ending encounter an unresolved mystery.
topics.confusion: Jauss stresses historical reception; individual preference alone is too narrow.

topics.title: Reception theory and gaps
topics.core: Iser treats reading as an interaction in which readers realise a text's possibilities.
topics.explanation: Texts guide inference while leaving gaps. The implied reader is a role structured by the text, distinct from any actual individual.
topics.example: Teaching illustration: Readers infer a character's motive from incomplete dialogue and action.
topics.confusion: Gaps permit interpretation but do not make every reading equally well supported.

questions.shortAnswer: No.

topics.title: Speech acts
topics.core: Speech acts are actions performed through utterances.
topics.explanation: Distinguish locution, illocution and perlocution: what is said, the act performed, and its effect. Appropriate conditions matter to the act's success.
topics.example: Teaching illustration: I promise to return performs a commitment rather than merely describing one.
topics.confusion: An intended effect is not guaranteed to occur.

topics.title: Dialectical materialism
topics.core: Dialectical materialism examines change through contradictions in material conditions.
topics.explanation: In Marxist analysis, economic organisation and conflict help explain social transformation. Avoid treating thesis–antithesis–synthesis as a mechanical formula for every event.
topics.example: Teaching illustration: Conflicting interests of workers and owners generate tensions within production.
topics.confusion: Materialism here concerns explanatory priority, not a personal love of possessions.

topics.title: Base and superstructure
topics.core: The base concerns economic production relations; superstructure concerns institutions and cultural forms.
topics.explanation: The relation is complex rather than a one-way copying process. Art and institutions can have relative autonomy while remaining socially situated.
topics.example: Teaching illustration: A novel's publication depends on markets, yet its form can challenge dominant values.
topics.confusion: Economic influence does not mean every artistic detail is mechanically caused by economics.

topics.core: Alienation describes estrangement from one's labour, its products, other people or human capacities.
topics.explanation: In Marx's account, capitalist labour can confront workers as an externally controlled activity whose products belong to others.
topics.example: Teaching illustration: A worker makes one component repeatedly without control over the finished product or working process.

topics.explanation: Marx examines how commodity exchange obscures the social labour relations through which value is organised.

topics.core: Hegemony is leadership and dominance maintained through consent as well as power.
topics.explanation: Gramsci highlights how institutions and common sense secure acceptance of a social order. Consent can coexist with coercion and resistance.
topics.example: Teaching illustration: An unequal hierarchy is accepted as natural merit through repeated cultural messages.
topics.confusion: Hegemony does not imply that force disappears or consent is unanimous.

topics.title: Standardization
topics.core: Standardization develops shared norms through selection, codification, functional elaboration and acceptance.
topics.explanation: These processes can overlap and be contested. Codification records norms; elaboration extends their use into new domains.

topics.title: Pidgins and pidginization
topics.core: A pidgin is a contact variety conventionally used as an additional means of communication among groups.
topics.explanation: Pidginization concerns its development in contact settings. Pidgins have structured grammars; some expand across functions and persist over time.
topics.example: Teaching illustration: A contact variety develops for communication among speakers without a shared first language.
topics.confusion: Pidgins are not random broken speech, and not all are temporary.

topics.title: Creoles and creolization
topics.core: Creoles are established community languages that developed in particular language-contact histories.

topics.title: Post-creole continuum

topics.explanation: Basilect, mesolect and acrolect name relative positions in such a continuum. Speakers may vary by situation and access.

topics.explanation: The contribution of vocabulary does not make the resulting language merely a corrupt form of its lexifier. Social conditions shape convergence and maintenance.

topics.title: Tree and wave models
topics.core: A tree represents genealogical branching; a wave represents diffusion of innovations across communities.
topics.explanation: The models emphasise inheritance and contact respectively. Contact can cross genealogical boundaries, so neither model alone captures every relation.
topics.example: Teaching illustration: A pronunciation innovation spreads across neighbouring dialects while their genealogical histories remain distinct.
topics.confusion: The wave model complements rather than simply disproves genealogical classification.

topics.title: Isogloss
topics.core: An isogloss maps the geographical distribution boundary of a linguistic feature.
topics.explanation: Several isoglosses may cluster into a bundle, helping identify dialect areas. Different features need not have identical boundaries.
topics.example: Teaching illustration: Map where one word for an everyday object gives way to another.
topics.confusion: One isogloss does not by itself define a complete language or dialect boundary.

topics.title: Diffusion and social networks
topics.core: Diffusion is the spread of linguistic innovations through contact and social relations.
topics.explanation: Access, prestige, identity and networks affect adoption. Spread need not be uniform or form perfectly circular waves.

topics.confusion: Geographical proximity alone does not guarantee adoption.

topics.title: Diglossia
topics.core: Diglossia involves a relatively stable functional distribution of varieties or languages within a community.
topics.explanation: Ferguson's classic account contrasts high and low varieties; later usage extends the concept. The labels refer to social functions and prestige.

topics.title: Bilingualism

topics.example: Teaching illustration: A person reads academic material in one language and talks with family in another.

topics.title: Simultaneous and sequential bilingualism
topics.core: Simultaneous bilingual development begins with two languages early together; sequential development adds another after initial first-language development.

questions.answer: Sense is the semantic content through which an expression is understood, distinct from a particular referent. Expressions can share a referent while presenting it differently. The guide gives limited technical coverage of sense.

topics.title: Reference and denotation
topics.core: Reference identifies an entity in use; denotation concerns what an expression conventionally applies to.
topics.explanation: A common noun can denote a category, while a speaker uses a noun phrase to identify a particular member.
topics.example: Teaching example: Cat applies to cats generally; that cat can refer to a particular animal in context.
topics.confusion: Reference needs not be fixed solely by dictionary meaning.

topics.title: Propositions
topics.core: A proposition is the content that can be asserted, denied or evaluated for truth.
topics.explanation: Different sentence forms can be related to the same situation content, while questions need not assert it.
topics.example: Teaching example: The door is open and Is the door open? concern the same possible state.
topics.confusion: A proposition is not simply the sequence of words in a sentence.

topics.title: Ambiguity, homonymy and polysemy
topics.core: Ambiguity allows distinct readings; homonymy involves unrelated lexical meanings, while polysemy involves related meanings.
topics.explanation: Lexical ambiguity can come from homonymy or polysemy; structural ambiguity comes from alternative grammatical organisation.
topics.example: Teaching example: Bank can mean a financial institution or a river edge; head has several related uses.
topics.confusion: Relatedness is sometimes debatable; contextual variation does not always establish a stored lexical sense.

topics.title: Vagueness
topics.core: Vagueness concerns unclear boundaries within a reading rather than several distinct readings.

topics.title: Componential analysis
topics.core: Componential analysis represents word meanings through combinations of semantic features.

topics.title: Semantic roles
topics.core: Semantic roles describe how participants relate to an event, such as agent, theme or patient.
topics.explanation: An agent typically initiates an action; a patient is affected; a theme is involved or moved. Role inventories differ across frameworks.
topics.example: Teaching example: In The child broke the cup, child is agent and cup is patient.
topics.confusion: Semantic roles do not equal grammatical functions: a subject need not be an agent.

topics.title: Synonymy and near-synonymy
topics.core: Synonymy concerns sameness or close similarity of meaning between expressions.
topics.explanation: Near synonyms can differ in register, distribution, connotation or collocation, so complete interchangeability is unusual.

topics.title: Hyponymy and meronymy
topics.core: Hyponymy is a kind-of relation; meronymy is a part-of relation.
topics.explanation: These organise vocabulary in different ways and should be identified by the relevant conceptual link.

topics.title: Antonymy and complementarity

topics.title: Conventional and conversational implicature
topics.core: Conventional implicature is tied to particular expressions; conversational implicature is inferred through context and communicative expectations.
topics.explanation: Conversational implicatures can often be cancelled or changed by context. A generalized inference needs less special context than a particularized one.
topics.example: Teaching example: Some passed may suggest not all, yet 'in fact, all did' can cancel that inference.
topics.confusion: Conversational implicature is not a strict logical entailment.

questions.prompt: Explain conventional and conversational implicature briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Conventional implicature is tied to particular expressions; conversational implicature is inferred through context and communicative expectations.
questions.answer: Conventional implicature is tied to particular expressions; conversational implicature is inferred through context and communicative expectations. Conversational implicatures can often be cancelled or changed by context. A generalized inference needs less special context than a particularized one.
keyPoints: Conventional implicature is tied to particular expressions; conversational implicature is inferred through context and communicative expectations.
Conversational implicature is not a strict logical entailment.

questions.prompt: Why can 'Some students passed—in fact, all did' be consistent?
questions.shortAnswer: Some does not semantically exclude all in the relevant logical reading.
questions.answer: Some does not semantically exclude all in the relevant logical reading. The not-all suggestion is normally an implicature that the continuation can cancel.
keyPoints: Some does not semantically exclude all in the relevant logical reading.
The not-all suggestion is normally an implicature that the continuation can cancel.

topics.title: Cooperation and conversational maxims
topics.core: Grice's Cooperative Principle describes an expectation of contributions appropriate to an exchange's purpose.
topics.explanation: The maxims concern Quality, Quantity, Relation and Manner: truthfulness, informativeness, relevance and clarity.
topics.example: Teaching example: A concise relevant answer supports the current task.
topics.confusion: Cooperation is a framework for interpreting conversation, not a rule requiring social agreement.

questions.prompt: Explain cooperation and conversational maxims briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Grice's Cooperative Principle describes an expectation of contributions appropriate to an exchange's purpose.
questions.answer: Grice's Cooperative Principle describes an expectation of contributions appropriate to an exchange's purpose. The maxims concern Quality, Quantity, Relation and Manner: truthfulness, informativeness, relevance and clarity.
keyPoints: Grice's Cooperative Principle describes an expectation of contributions appropriate to an exchange's purpose.
Cooperation is a framework for interpreting conversation, not a rule requiring social agreement.

questions.prompt: Which maxim is relevant if someone knowingly supplies false information?
questions.shortAnswer: Quality, because it concerns truthfulness and adequate evidence.
questions.answer: Quality, because it concerns truthfulness and adequate evidence. The interpretation also depends on whether deception or an openly recognisable nonliteral use is involved.
keyPoints: Quality, because it concerns truthfulness and adequate evidence.
The interpretation also depends on whether deception or an openly recognisable nonliteral use is involved.

topics.title: Flouting and violating maxims
topics.core: Flouting makes a mismatch conspicuous so an implicature can be inferred; violating covertly fails an expectation.
topics.explanation: A hearer may infer irony or an indirect message when the apparent mismatch is openly recognisable.
topics.example: Teaching example: Lovely weather as a reply to a sensitive question may signal a wish to change topic.
topics.confusion: A maxim departure is not automatically deliberate or interpretable as one fixed message.

questions.prompt: Explain flouting and violating maxims briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Flouting makes a mismatch conspicuous so an implicature can be inferred; violating covertly fails an expectation.
questions.answer: Flouting makes a mismatch conspicuous so an implicature can be inferred; violating covertly fails an expectation. A hearer may infer irony or an indirect message when the apparent mismatch is openly recognisable.
keyPoints: Flouting makes a mismatch conspicuous so an implicature can be inferred; violating covertly fails an expectation.
A maxim departure is not automatically deliberate or interpretable as one fixed message.

questions.prompt: How does an obvious ironic compliment differ from a successful lie in Gricean terms?
questions.shortAnswer: The ironic mismatch is meant to be noticed and can flout Quality.
questions.answer: The ironic mismatch is meant to be noticed and can flout Quality. A lie covertly violates truthfulness while aiming to be accepted as true.
keyPoints: The ironic mismatch is meant to be noticed and can flout Quality.
A lie covertly violates truthfulness while aiming to be accepted as true.

topics.title: Deixis and the deictic centre
topics.core: Deixis links interpretation to an utterance's participants, time, place or related contextual coordinates.
topics.explanation: The ordinary centre is speaker, here and now. Some uses are anaphoric rather than deictic, depending on how a referent is identified.
topics.example: Teaching example: I will meet you here tomorrow needs a speaker, addressee, location and date.
topics.confusion: A form such as that can have deictic or anaphoric uses.

questions.prompt: Explain deixis and the deictic centre briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Deixis links interpretation to an utterance's participants, time, place or related contextual coordinates.
questions.answer: Deixis links interpretation to an utterance's participants, time, place or related contextual coordinates. The ordinary centre is speaker, here and now. Some uses are anaphoric rather than deictic, depending on how a referent is identified.
keyPoints: Deixis links interpretation to an utterance's participants, time, place or related contextual coordinates.
A form such as that can have deictic or anaphoric uses.

questions.prompt: Why can 'I'll be here tomorrow' become unclear when read days later?
questions.shortAnswer: Here and tomorrow depend on the relevant contextual centre.
questions.answer: Here and tomorrow depend on the relevant contextual centre. The reader must recover the intended place and time instead of automatically using their own current coordinates.
keyPoints: Here and tomorrow depend on the relevant contextual centre.
The reader must recover the intended place and time instead of automatically using their own current coordinates.

topics.title: Deictic projection
topics.core: Deictic projection shifts the interpretive centre away from the speaker's immediate here and now.
topics.explanation: A narrative or represented viewpoint can organise deictic expressions around another participant, time or location.
topics.example: Teaching example: A narrator may use now from a character's represented moment.
topics.confusion: Deictic projection shifts viewpoint; presupposition projection concerns background assumptions in larger constructions.

questions.prompt: What is deictic projection?
questions.shortAnswer: Deictic projection shifts the interpretive centre away from the speaker's immediate here and now.
questions.answer: Deictic projection shifts the interpretive centre away from the speaker's immediate here and now. A narrative or represented viewpoint can organise deictic expressions around another participant, time or location.
keyPoints: Deictic projection shifts the interpretive centre away from the speaker's immediate here and now.
Deictic projection shifts viewpoint; presupposition projection concerns background assumptions in larger constructions.

questions.prompt: How does deictic projection differ from presupposition projection?
questions.shortAnswer: Deictic projection shifts the contextual viewpoint used to interpret expressions such as here or now.
questions.answer: Deictic projection shifts the contextual viewpoint used to interpret expressions such as here or now. Presupposition projection concerns whether an assumption is inherited by a larger sentence.
keyPoints: Deictic projection shifts the contextual viewpoint used to interpret expressions such as here or now.
Presupposition projection concerns whether an assumption is inherited by a larger sentence.

topics.title: Types of deixis
topics.core: Major categories include person, place, time, discourse and social deixis.
topics.explanation: Person concerns participant roles, place and time locate events, discourse points within communication and social deixis encodes relationships.
topics.example: Teaching example: The next paragraph is discourse-deictic, while tomorrow is time-deictic.
topics.confusion: A demonstrative's grammatical form alone does not settle which deictic function it performs.

questions.prompt: Explain types of deixis briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Major categories include person, place, time, discourse and social deixis.
questions.answer: Major categories include person, place, time, discourse and social deixis. Person concerns participant roles, place and time locate events, discourse points within communication and social deixis encodes relationships.
keyPoints: Major categories include person, place, time, discourse and social deixis.
A demonstrative's grammatical form alone does not settle which deictic function it performs.

questions.prompt: What kind of deixis appears in 'As explained above'?
questions.shortAnswer: Discourse deixis: above points to a location in the text rather than an ordinary physical place.
questions.answer: Discourse deixis: above points to a location in the text rather than an ordinary physical place. Interpretation depends on the organisation of the discourse.
keyPoints: Discourse deixis: above points to a location in the text rather than an ordinary physical place.
Interpretation depends on the organisation of the discourse.

topics.title: Honorifics
topics.core: Honorifics conventionally encode social relationships such as respect, status or formality.
topics.explanation: They can concern the addressee or a person being referred to; their precise forms and meanings are language-specific.
topics.example: Teaching example: A socially marked title can position the relationship between speaker and referent.
topics.confusion: An honorific does not guarantee sincere respect or a polite overall interaction.

questions.prompt: Explain honorifics briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Honorifics conventionally encode social relationships such as respect, status or formality.
questions.answer: Honorifics conventionally encode social relationships such as respect, status or formality. They can concern the addressee or a person being referred to; their precise forms and meanings are language-specific.
keyPoints: Honorifics conventionally encode social relationships such as respect, status or formality.
An honorific does not guarantee sincere respect or a polite overall interaction.

questions.prompt: Why are honorifics related to social deixis?
questions.shortAnswer: Their interpretation depends on socially organised relations among participants or referents.
questions.answer: Their interpretation depends on socially organised relations among participants or referents. They can encode status or deference rather than merely describing an object.
keyPoints: Their interpretation depends on socially organised relations among participants or referents.
They can encode status or deference rather than merely describing an object.

topics.title: Performatives and constatives
topics.core: A performative utterance can enact an action under suitable conditions; a constative is presented as a statement describing a situation.
topics.explanation: Austin's initial distinction motivated a wider theory in which ordinary assertions are also actions.
topics.example: Teaching example: I promise to return it can make a promise, rather than merely report one.
topics.confusion: The presence of I plus a verb alone does not guarantee successful performance.

questions.prompt: Explain performatives and constatives briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: A performative utterance can enact an action under suitable conditions; a constative is presented as a statement describing a situation.
questions.answer: A performative utterance can enact an action under suitable conditions; a constative is presented as a statement describing a situation. Austin's initial distinction motivated a wider theory in which ordinary assertions are also actions.
keyPoints: A performative utterance can enact an action under suitable conditions; a constative is presented as a statement describing a situation.
The presence of I plus a verb alone does not guarantee successful performance.

questions.prompt: Why does 'I apologise' differ from 'I apologised yesterday'?
questions.shortAnswer: The first can perform an apology in the current interaction.
questions.answer: The first can perform an apology in the current interaction. The second ordinarily reports a past event, though both are utterances performing some communicative action.
keyPoints: The first can perform an apology in the current interaction.
The second ordinarily reports a past event, though both are utterances performing some communicative action.

topics.title: Felicity conditions
topics.core: Felicity conditions are the contextual and procedural requirements for a speech act to be appropriate or successfully performed.
topics.explanation: They may involve authority, circumstances, procedure, sincerity and subsequent conduct. Failures differ in kind.
topics.example: Teaching example: A marriage declaration requires an appropriate authorised procedure and setting.
topics.confusion: Insincerity and lack of institutional authority are different kinds of failure.

questions.prompt: Why can a random spectator not successfully declare two people married merely by saying the words?
questions.shortAnswer: The required authority and institutional circumstances are absent.
questions.answer: The required authority and institutional circumstances are absent. The formula alone cannot satisfy the felicity conditions for that act.
keyPoints: The required authority and institutional circumstances are absent.
The formula alone cannot satisfy the felicity conditions for that act.

topics.title: Locution, illocution and perlocution
topics.core: Locution concerns producing meaningful words; illocution concerns the act performed; perlocution concerns its effects.
topics.explanation: Distinguish the linguistic content, communicative force and actual consequences.
topics.example: Teaching example: It's hot may state a temperature, request ventilation and persuade someone to open a window.
topics.confusion: A speaker's intended effect need not actually occur.

questions.prompt: Explain locution, illocution and perlocution briefly.

questions.prompt: If a warning is ignored, has it necessarily failed to be a warning?
questions.shortAnswer: No.
questions.answer: No. Its illocutionary force can still be a warning even if it fails to produce the desired perlocutionary effect, such as making the hearer avoid danger.
keyPoints: No.
Its illocutionary force can still be a warning even if it fails to produce the desired perlocutionary effect, such as making the hearer avoid danger.

topics.title: Searle's speech-act categories
topics.core: Searle distinguishes representatives, directives, commissives, expressives and declarations.
topics.explanation: These concern commitments to truth, attempts to get action, future commitments, expressed attitudes and institutionally effective changes.
topics.example: Teaching example: An assertion represents; a request directs; a promise commits; thanks expresses; an authorised verdict declares.
topics.confusion: A declarative grammatical sentence need not perform a declaration.

questions.prompt: Explain searle's speech-act categories briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Searle distinguishes representatives, directives, commissives, expressives and declarations.
questions.answer: Searle distinguishes representatives, directives, commissives, expressives and declarations. These concern commitments to truth, attempts to get action, future commitments, expressed attitudes and institutionally effective changes.

questions.prompt: Why is 'The room is empty' not automatically a declaration in Searle's sense?
questions.shortAnswer: It normally represents a state of affairs rather than changing an institutional state through authorised utterance.
questions.answer: It normally represents a state of affairs rather than changing an institutional state through authorised utterance. Grammatical declarative form and speech-act category are different classifications.
keyPoints: It normally represents a state of affairs rather than changing an institutional state through authorised utterance.
Grammatical declarative form and speech-act category are different classifications.

topics.title: Indirect speech acts
topics.core: An indirect speech act performs an action through a form conventionally associated with another action.
topics.explanation: Interpretation relies on context and familiar patterns, not only on literal sentence type.
topics.example: Teaching example: Can you pass the salt? is often a request rather than a genuine ability inquiry.
topics.confusion: Indirectness does not automatically mean greater politeness in every context.

questions.shortAnswer: An indirect speech act performs an action through a form conventionally associated with another action.

questions.prompt: What makes 'Can you open the window?' an indirect request in an ordinary room?
questions.shortAnswer: Its literal form asks about ability, but the context makes a request for action the relevant interpretation.
questions.answer: Its literal form asks about ability, but the context makes a request for action the relevant interpretation. The hearer need not stop at answering yes.
keyPoints: Its literal form asks about ability, but the context makes a request for action the relevant interpretation.
The hearer need not stop at answering yes.

topics.title: Politeness and context
topics.core: Politeness concerns how interaction attends to social relations and participants' expectations.
topics.explanation: Interpretation depends on relationship, activity, wording and context. Face-based theory is one influential account, not the only account.
topics.example: Teaching example: Please can soften a request, but an aggressive context may undermine it.
topics.confusion: Formality, indirectness and politeness are related but not equivalent.

questions.prompt: Does adding please guarantee that a request is polite?
questions.shortAnswer: No.
questions.answer: No. The relationship, entitlement, tone and wider interaction affect its interpretation. One word does not determine the social effect of the whole act.
keyPoints: No.
The relationship, entitlement, tone and wider interaction affect its interpretation.
One word does not determine the social effect of the whole act.

topics.title: Positive and negative face
topics.core: In Brown and Levinson's framework, positive face concerns approval and negative face concerns freedom from imposition.
topics.explanation: Face wants motivate ways of managing potentially threatening acts.
topics.example: Teaching example: A criticism can threaten approval; a demanding request can threaten freedom of action.
topics.confusion: Positive and negative do not mean good and bad personalities.

questions.shortAnswer: It can impose on the hearer's time or choices even when it expresses warmth and approval.
questions.answer: It can impose on the hearer's time or choices even when it expresses warmth and approval. The two face dimensions are analytically different.

topics.title: Positive and negative politeness
topics.core: Positive politeness attends to approval or solidarity; negative politeness attends to non-imposition.
topics.explanation: Strategies can include common-ground appeals or respectful mitigation, depending on context.
topics.example: Teaching example: Could you possibly help, if you have time? acknowledges a potential imposition.
topics.confusion: Negative politeness is not rudeness; positive politeness is not simply praise.

questions.prompt: How does offering an easy refusal help manage a request?
questions.shortAnswer: It acknowledges the hearer's autonomy and reduces pressure to comply, which fits negative-politeness concerns in the face-based framework.

topics.title: Impoliteness
topics.core: Impoliteness involves behaviour interpreted as damaging or attacking social relations or face in context.
topics.explanation: Insults, exclusion and dismissive wording can contribute, but interpretation depends on the activity and participants.
topics.example: Teaching example: Go away, nobody wants you here can explicitly exclude a participant.
topics.confusion: Directness alone is not proof of impoliteness.

questions.prompt: Why might the same direct command be acceptable in an emergency but offensive in ordinary conversation?
questions.shortAnswer: Urgency and shared activity change expectations and entitlement.
questions.answer: Urgency and shared activity change expectations and entitlement. Its social meaning depends on the situation rather than sentence form alone.

topics.title: Topic management
topics.core: Conversation participants establish, maintain, shift and negotiate what their talk is about.
topics.explanation: Topic conflict can arise when speakers pursue incompatible agendas or resist each other's proposed direction.
topics.example: Teaching example: An evasive weather comment can redirect a sensitive discussion.
topics.confusion: A topic shift can still belong to an orderly conversational sequence.

questions.prompt: Why should a change of subject not automatically be labelled incoherent?
questions.shortAnswer: A shift may be understood as avoidance, a new proposal or part of a sequence.
questions.answer: A shift may be understood as avoidance, a new proposal or part of a sequence. Participants can make sense of it through its interactional position and context.
keyPoints: A shift may be understood as avoidance, a new proposal or part of a sequence.

topics.title: Repair
topics.core: Repair addresses problems in speaking, hearing or understanding.
topics.explanation: Distinguish who initiates repair from who supplies the solution.
topics.example: Teaching example: A says Tuesday—sorry, Thursday: the speaker initiates and completes self-repair.
topics.confusion: Repair is broader than correcting grammar mistakes.

topics.title: Insertion sequences
topics.core: An insertion sequence occurs between the parts of a base adjacency pair.
topics.explanation: The inserted exchange can resolve something needed before the pending response.
topics.example: Teaching example: A: Can I borrow it? B: When? A: Tonight. B: Yes.
topics.confusion: The inserted turns delay, rather than necessarily abandon, the original response.

questions.prompt: Why does asking 'When?' before answering a borrowing request not necessarily change the topic?
questions.shortAnswer: It can be an inserted clarification needed to decide the response.

topics.title: Adjacency pairs
topics.core: An adjacency pair links a first action with a relevant responsive action by another speaker.
topics.explanation: A first pair part makes a limited range of second actions relevant, such as a greeting and return greeting.
topics.example: Teaching example: A question makes an answer relevant, though an insertion may intervene.
topics.confusion: Adjacency is an organisational relation, not a claim that the turns must always be physically next to each other.

questions.shortAnswer: Yes.

topics.title: The semantics–pragmatics interface
topics.core: Semantics and pragmatics distinguish conventional linguistic contributions from context-sensitive use and inference, while interacting in interpretation.
topics.explanation: Deictic reference and implied messages show why the boundary is analytically useful but theoretically debated.
topics.example: Teaching example: The conventional meaning of I identifies a speaker role; context determines its referent.
topics.confusion: Semantics is not wholly unrelated to context, and pragmatics is not unrestricted guesswork.

questions.prompt: Why is 'semantics is completely context-free' an oversimplification?
questions.shortAnswer: Expressions such as pronouns and indexicals require contextual values even when their conventional meaning supplies a rule.
questions.answer: Expressions such as pronouns and indexicals require contextual values even when their conventional meaning supplies a rule. Theories differ on where to locate particular contextual contributions.

topics.title: Cohesion
topics.core: Cohesion consists of identifiable linguistic ties connecting parts of a text.
topics.explanation: Reference, substitution, ellipsis, lexical relations and conjunction can link clauses or turns.
topics.example: Teaching example: A student arrived. She sat down uses an anaphoric reference tie.
topics.confusion: Cohesive devices alone do not guarantee a sensible overall message.

questions.prompt: Can a passage contain many connectives yet remain incoherent?
questions.shortAnswer: Yes.
questions.answer: Yes. Explicit ties can link sentences formally while their ideas fail to make sense together. Coherence needs an interpretable relationship, not only markers.
keyPoints: Yes.
Explicit ties can link sentences formally while their ideas fail to make sense together.

topics.title: Reference ties
topics.core: Reference ties connect an expression with an entity interpreted through text or situation.
topics.explanation: Anaphora points back; cataphora points forward. Endophoric reference is text-internal, while exophoric reference depends on the situation.
topics.example: Teaching example: When she entered, Amina smiled can use a following name to resolve she.
topics.confusion: Exophoric reference may support interpretation without forming a text-internal tie.

questions.prompt: How do anaphora and deixis differ?
questions.shortAnswer: Anaphora retrieves a referent through discourse, while deixis anchors interpretation to contextual coordinates.
questions.answer: Anaphora retrieves a referent through discourse, while deixis anchors interpretation to contextual coordinates. Some expressions can serve either role depending on use.

topics.title: Substitution and ellipsis
topics.core: Substitution replaces material with a grammatical substitute; ellipsis leaves recoverable material unspoken.
topics.explanation: They can involve nominal, verbal or clausal material, depending on the construction.
topics.example: Teaching example: I need a pen. Have you got one? substitutes one; Have you finished? Yes, I have leaves finished understood.
topics.confusion: A pronoun's reference relation is not automatically the same as grammatical substitution.

questions.answer: Substitution replaces material with a grammatical substitute; ellipsis leaves recoverable material unspoken. They can involve nominal, verbal or clausal material, depending on the construction.

questions.prompt: What is omitted in 'Has she finished the essay? Yes, she has'?

topics.title: Lexical cohesion
topics.core: Lexical cohesion connects a text through vocabulary relations and associations.
topics.explanation: Reiteration can use repetition, near synonyms, superordinates or general words. Associated vocabulary can also establish links.
topics.example: Teaching example: A sparrow landed. The bird rested uses a superordinate to maintain the referent.
topics.confusion: Related words need not be interchangeable synonyms.

topics.title: Conjunction in discourse
topics.core: Conjunction marks relations such as addition, contrast, cause or sequence between discourse parts.

topics.title: Coherence
topics.core: Coherence is the meaningful connectedness that makes discourse interpretable as a whole.
topics.explanation: Hearers use context, shared knowledge and inference to connect ideas, including brief exchanges with few overt ties.

courses.title: Phonetics and Phonology
courses.overview: Speech has a physical form and a patterned organisation. Begin with phonetic description and phonological contrast, then build syllables, word stress and connected speech. Intonation and transcription connect the sound system with meaning in actual interaction.
journey: Describe speech physically: articulation, sound signals and perception.
Identify contrasts and patterns: phonemes, features, vowels and consonants.
Build larger units: syllables, stress, tone and intonation.
Explain an actual utterance: reduction, assimilation, linking and IPA.

topics.title: Phonetics
topics.core: Phonetics studies the production, transmission and perception of speech sounds.
topics.explanation: It describes physical speech events, including articulatory movements, acoustic properties and auditory processing.
topics.example: Teaching example: The aspiration after [p] in pin can be measured as a physical feature.
topics.confusion: Phonetics is not restricted to spelling or to sounds that distinguish words.

questions.shortAnswer: Phonetics studies the production, transmission and perception of speech sounds.

questions.prompt: What would an articulatory phonetician examine when you say pin?
questions.shortAnswer: They would examine how the lips close and release, how the vocal folds behave and how the tongue forms the following vowel.

topics.title: Phonology
topics.core: Phonology studies how sounds are organised and patterned in a language.
topics.explanation: It concerns contrasts, distribution, syllable patterns and sound processes. Phonetic evidence helps explain these patterns.
topics.example: Teaching example: English pin and bin contrast through /p/ and /b/.
topics.confusion: Phonology also studies non-contrastive patterns such as allophony.

topics.title: Branches of phonetics
topics.core: The three main branches are articulatory, acoustic and auditory phonetics.
topics.explanation: They study sound production, physical sound signals and sound perception respectively.
topics.example: Teaching example: A spectrogram supports acoustic analysis; tongue position supports articulatory analysis.
topics.confusion: The branches examine related stages of speech rather than unrelated kinds of language.

topics.title: Phone and phoneme
topics.core: A phone is a speech sound; a phoneme is an abstract contrastive unit in a language.
topics.explanation: Phones are conventionally written in brackets and phonemes in slashes. A phoneme can have different phonetic realisations.
topics.example: Teaching example: [pʰ] can realise English /p/ in pin.
topics.confusion: A letter is not a phoneme: spelling and sound units do not correspond one to one.

topics.title: Minimal pairs
topics.core: A minimal pair consists of words differing in one sound in the same position, with different meanings.
topics.explanation: It provides evidence that the sound difference is contrastive in the language.
topics.example: Teaching example: Pin and bin differ initially in /p/ and /b/.
topics.confusion: Two words differing in several sounds do not form a minimal pair.

topics.title: Allophones
topics.core: Allophones are phonetic variants of a phoneme that do not establish a lexical contrast in the relevant language.
topics.explanation: Their occurrence may depend on context or vary with speaker and style.

topics.confusion: Sounds that are allophones in one language may contrast in another.

topics.title: Complementary distribution
topics.core: Complementary distribution means two sounds occur in non-overlapping environments.
topics.explanation: It supports an allophonic analysis when combined with a plausible phonetic relationship and wider evidence.

topics.title: Free variation
topics.core: Free variation is non-contrastive variation in a comparable environment.
topics.explanation: A speaker may produce a final stop with or without an audible release without changing the intended word.

topics.title: Trubetzkoy and phonological opposition

topics.explanation: He analysed phonological systems through distinctive contrasts and discussed neutralisation and markedness.

topics.title: Tag questions and interpretation
topics.core: Tag-question intonation can contribute to whether a speaker seeks information or invites agreement.
topics.explanation: A rising tag often seeks confirmation, while a falling tag often displays a stronger expectation of agreement; these are tendencies.
topics.example: Teaching example: It's cold, isn't it? can be spoken with different expectations.
topics.confusion: A contour is a cue rather than conclusive evidence of certainty.

topics.title: IPA and transcription levels
topics.core: The IPA represents speech sounds; broad transcription abstracts categories while narrow transcription adds phonetic detail.
topics.explanation: Slashes conventionally mark phonemic analysis, while brackets permit more detailed phonetic description.
topics.example: Teaching example: /pɪn/ is broad; [pʰɪn] adds aspiration.
topics.confusion: IPA transcription represents sounds rather than converting each written letter into a symbol.

questions.prompt: Why would an aspiration study need more detail than a pronunciation dictionary?

topics.title: Connected-speech transcription
topics.core: Connected-speech transcription represents sounds in a continuous utterance rather than isolated dictionary forms.
topics.explanation: Account for weak forms, possible assimilation or elision, linking and prominence. State the accent and level of detail.
topics.example: Teaching example: A possible British rendering of I can go is /aɪ kən ɡəʊ/.

questions.shortAnswer: Accent, focus, speed and style affect pronunciation.

topics.title: Linking and intrusive r
topics.core: In non-rhotic accents, linking /r/ appears before a following vowel where historical or spelling r supports it.
topics.explanation: Intrusive /r/ occurs in comparable vowel-linking contexts without a written r. Both vary across speakers and styles.
topics.example: Teaching example: Far away may have linking [r]; law and order may have intrusive [r].

questions.prompt: How do far away and law and order illustrate different r-linking labels?
questions.shortAnswer: Far away can have linking r associated with the word far.

courses.title: Morphology and Syntax
courses.overview: Morphology explains the structure of words; syntax explains how words form larger structures. Track meaningful units, grammatical categories and hierarchical relationships, then connect form with sound, meaning and clause organisation.
journey: Identify the pieces: lexemes, morphemes, bases and affixes.
Explain the patterns: formation, allomorphy and interfaces.
Build larger structures: categories, phrases, clauses and dependencies.
Compare analyses: structural rules and alternative syntactic theories.

topics.title: Morphology
topics.core: Morphology studies the internal structure of words and how their forms relate to meaning and grammar.
topics.explanation: It identifies recurring meaningful units and the rules or patterns that combine or alter them.
topics.example: Teaching example: Teachers contains teach, -er and plural -s; the parts contribute a lexical base, an agent noun and number.
topics.confusion: A meaningful unit need not be a whole word.

questions.prompt: What is morphology?
questions.shortAnswer: Morphology studies the internal structure of words and how their forms relate to meaning and grammar.
questions.answer: Morphology studies the internal structure of words and how their forms relate to meaning and grammar. It identifies recurring meaningful units and the rules or patterns that combine or alter them.
keyPoints: Morphology studies the internal structure of words and how their forms relate to meaning and grammar.

questions.prompt: Why is teachers a useful example of morphology?
questions.shortAnswer: It combines a root with derivational -er and inflectional -s.
questions.answer: It combines a root with derivational -er and inflectional -s. Their order and contribution show how word structure expresses both lexical and grammatical information.
keyPoints: It combines a root with derivational -er and inflectional -s.
Their order and contribution show how word structure expresses both lexical and grammatical information.

topics.title: Inflection and derivation
topics.core: Inflection expresses grammatical forms of a lexeme; derivation typically creates a new lexeme.
topics.explanation: Derivation can change word class or meaning; inflection normally supplies contrasts such as number or tense within a paradigm.
topics.example: Teaching example: Teach to teacher is derivation; teacher to teachers is inflection.
topics.confusion: A derivational affix need not change word class.

questions.prompt: Explain inflection and derivation briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Inflection expresses grammatical forms of a lexeme; derivation typically creates a new lexeme.
questions.answer: Inflection expresses grammatical forms of a lexeme; derivation typically creates a new lexeme. Derivation can change word class or meaning; inflection normally supplies contrasts such as number or tense within a paradigm.
keyPoints: Inflection expresses grammatical forms of a lexeme; derivation typically creates a new lexeme.

questions.prompt: Does unhappy show derivation although happy and unhappy are both adjectives?
questions.shortAnswer: Yes.
questions.answer: Yes. Derivation can change lexical meaning without changing word class. Unhappy is a distinct adjective lexeme, while happier is normally an inflected comparative form.
keyPoints: Yes.
Derivation can change lexical meaning without changing word class.
Unhappy is a distinct adjective lexeme, while happier is normally an inflected comparative form.

topics.title: Word, word form and lexeme
topics.core: A lexeme is an abstract vocabulary item; a word form is one grammatical realisation of it.
topics.explanation: Orthographic, phonological and grammatical notions of a word do not always coincide.
topics.example: Teaching example: Sing, sings, sang and sung are forms associated with the lexeme SING.
topics.confusion: A lexeme is not just a spelling stripped of its final letters.

questions.prompt: Explain word, word form and lexeme briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: A lexeme is an abstract vocabulary item; a word form is one grammatical realisation of it.
questions.answer: A lexeme is an abstract vocabulary item; a word form is one grammatical realisation of it. Orthographic, phonological and grammatical notions of a word do not always coincide.
keyPoints: A lexeme is an abstract vocabulary item; a word form is one grammatical realisation of it.

questions.prompt: Are went and goes different lexemes merely because they look different?
questions.shortAnswer: No.
questions.answer: No. They are grammatical forms of GO. Lexeme identity concerns the vocabulary item and its paradigm, not visual similarity alone.
keyPoints: No.
They are grammatical forms of GO.
Lexeme identity concerns the vocabulary item and its paradigm, not visual similarity alone.

topics.title: Wordhood diagnostics
topics.core: Wordhood diagnostics examine properties such as internal cohesion, stress and independent occurrence.
topics.explanation: No single diagnostic works without exceptions across all languages and constructions; combine evidence.
topics.example: Teaching example: The insertion test distinguishes a typical compound blackbird from the phrase very black bird.
topics.confusion: Space in writing is an orthographic convention, not a universal linguistic definition.

questions.prompt: Explain wordhood diagnostics briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Wordhood diagnostics examine properties such as internal cohesion, stress and independent occurrence.
questions.answer: Wordhood diagnostics examine properties such as internal cohesion, stress and independent occurrence. No single diagnostic works without exceptions across all languages and constructions; combine evidence.
keyPoints: Wordhood diagnostics examine properties such as internal cohesion, stress and independent occurrence.

questions.prompt: Can a space in writing settle whether an expression is one linguistic word?
questions.shortAnswer: No.
questions.answer: No. Writing conventions vary, and compounds may be spaced. Consider grammatical cohesion, possible internal modification and relevant phonological evidence together.
keyPoints: No.
Writing conventions vary, and compounds may be spaced.
Consider grammatical cohesion, possible internal modification and relevant phonological evidence together.

topics.title: Simple, complex and compound words
topics.core: A simple word has one morpheme; a complex word contains multiple morphemes; a compound combines bases.
topics.explanation: Terminology varies: compound words can also be described as morphologically complex in a broad sense.
topics.example: Teaching example: Cat is simple, unhappy is derived, and blackboard is a compound.
topics.confusion: Long words are not necessarily morphologically complex.

questions.prompt: Explain simple, complex and compound words briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: A simple word has one morpheme; a complex word contains multiple morphemes; a compound combines bases.
questions.answer: A simple word has one morpheme; a complex word contains multiple morphemes; a compound combines bases. Terminology varies: compound words can also be described as morphologically complex in a broad sense.
keyPoints: A simple word has one morpheme; a complex word contains multiple morphemes; a compound combines bases.

questions.prompt: Is elephant complex because it has several syllables?
questions.shortAnswer: No.
questions.answer: No. Syllable count concerns sound structure. In ordinary modern English analysis elephant is a single morpheme despite its multiple syllables.
keyPoints: No.
Syllable count concerns sound structure.
In ordinary modern English analysis elephant is a single morpheme despite its multiple syllables.

topics.title: Root, base and stem
topics.core: A root is the central lexical element; a base accepts a morphological process; a stem accepts inflection.
topics.explanation: A base can be larger than a root. The terms describe different roles in a derivation.
topics.example: Teaching example: In teachers, teach is the root and teacher is the stem to which plural -s attaches.
topics.confusion: Base and root are not always interchangeable.

questions.prompt: Explain root, base and stem briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: A root is the central lexical element; a base accepts a morphological process; a stem accepts inflection.
questions.answer: A root is the central lexical element; a base accepts a morphological process; a stem accepts inflection. A base can be larger than a root. The terms describe different roles in a derivation.
keyPoints: A root is the central lexical element; a base accepts a morphological process; a stem accepts inflection.

questions.prompt: In unhappiness, can unhappy be a base although it is not the root?
questions.shortAnswer: Yes.
questions.answer: Yes. Unhappy is the base for suffix -ness, while happy is the root. Bases can already contain affixes.
keyPoints: Yes.
Unhappy is the base for suffix -ness, while happy is the root.
Bases can already contain affixes.

topics.title: Affix types
topics.core: An affix is a bound formative attached to a base, such as a prefix or suffix.
topics.explanation: An infix occurs within a base; a circumfix has discontinuous parts surrounding it. Languages vary in their affix systems.
topics.example: Teaching example: English un- precedes happy and -ness follows it.
topics.confusion: Not every bound morpheme is necessarily an affix; some are bound roots.

questions.prompt: Explain affix types briefly.

keyPoints: An affix is a bound formative attached to a base, such as a prefix or suffix.

questions.prompt: Why are un- and -ness both affixes despite different positions?
questions.shortAnswer: Both are bound units attached to a base.
questions.answer: Both are bound units attached to a base. Their position distinguishes prefix un- from suffix -ness.
keyPoints: Both are bound units attached to a base.
Their position distinguishes prefix un- from suffix -ness.

topics.title: Compounding and headedness
topics.core: Compounding forms a word from two or more bases.
topics.explanation: An endocentric compound has an internal head defining its type; an exocentric compound lacks that straightforward internal semantic head.
topics.example: Teaching example: A blackboard is a kind of board; a pickpocket is a person, not a kind of pocket.
topics.confusion: Compound stress is a useful tendency, not an exception-free rule.

questions.prompt: Explain compounding and headedness briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Compounding forms a word from two or more bases.
questions.answer: Compounding forms a word from two or more bases. An endocentric compound has an internal head defining its type; an exocentric compound lacks that straightforward internal semantic head.

questions.prompt: What makes blackboard endocentric and pickpocket exocentric?
questions.shortAnswer: Blackboard names a type of board, so board is its semantic head.
questions.answer: Blackboard names a type of board, so board is its semantic head. Pickpocket names a person rather than a type of pocket or picking.
keyPoints: Blackboard names a type of board, so board is its semantic head.
Pickpocket names a person rather than a type of pocket or picking.

topics.title: Conversion
topics.core: Conversion creates a new word-class use without an overt derivational affix.
topics.explanation: It is also called zero derivation, though analyses differ on whether a silent affix should be posited.
topics.example: Teaching example: Email functions as a noun in an email and as a verb in email me.
topics.confusion: Conversion concerns lexical category change, not ordinary inflection.

questions.prompt: What is conversion?
questions.shortAnswer: Conversion creates a new word-class use without an overt derivational affix.
questions.answer: Conversion creates a new word-class use without an overt derivational affix. It is also called zero derivation, though analyses differ on whether a silent affix should be posited.
keyPoints: Conversion creates a new word-class use without an overt derivational affix.

questions.prompt: What process turns bottle into a verb in bottle the juice?
questions.shortAnswer: Conversion: a noun base is used as a verb without an overt category-changing suffix.
questions.answer: Conversion: a noun base is used as a verb without an overt category-changing suffix.
keyPoints: Conversion: a noun base is used as a verb without an overt category-changing suffix.

topics.title: Clipping and blending
topics.core: Clipping shortens a word; blending combines parts of words into a new form.
topics.explanation: The new forms preserve enough source material for their origin to be recognised, but the processes differ.
topics.example: Teaching example: Lab clips laboratory; brunch blends breakfast and lunch.
topics.confusion: A blend does not simply concatenate two complete bases.

questions.prompt: Explain clipping and blending briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Clipping shortens a word; blending combines parts of words into a new form.
questions.answer: Clipping shortens a word; blending combines parts of words into a new form. The new forms preserve enough source material for their origin to be recognised, but the processes differ.
keyPoints: Clipping shortens a word; blending combines parts of words into a new form.

questions.prompt: How do lab and brunch illustrate different processes?
questions.shortAnswer: Lab is a shortened form of one source word.
questions.answer: Lab is a shortened form of one source word. Brunch merges portions of two source words into a new word.
keyPoints: Lab is a shortened form of one source word.
Brunch merges portions of two source words into a new word.

topics.title: Acronyms and initialisms
topics.core: Acronyms and initialisms use initial letters of longer expressions.
topics.explanation: Acronyms are pronounced as words, whereas initialisms are pronounced as letter names under a common terminology.
topics.example: Teaching example: NATO is pronounced as a word; BBC uses individual letter names.
topics.confusion: Usage of acronym as an umbrella term varies, so state the distinction intended.

questions.prompt: Explain acronyms and initialisms briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Acronyms and initialisms use initial letters of longer expressions.
questions.answer: Acronyms and initialisms use initial letters of longer expressions. Acronyms are pronounced as words, whereas initialisms are pronounced as letter names under a common terminology.
keyPoints: Acronyms and initialisms use initial letters of longer expressions.

questions.prompt: How would you distinguish NATO from BBC as word-formation examples?
questions.shortAnswer: Both originate from initials, but NATO is a word-pronounced acronym and BBC a letter-pronounced initialism in the narrower distinction.
questions.answer: Both originate from initials, but NATO is a word-pronounced acronym and BBC a letter-pronounced initialism in the narrower distinction.
keyPoints: Both originate from initials, but NATO is a word-pronounced acronym and BBC a letter-pronounced initialism in the narrower distinction.

topics.title: Back-formation
topics.core: Back-formation creates a new word by removing a part interpreted as an affix.
topics.explanation: The historical direction matters: apparent morphological simplicity does not prove which form came first.
topics.example: Teaching example: Edit was formed historically from editor, rather than editor simply being formed from edit.
topics.confusion: Back-formation is not the same as clipping a word casually.

questions.prompt: What is back-formation?

questions.answer: Back-formation creates a new word by removing a part interpreted as an affix. The historical direction matters: apparent morphological simplicity does not prove which form came first.
keyPoints: Back-formation creates a new word by removing a part interpreted as an affix.

questions.prompt: Why is edit from editor back-formation rather than ordinary suffixation?
questions.shortAnswer: The longer noun existed first; speakers interpreted its ending as removable and created the verb.
questions.answer: The longer noun existed first; speakers interpreted its ending as removable and created the verb. The historical direction is from the longer form to the shorter one.
keyPoints: The longer noun existed first; speakers interpreted its ending as removable and created the verb.

topics.title: Borrowing and reduplication
topics.core: Borrowing adopts linguistic material from another language; reduplication repeats all or part of a form.
topics.explanation: Borrowed forms may become adapted to the receiving language. Reduplication can serve grammatical or expressive functions, depending on the language.
topics.example: Teaching example: English borrowed bungalow; expressive forms such as bye-bye repeat material.
topics.confusion: Borrowing describes historical source, while derivation describes internal formation.

questions.prompt: Can a borrowed word later take English affixes?
questions.shortAnswer: Yes.

topics.title: Words and phrases
topics.core: Words show internal cohesion; phrases are syntactic combinations whose parts can often be independently modified.
topics.explanation: Stress, meaning, inflection and insertion provide relevant evidence, but compound–phrase boundaries can be difficult.
topics.example: Teaching example: A greenhouse is a building for plants; a green house is a house described as green.

questions.prompt: Explain words and phrases briefly.

questions.prompt: Why can greenhouse and green house differ despite sharing the same bases?

topics.title: Morphological segmentation
topics.core: Morphological analysis identifies meaningful components and their structural relationships.
topics.explanation: Use recurring form–meaning correspondences and category information rather than splitting wherever letters happen to repeat.
topics.example: Teaching example: Teachers can be segmented teach-er-s; corner is not ordinarily corn-er.

questions.prompt: What is morphological segmentation?
questions.shortAnswer: Morphological analysis identifies meaningful components and their structural relationships.

topics.title: Morphological rules
topics.core: A morphological rule states a pattern relating bases and formed words, including meaning and category.
topics.explanation: For example, agentive -er commonly attaches to verbs to create nouns; productivity is restricted and exceptions matter.

questions.prompt: Explain morphological rules briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: A morphological rule states a pattern relating bases and formed words, including meaning and category.

topics.title: Morphological trees and ambiguity
topics.core: Morphological trees show hierarchical grouping and the order in which bases and affixes combine.

questions.prompt: Explain morphological trees and ambiguity briefly.

topics.title: Syntagmatic and paradigmatic relations
topics.core: Syntagmatic relations concern combination; paradigmatic relations concern alternatives in a structural position.
topics.explanation: In morphology, affixes combine with bases while related forms contrast within a paradigm or word family.
topics.example: Teaching example: Teach-er-s illustrates combination; cat/cats illustrates a number contrast.

topics.title: Morpheme, morph and allomorph

questions.prompt: Why are /s/, /z/ and /ɪz/ in regular English plurals allomorphs?

topics.title: Prosodic morphology
topics.core: Prosodic morphology studies how morphological patterns interact with units such as syllables, feet and stress.
topics.explanation: Morphological contrasts can involve changes in prosody rather than the addition of a straightforward segmental suffix.
