questions.shortAnswer: Triangulation examines a phenomenon using multiple evidence sources or approaches.
questions.answer: Triangulation examines a phenomenon using multiple evidence sources or approaches. Comparing perspectives can strengthen an interpretation or expose contradictions.
keyPoints: Triangulation examines a phenomenon using multiple evidence sources or approaches.

questions.prompt: What should you do if interviews report high participation but observation shows little?
questions.shortAnswer: Examine the timeframe, definitions, observer effects and participants' interpretations.
questions.answer: Examine the timeframe, definitions, observer effects and participants' interpretations. The disagreement is evidence to explain, not a reason to discard an inconvenient source.
keyPoints: Examine the timeframe, definitions, observer effects and participants' interpretations.
The disagreement is evidence to explain, not a reason to discard an inconvenient source.

topics.title: Ethics and consent
topics.core: Research ethics requires informed, voluntary participation and appropriate protection of people and data.
topics.explanation: Explain the tasks, uses, risks, withdrawal conditions and privacy arrangements. Confidentiality protects identifiable information; anonymity means identities are not known or recorded in the relevant process.
topics.example: Explain recording use before an interview and avoid coercing students whose grades you control.
topics.confusion: Researchers cannot guarantee what fellow focus-group members will disclose later.

questions.prompt: Explain ethics and consent briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Research ethics requires informed, voluntary participation and appropriate protection of people and data.
questions.answer: Research ethics requires informed, voluntary participation and appropriate protection of people and data. Explain the tasks, uses, risks, withdrawal conditions and privacy arrangements.
keyPoints: Research ethics requires informed, voluntary participation and appropriate protection of people and data.

questions.prompt: Why is teacher-led research with the teacher's own students ethically sensitive?
questions.shortAnswer: The power relationship may make refusal feel unsafe.
questions.answer: The power relationship may make refusal feel unsafe. Participation and assessment should be separated, and students need a credible way to decline without disadvantage.
keyPoints: The power relationship may make refusal feel unsafe.
Participation and assessment should be separated, and students need a credible way to decline without disadvantage.

topics.title: Research transcription
topics.core: Transcription represents recorded speech in written form using conventions appropriate to the research question.
topics.explanation: Verbatim records retain relevant repetitions, pauses and false starts. Intelligent-verbatim and edited versions improve readability but may remove interactional evidence. Document decisions and check the record against the recording.
topics.example: Preserve a pause and self-correction when investigating repair, because their placement can explain how the exchange develops.
topics.confusion: A cleaned transcript is not a neutral copy: removing a feature can remove evidence.

questions.prompt: What is research transcription?
questions.shortAnswer: Transcription represents recorded speech in written form using conventions appropriate to the research question.
questions.answer: Transcription represents recorded speech in written form using conventions appropriate to the research question. Verbatim records retain relevant repetitions, pauses and false starts.
keyPoints: Transcription represents recorded speech in written form using conventions appropriate to the research question.

questions.prompt: Why might edited transcription be unsuitable for conversation analysis?
questions.shortAnswer: Editing can erase pauses, overlaps and repairs that show how turns and actions are organised.
questions.answer: Editing can erase pauses, overlaps and repairs that show how turns and actions are organised. Preserve the details needed by the analysis and state the transcription conventions.
keyPoints: Editing can erase pauses, overlaps and repairs that show how turns and actions are organised.
Preserve the details needed by the analysis and state the transcription conventions.

topics.title: Qualitative coding
topics.core: Coding labels meaningful data segments; analysis develops relationships and interpretations from those labels.
topics.explanation: Codes can form categories and themes. A theme should address a meaningful pattern relevant to the question, supported by extracts and checked against contrary cases.
topics.example: Code 'I stay quiet because classmates laugh' as fear of peer judgment.
topics.confusion: A frequent word or broad topic is not automatically an analytical theme.

questions.prompt: What is qualitative coding?
questions.shortAnswer: Coding labels meaningful data segments; analysis develops relationships and interpretations from those labels.
questions.answer: Coding labels meaningful data segments; analysis develops relationships and interpretations from those labels. Codes can form categories and themes.
keyPoints: Coding labels meaningful data segments; analysis develops relationships and interpretations from those labels.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between the code 'anxiety' and a developed theme?
questions.shortAnswer: A code labels a segment or idea.
questions.answer: A code labels a segment or idea. A theme articulates a broader pattern, such as peer judgment limiting participation, and explains its relevance across the evidence.
keyPoints: A code labels a segment or idea.
A theme articulates a broader pattern, such as peer judgment limiting participation, and explains its relevance across the evidence.

topics.title: Frequency and distributions
topics.core: Frequency counts occurrences; a distribution shows how observations are spread across values or categories.
topics.explanation: Tables and graphs reveal patterns, concentrations and variation. Percentages express counts relative to a total; check the denominator and missing data.
topics.example: 18 of 30 learners is 60 percent, provided all 30 supplied relevant responses.
topics.confusion: A numeric code for a category is not a measured quantity.

questions.prompt: Explain frequency and distributions briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Frequency counts occurrences; a distribution shows how observations are spread across values or categories.
questions.answer: Frequency counts occurrences; a distribution shows how observations are spread across values or categories. Tables and graphs reveal patterns, concentrations and variation.
keyPoints: Frequency counts occurrences; a distribution shows how observations are spread across values or categories.

questions.prompt: If 18 of 30 students use a dictionary daily, what percentage is that?
questions.shortAnswer: It is 60 percent: 18 divided by 30, multiplied by 100.
questions.answer: It is 60 percent: 18 divided by 30, multiplied by 100. State the sample and what daily use means.
keyPoints: It is 60 percent: 18 divided by 30, multiplied by 100.
State the sample and what daily use means.

topics.title: Central tendency and spread
topics.core: Mean, median and mode describe central tendency; range and standard deviation describe spread.
topics.explanation: The mean uses all values, the median is the sorted middle, and the mode is most frequent. Standard deviation summarises dispersion around the mean.
topics.example: For 2, 4, 4, 6: mean 4, median 4, mode 4 and range 4.
topics.confusion: Two groups with equal means can have very different distributions.

questions.prompt: Explain central tendency and spread briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Mean, median and mode describe central tendency; range and standard deviation describe spread.
questions.answer: Mean, median and mode describe central tendency; range and standard deviation describe spread. The mean uses all values, the median is the sorted middle, and the mode is most frequent.
keyPoints: Mean, median and mode describe central tendency; range and standard deviation describe spread.

questions.prompt: Why report standard deviation alongside a mean speaking score?
questions.shortAnswer: The mean gives the centre but not how varied learners are.
questions.answer: The mean gives the centre but not how varied learners are. Standard deviation helps describe the spread and prevents equal means from hiding different patterns.
keyPoints: The mean gives the centre but not how varied learners are.
Standard deviation helps describe the spread and prevents equal means from hiding different patterns.

topics.title: Chi-square
topics.core: A chi-square test of independence assesses association between categorical variables using observed and expected counts.
topics.explanation: The test compares counts with those expected under independence. Use a suitable contingency table and check expected-count and independence assumptions.
topics.example: Test whether preferred feedback type is associated with year of study.
topics.confusion: A significant association does not establish causation or its strength by itself.

questions.prompt: What is chi-square?
questions.shortAnswer: A chi-square test of independence assesses association between categorical variables using observed and expected counts.
questions.answer: A chi-square test of independence assesses association between categorical variables using observed and expected counts. The test compares counts with those expected under independence.
keyPoints: A chi-square test of independence assesses association between categorical variables using observed and expected counts.

questions.prompt: Would chi-square normally compare two mean fluency scores?
questions.shortAnswer: No.
questions.answer: No. A chi-square independence test is for categorical counts. A comparison of means requires an appropriate mean-comparison procedure and its assumptions.
keyPoints: No.
A chi-square independence test is for categorical counts.
A comparison of means requires an appropriate mean-comparison procedure and its assumptions.

topics.title: Pearson correlation
topics.core: Pearson's r measures the direction and strength of a linear relationship between two quantitative variables.
topics.explanation: It ranges from minus one to plus one. Zero indicates no linear association, not necessarily no relationship. Outliers and nonlinearity can make a summary misleading.
topics.example: A negative relationship could link higher anxiety scores with lower participation counts.
topics.confusion: Correlation does not by itself show that one variable causes another.

questions.prompt: What is pearson correlation?
questions.shortAnswer: Pearson's r measures the direction and strength of a linear relationship between two quantitative variables.
questions.answer: Pearson's r measures the direction and strength of a linear relationship between two quantitative variables. It ranges from minus one to plus one.
keyPoints: Pearson's r measures the direction and strength of a linear relationship between two quantitative variables.

questions.prompt: If r is zero, must two variables be unrelated?
questions.shortAnswer: No.
questions.answer: No. There may be a nonlinear relationship. Inspect the pattern and the measurement context instead of treating zero correlation as proof of complete independence.
keyPoints: No.
There may be a nonlinear relationship.
Inspect the pattern and the measurement context instead of treating zero correlation as proof of complete independence.

topics.title: Z-tests and t-tests
topics.core: A z-test uses the standard normal reference distribution; a t-test for a mean uses a t distribution when population variation is estimated.
topics.explanation: For the classic one-sample mean z-test, the population standard deviation is known and other distributional conditions must hold. A t-test uses sample variation. Test selection is not determined by sample size alone.
topics.example: Use a paired t-test to examine within-person pretest–posttest differences when its assumptions fit.
topics.confusion: A sample above 30 does not automatically require a z-test.

questions.prompt: Explain z-tests and t-tests briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: A z-test uses the standard normal reference distribution; a t-test for a mean uses a t distribution when population variation is estimated.
questions.answer: A z-test uses the standard normal reference distribution; a t-test for a mean uses a t distribution when population variation is estimated. For the classic one-sample mean z-test, the population standard deviation is known and other distributional conditions must hold.
keyPoints: A z-test uses the standard normal reference distribution; a t-test for a mean uses a t distribution when population variation is estimated.

questions.prompt: Would you use an independent or paired t-test for the same learners' pretest and posttest scores?
questions.shortAnswer: A paired t-test treats each learner's two scores as a matched pair and analyses the differences, assuming the difference scores meet the required conditions.
questions.answer: A paired t-test treats each learner's two scores as a matched pair and analyses the differences, assuming the difference scores meet the required conditions.
keyPoints: A paired t-test treats each learner's two scores as a matched pair and analyses the differences, assuming the difference scores meet the required conditions.

topics.title: Factor analysis
topics.core: Factor analysis models shared patterns among observed variables using a smaller number of latent factors.
topics.explanation: It can explore whether questionnaire items reflect underlying constructs. The number and interpretation of factors require evidence and theoretical judgment.
topics.example: An anxiety questionnaire may contain related items about communication apprehension and evaluation fears.
topics.confusion: A statistical factor is not automatically a proven psychological cause.

questions.prompt: Explain factor analysis briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Factor analysis models shared patterns among observed variables using a smaller number of latent factors.
questions.answer: Factor analysis models shared patterns among observed variables using a smaller number of latent factors. It can explore whether questionnaire items reflect underlying constructs.
keyPoints: Factor analysis models shared patterns among observed variables using a smaller number of latent factors.

questions.prompt: Why use factor analysis while developing a learner-attitude questionnaire?
questions.shortAnswer: To examine patterns of shared variation and whether items cluster into plausible underlying dimensions, while also considering theory and other validity evidence.
questions.answer: To examine patterns of shared variation and whether items cluster into plausible underlying dimensions, while also considering theory and other validity evidence.
keyPoints: To examine patterns of shared variation and whether items cluster into plausible underlying dimensions, while also considering theory and other validity evidence.

topics.title: Results and discussion
topics.core: Results present the evidence; discussion explains what the findings mean in relation to questions and prior research.
topics.explanation: Use tables, figures, extracts and clear prose as appropriate. Interpretation should address alternative explanations and limits, not simply repeat the numbers.
topics.example: Report an observed score change, then discuss its possible meaning and relation to earlier findings.
topics.confusion: Qualitative findings are results too; results are not only statistical tables.

questions.prompt: Explain results and discussion briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Results present the evidence; discussion explains what the findings mean in relation to questions and prior research.
questions.answer: Results present the evidence; discussion explains what the findings mean in relation to questions and prior research. Use tables, figures, extracts and clear prose as appropriate.
keyPoints: Results present the evidence; discussion explains what the findings mean in relation to questions and prior research.

questions.prompt: How does 'the mean increased by 15' differ from a discussion claim?
questions.shortAnswer: The first describes a result.
questions.answer: The first describes a result. Discussion explains its significance and possible reasons, compares it with prior work and considers whether the design supports a causal interpretation.
keyPoints: The first describes a result.
Discussion explains its significance and possible reasons, compares it with prior work and considers whether the design supports a causal interpretation.

topics.title: Inference and recommendations
topics.core: Inference draws conclusions from evidence; recommendations propose actions supported by those conclusions.
topics.explanation: Keep claims within the design, sample and measurement limits. Recommendations can address practice or future research and should specify the context in which they apply.
topics.example: A small local case may suggest testing a strategy in other settings before wider adoption.
topics.confusion: A promising local result is not a universal teaching prescription.

questions.prompt: Explain inference and recommendations briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Inference draws conclusions from evidence; recommendations propose actions supported by those conclusions.
questions.answer: Inference draws conclusions from evidence; recommendations propose actions supported by those conclusions. Keep claims within the design, sample and measurement limits.
keyPoints: Inference draws conclusions from evidence; recommendations propose actions supported by those conclusions.

questions.prompt: Can a study of one class justify a policy for every university?
questions.shortAnswer: Not by itself.
questions.answer: Not by itself. It can provide contextual insight and motivate broader investigation, but sweeping recommendations exceed the evidence's scope.
keyPoints: Not by itself.
It can provide contextual insight and motivate broader investigation, but sweeping recommendations exceed the evidence's scope.

topics.title: Citation and plagiarism
topics.core: Citation credits borrowed ideas and words; plagiarism presents another person's work as one's own.
topics.explanation: A genuine paraphrase changes the structure and wording while retaining the meaning and citing the source. Exact wording requires quotation treatment and a locator.
topics.example: After explaining an author's idea in your own words, include author and year and a matching reference.
topics.confusion: Changing a few words does not turn copied structure into an adequate paraphrase.

questions.prompt: Explain citation and plagiarism briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Citation credits borrowed ideas and words; plagiarism presents another person's work as one's own.
questions.answer: Citation credits borrowed ideas and words; plagiarism presents another person's work as one's own. A genuine paraphrase changes the structure and wording while retaining the meaning and citing the source.
keyPoints: Citation credits borrowed ideas and words; plagiarism presents another person's work as one's own.

questions.prompt: Does paraphrasing remove the need for a citation?
questions.shortAnswer: No.
questions.answer: No. The idea still comes from a source. Credit the author and year even when using your own wording.
keyPoints: No.
The idea still comes from a source.
Credit the author and year even when using your own wording.

topics.title: APA in-text citation and quotation
topics.core: APA uses author–date in-text citations linked to entries in a reference list.
topics.explanation: Ordinary three-or-more-author in-text citations use the first surname and et al. Direct quotations need a page or other suitable locator. Quotations of 40 words or more use block format.
topics.example: A fictional example is (Rahman et al., 2024); a quotation might add p. 12.
topics.confusion: The reference list uses full author details under APA rules, not ordinary in-text et al. shortening.

questions.prompt: Explain apa in-text citation and quotation briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: APA uses author–date in-text citations linked to entries in a reference list.
questions.answer: APA uses author–date in-text citations linked to entries in a reference list. Ordinary three-or-more-author in-text citations use the first surname and et al.
keyPoints: APA uses author–date in-text citations linked to entries in a reference list.

questions.prompt: What extra information does a direct quotation need compared with an ordinary paraphrase?
questions.shortAnswer: It needs quotation formatting and a specific locator such as a page number, as well as the author and year.
questions.answer: It needs quotation formatting and a specific locator such as a page number, as well as the author and year. A locator is optional but often useful for a paraphrase.
keyPoints: It needs quotation formatting and a specific locator such as a page number, as well as the author and year.
A locator is optional but often useful for a paraphrase.

topics.title: APA reference entries
topics.core: A reference entry identifies a source through its author, date, title and publication information.
topics.explanation: Identify the source type first. Books, journal articles and chapters require different arrangements. APA 7 omits a publisher's city and presents available DOIs as URLs.
topics.example: A chapter entry starts with its chapter author, then identifies the editor and book.
topics.confusion: Do not invent missing dates, page ranges, journals or DOIs to fill a format.

questions.prompt: Explain apa reference entries briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: A reference entry identifies a source through its author, date, title and publication information.
questions.answer: A reference entry identifies a source through its author, date, title and publication information. Identify the source type first.
keyPoints: A reference entry identifies a source through its author, date, title and publication information.

questions.prompt: Who appears first in an APA reference for a chapter in an edited book?
questions.shortAnswer: The chapter author.
questions.answer: The chapter author. The editor appears later with the book information because the specific cited contribution is the chapter.
keyPoints: The chapter author.
The editor appears later with the book information because the specific cited contribution is the chapter.

topics.title: Research proposals and frameworks
topics.core: A proposal explains what a study plans to investigate, why it matters and how it will be conducted.
topics.explanation: Include the problem, literature, questions, framework, methods, ethics, expected contribution, timeline and references. A theoretical framework draws on theory; a conceptual framework specifies the study's concepts and relationships.
topics.example: Plan a study of role-play and fluency with participants, measures, comparison and analysis.
topics.confusion: A proposal must not present invented results as if the study has happened.

questions.prompt: Explain research proposals and frameworks briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: A proposal explains what a study plans to investigate, why it matters and how it will be conducted.
questions.answer: A proposal explains what a study plans to investigate, why it matters and how it will be conducted. Include the problem, literature, questions, framework, methods, ethics, expected contribution, timeline and references.
keyPoints: A proposal explains what a study plans to investigate, why it matters and how it will be conducted.

questions.prompt: What should a proposal say about findings before data are collected?
questions.shortAnswer: It may state hypotheses or expected contributions, clearly as expectations.
questions.answer: It may state hypotheses or expected contributions, clearly as expectations. It must not fabricate findings; it should explain how the eventual evidence will answer the questions.
keyPoints: It may state hypotheses or expected contributions, clearly as expectations.
It must not fabricate findings; it should explain how the eventual evidence will answer the questions.

topics.title: Research papers and dissertations
topics.core: A research report explains the question, methods, evidence and reasoned conclusions of a completed study.
topics.explanation: A common dissertation structure includes introduction, literature review, methodology, results, discussion and conclusion. Articles often compress these functions; requirements vary by discipline and venue.
topics.example: A report connects its discussion back to the research questions and ends with implications and limits.
topics.confusion: An abstract summarises the whole study rather than serving as another general introduction.
syllabusTerms: Structures of research papers and dissertations

questions.prompt: Explain research papers and dissertations briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: A research report explains the question, methods, evidence and reasoned conclusions of a completed study.
questions.answer: A research report explains the question, methods, evidence and reasoned conclusions of a completed study. A common dissertation structure includes introduction, literature review, methodology, results, discussion and conclusion.
keyPoints: A research report explains the question, methods, evidence and reasoned conclusions of a completed study.

questions.prompt: What should a concise research-article abstract normally cover?
questions.shortAnswer: The problem or purpose, the main methods, central findings and conclusion or implication.
questions.answer: The problem or purpose, the main methods, central findings and conclusion or implication. For a proposal, describe planned work and omit invented findings.
keyPoints: The problem or purpose, the main methods, central findings and conclusion or implication.
For a proposal, describe planned work and omit invented findings.

topics.title: Defamiliarization
topics.core: Defamiliarization makes familiar things seem unfamiliar, renewing perception.
topics.explanation: Shklovsky associates art with slowing habitual perception through unusual perspective, description or form.
topics.example: Teaching illustration: Describe a lift as a small room that carries people through a building; the unfamiliar wording renews attention.
topics.confusion: It concerns an effect on perception, not simply using difficult vocabulary.

questions.prompt: Explain defamiliarization briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Defamiliarization makes familiar things seem unfamiliar, renewing perception.
questions.answer: Defamiliarization makes familiar things seem unfamiliar, renewing perception. Shklovsky associates art with slowing habitual perception through unusual perspective, description or form.
keyPoints: Defamiliarization makes familiar things seem unfamiliar, renewing perception.
Shklovsky associates art with slowing habitual perception through unusual perspective, description or form.

questions.prompt: How could a familiar bus journey be defamiliarized?
questions.shortAnswer: Describe it through someone encountering buses for the first time, attending to its sounds and rituals.
questions.answer: Describe it through someone encountering buses for the first time, attending to its sounds and rituals. The unusual perspective interrupts habitual recognition.
keyPoints: Describe it through someone encountering buses for the first time, attending to its sounds and rituals. The unusual perspective interrupts habitual recognition.

questions.prompt: What is Formalism?
questions.shortAnswer: Formalism studies the devices and organisation that create literary effects.
questions.answer: Formalism studies the devices and organisation that create literary effects. It foregrounds how a work uses language and form, including literariness and defamiliarization.
keyPoints: Formalism studies the devices and organisation that create literary effects.
It foregrounds how a work uses language and form, including literariness and defamiliarization.

topics.title: Foregrounding
topics.core: Foregrounding makes features of language especially noticeable.
topics.explanation: Deviation or patterned repetition can draw attention to sound, syntax or wording. Mayakovsky illustrates startling poetic language; the concept is associated with Prague School work.
topics.example: Teaching illustration: Repeated initial sounds in a slogan make its wording prominent.
topics.confusion: Foregrounding can occur outside poetry and need not depend only on deviation.

questions.prompt: Explain foregrounding briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Foregrounding makes features of language especially noticeable.
questions.answer: Foregrounding makes features of language especially noticeable. Deviation or patterned repetition can draw attention to sound, syntax or wording. Mayakovsky illustrates startling poetic language; the concept is associated with Prague School work.
keyPoints: Foregrounding makes features of language especially noticeable.
Deviation or patterned repetition can draw attention to sound, syntax or wording. Mayakovsky illustrates startling poetic language; the concept is associated with Prague School work.

questions.prompt: Does repeated alliteration count as foregrounding even without unusual grammar?
questions.shortAnswer: Yes.
questions.answer: Yes. Repetition can make a sound pattern salient. Foregrounding includes parallelism as well as departures from expected language.
keyPoints: Yes. Repetition can make a sound pattern salient. Foregrounding includes parallelism as well as departures from expected language.

topics.title: Practical criticism
topics.core: Practical criticism closely analyses a text with external identifying information withheld.
topics.explanation: Richards used anonymous poems to investigate readers' responses and misunderstandings. Attention falls on words, tone, imagery and their relations.
topics.example: Teaching illustration: Read a poem without knowing its author, then justify a reading from its wording.
topics.confusion: A reading exercise without biography does not establish that historical context never matters.

questions.prompt: Explain practical criticism briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Practical criticism closely analyses a text with external identifying information withheld.
questions.answer: Practical criticism closely analyses a text with external identifying information withheld. Richards used anonymous poems to investigate readers' responses and misunderstandings. Attention falls on words, tone, imagery and their relations.
keyPoints: Practical criticism closely analyses a text with external identifying information withheld.
Richards used anonymous poems to investigate readers' responses and misunderstandings. Attention falls on words, tone, imagery and their relations.

questions.prompt: Why did Richards withhold authors' names in his reading experiments?
questions.shortAnswer: It reduced reliance on reputation and background knowledge, making readers' textual judgments and interpretive difficulties more visible.
questions.answer: It reduced reliance on reputation and background knowledge, making readers' textual judgments and interpretive difficulties more visible.
keyPoints: It reduced reliance on reputation and background knowledge, making readers' textual judgments and interpretive difficulties more visible.

topics.title: New Criticism and close reading
topics.core: New Criticism studies the internal relations of literary language through close reading.
topics.explanation: It often seeks organic unity through tensions, paradoxes and irony. Form and meaning are understood as closely interdependent.
topics.example: Teaching illustration: Explain how a poem's opposing images contribute to an overall interpretation.
topics.confusion: Close reading is a method used by many approaches, not the exclusive property of New Criticism.

questions.prompt: Explain new criticism and close reading briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: New Criticism studies the internal relations of literary language through close reading.
questions.answer: New Criticism studies the internal relations of literary language through close reading. It often seeks organic unity through tensions, paradoxes and irony. Form and meaning are understood as closely interdependent.
keyPoints: New Criticism studies the internal relations of literary language through close reading.
It often seeks organic unity through tensions, paradoxes and irony. Form and meaning are understood as closely interdependent.

questions.prompt: What would a New Critic examine before discussing a poet's biography?
questions.shortAnswer: The work's diction, imagery, rhythm, ambiguities, irony and structure, explaining how these features interact within the text.
questions.answer: The work's diction, imagery, rhythm, ambiguities, irony and structure, explaining how these features interact within the text.
keyPoints: The work's diction, imagery, rhythm, ambiguities, irony and structure, explaining how these features interact within the text.

topics.title: Sign and signification
topics.core: A Saussurean sign links a signifier with a signified; signification is meaning production.
topics.explanation: The signifier is the form and the signified is the concept. Their association is conventional within a language system.
topics.example: Teaching illustration: The sound pattern of tree calls up a concept; another language uses a different form.
topics.confusion: The signified is a concept, not the physical object itself.

questions.prompt: Explain sign and signification briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: A Saussurean sign links a signifier with a signified; signification is meaning production.
questions.answer: A Saussurean sign links a signifier with a signified; signification is meaning production. The signifier is the form and the signified is the concept. Their association is conventional within a language system.
keyPoints: A Saussurean sign links a signifier with a signified; signification is meaning production.
The signifier is the form and the signified is the concept. Their association is conventional within a language system.

questions.prompt: Why does another language's different word for tree support arbitrariness?
questions.shortAnswer: It shows that the sound–concept association is socially conventional rather than a necessary natural resemblance.
questions.answer: It shows that the sound–concept association is socially conventional rather than a necessary natural resemblance.
keyPoints: It shows that the sound–concept association is socially conventional rather than a necessary natural resemblance.

questions.prompt: What is structuralism?
questions.shortAnswer: Structuralism examines how elements acquire meaning through relations within a system.
questions.answer: Structuralism examines how elements acquire meaning through relations within a system. In literary study, it investigates sign systems, narrative conventions and contrasts rather than treating each element as self-contained.
keyPoints: Structuralism examines how elements acquire meaning through relations within a system.
In literary study, it investigates sign systems, narrative conventions and contrasts rather than treating each element as self-contained.

topics.title: Paradigm and syntagm
topics.core: A paradigm concerns alternatives; a syntagm concerns combinations.
topics.explanation: A speaker selects among possible items and combines selected items into an organised sequence.
topics.example: Teaching illustration: In the dog sleeps, cat can replace dog paradigmatically; the whole sequence is syntagmatic.
topics.confusion: Selection and combination are related axes, not two separate kinds of language.

questions.prompt: Explain paradigm and syntagm briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: A paradigm concerns alternatives; a syntagm concerns combinations.
questions.answer: A paradigm concerns alternatives; a syntagm concerns combinations. A speaker selects among possible items and combines selected items into an organised sequence.
keyPoints: A paradigm concerns alternatives; a syntagm concerns combinations.
A speaker selects among possible items and combines selected items into an organised sequence.

questions.prompt: Identify both axes in the phrase a bright student.
questions.shortAnswer: Bright could be replaced by quiet or talented on the selection axis.
questions.answer: Bright could be replaced by quiet or talented on the selection axis. The ordered combination of determiner, adjective and noun is the syntagmatic axis.
keyPoints: Bright could be replaced by quiet or talented on the selection axis. The ordered combination of determiner, adjective and noun is the syntagmatic axis.

topics.title: Binary oppositions
topics.core: Binary oppositions organise meaning through paired contrasts.
topics.explanation: Structuralist analysis examines how contrasts such as nature/culture organise a text. Later critics ask whether one term is privileged and how the opposition is unsettled.
topics.example: Teaching illustration: A story opposes city and village, associating each with different values.
topics.confusion: A contrast need not be a simple or universal natural division.

questions.prompt: Explain binary oppositions briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Binary oppositions organise meaning through paired contrasts.
questions.answer: Binary oppositions organise meaning through paired contrasts. Structuralist analysis examines how contrasts such as nature/culture organise a text. Later critics ask whether one term is privileged and how the opposition is unsettled.
keyPoints: Binary oppositions organise meaning through paired contrasts.
Structuralist analysis examines how contrasts such as nature/culture organise a text. Later critics ask whether one term is privileged and how the opposition is unsettled.

questions.prompt: How could a character undermine a city/village binary?
questions.shortAnswer: A character may combine traits assigned to both sides, revealing that the text's supposedly separate categories depend on exclusions and overlaps.
questions.answer: A character may combine traits assigned to both sides, revealing that the text's supposedly separate categories depend on exclusions and overlaps.
keyPoints: A character may combine traits assigned to both sides, revealing that the text's supposedly separate categories depend on exclusions and overlaps.

topics.title: Mythoi and archetypal criticism
topics.core: Frye's mythoi are recurring narrative patterns used in archetypal criticism.
topics.explanation: His seasonal scheme associates comedy with spring, romance with summer, tragedy with autumn, and irony/satire with winter.
topics.example: Teaching illustration: A story of social renewal ending in celebration fits a comic pattern.
topics.confusion: A critical classification is an interpretive framework, not proof that every culture tells identical stories.

questions.prompt: Explain mythoi and archetypal criticism briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Frye's mythoi are recurring narrative patterns used in archetypal criticism.
questions.answer: Frye's mythoi are recurring narrative patterns used in archetypal criticism. His seasonal scheme associates comedy with spring, romance with summer, tragedy with autumn, and irony/satire with winter.
keyPoints: Frye's mythoi are recurring narrative patterns used in archetypal criticism.
His seasonal scheme associates comedy with spring, romance with summer, tragedy with autumn, and irony/satire with winter.

questions.prompt: Which Fryean mythos would a heroic quest ending in victory most readily suggest?
questions.shortAnswer: Romance, associated with summer and idealised adventure.
questions.answer: Romance, associated with summer and idealised adventure. The fit should be justified from the narrative rather than assumed from one isolated feature.
keyPoints: Romance, associated with summer and idealised adventure. The fit should be justified from the narrative rather than assumed from one isolated feature.

topics.title: Narratology and narrative order
topics.core: Narratology studies how narratives are structured and presented.
topics.explanation: Distinguish the chronological sequence of events from their artistic arrangement. Todorov's model describes equilibrium, disruption and a changed equilibrium.
topics.example: Teaching illustration: A novel starts with a death, then returns to the events that led to it.
topics.confusion: Narrative sequence is not necessarily chronological event order.

questions.answer: The Oedipus complex is Freud's theory of childhood desire, rivalry and identification within family relations. It has influenced interpretations of family conflict and Hamlet, but its universality and assumptions are contested.

questions.prompt: Does a son's closeness to his mother prove an Oedipus complex?
questions.shortAnswer: No.
questions.answer: No. Such closeness permits many explanations; an Oedipal interpretation needs careful textual support and acknowledgement of its theoretical assumptions.
keyPoints: No. Such closeness permits many explanations; an Oedipal interpretation needs careful textual support and acknowledgement of its theoretical assumptions.

topics.title: Drives and defenses
topics.core: Drives are motivating pressures; defenses manage anxiety and threatening psychic conflict in psychoanalytic theory.
topics.explanation: Repression excludes material from awareness; projection attributes unwanted feelings to others; sublimation redirects impulses into socially valued forms.
topics.example: Teaching illustration: A jealous character repeatedly accuses others of jealousy, suggesting projection as one reading.
topics.confusion: A defense is not necessarily a consciously planned lie.

questions.prompt: How do repression and projection differ?
questions.shortAnswer: Repression keeps threatening material out of awareness; projection locates an unwanted feeling or impulse in someone else.

topics.title: Dream-work
topics.core: Freudian dream-work transforms latent material into the dream's manifest form.
topics.explanation: Condensation brings several associations into one image; displacement shifts emphasis to an associated substitute.
topics.example: Teaching illustration: One dream figure combines traits of several important people.
topics.confusion: Manifest content is the remembered dream; latent content is the inferred material transformed by dream-work.

questions.shortAnswer: Several associations converge in a single image.

topics.title: Object relations theory
topics.core: Object relations theory examines how early relationships and their internal representations shape the self.
topics.explanation: Here an object is typically a person or part of a relationship as psychically represented, rather than a household item.
topics.example: Teaching illustration: Analyse a narrative's recurring attachment and separation patterns.
topics.confusion: It is not simply a theory about relations between physical objects.

topics.title: Imaginary, Symbolic and Real
topics.core: Lacan's three orders are the Imaginary, Symbolic and Real.
topics.explanation: The Imaginary concerns identification and images; the Symbolic concerns language, law and social relations; the Real names what resists symbolisation.
topics.example: Teaching illustration: A character's ideal self-image is challenged by their position in social language and rules.
topics.confusion: The Real is not everyday reality, and the three orders are not merely three successive life stages.

questions.prompt: How does Lacan's Real differ from ordinary reality?
questions.shortAnswer: Reality is experienced and organised through meanings and representations; the Real designates what resists full symbolisation within that organisation.

topics.title: Trauma
topics.core: Trauma theory considers overwhelming experience and difficulties of processing and representing it.
topics.explanation: Literary readings may examine repetition, silence or disrupted chronology as ways a text engages traumatic experience.
topics.example: Teaching illustration: A war narrative repeatedly returns to a scene without resolving it.
topics.confusion: Fragmented narration alone does not prove trauma; formal patterns need contextual interpretation.

questions.prompt: Can every gap in a narrative be treated as a symptom of trauma?

topics.title: Logocentrism
topics.core: Logocentrism privileges an ultimate foundation that supposedly guarantees meaning.
topics.explanation: Derrida questions claims to pure presence and the hierarchy of speech over writing, showing dependence on difference and mediation.
topics.example: Teaching illustration: A claim that only spoken words convey an author's meaning privileges presence.
topics.confusion: Questioning foundations does not mean ordinary communication never works.

questions.prompt: Why does Derrida question the supposed purity of speech?
questions.shortAnswer: Speech also relies on repeatable signs, differences and conventions; the speaker's presence does not make meaning completely self-contained or fully controllable.

questions.prompt: What does deconstruction examine?
questions.shortAnswer: Deconstruction examines tensions and dependencies that unsettle a text’s apparent conceptual stability.
questions.answer: Deconstruction examines tensions and dependencies that unsettle a text’s apparent conceptual stability. It attends to hierarchies, exclusions and aporias through close textual engagement; it is not arbitrary destruction of meaning.
keyPoints: Deconstruction examines tensions and dependencies that unsettle a text’s apparent conceptual stability.

topics.title: Differance and aporia
topics.core: Differance joins difference and deferral; aporia names a difficult interpretive impasse.
topics.explanation: Meaning depends on relations to other signs and cannot become completely self-sufficient. Deconstruction attends to tensions that unsettle a text's apparent assurances.
topics.example: Teaching illustration: A declaration of complete independence relies on terms and relations it rejects.
topics.confusion: Differance is not merely procrastination, and every hesitation is not an aporia.

topics.title: Jouissance
topics.core: Jouissance names an intense enjoyment that unsettles ordinary satisfaction and stable subjectivity.
topics.explanation: Kristeva connects disruptive bodily and rhythmic dimensions of signification with challenges to orderly symbolic structures.
topics.example: Teaching illustration: A text's rhythm and excess disturb a reader's secure interpretive position.
topics.confusion: The term is theory-dependent and is not simply a synonym for happiness.

topics.title: Death of the author
topics.core: Barthes challenges the author's intention as the final authority over a text's meaning.
topics.explanation: A text draws on multiple cultural voices; interpretation attends to their relations and the reader's encounter rather than seeking one biographical key.
topics.example: Teaching illustration: A writer's explanation does not exhaust the meanings readers can support from a text.
topics.confusion: It does not mean the author literally dies or evidence becomes irrelevant.

topics.title: Rhizome
topics.core: A rhizome models thought as multiple connections without one organising root.
topics.explanation: Deleuze and Guattari contrast it with hierarchical tree models. Connections can grow through diverse entry points rather than one required sequence.
topics.example: Teaching illustration: Map a cultural movement through intersecting music, migration, technology and politics.
topics.confusion: A rhizome is a conceptual model, not a claim that organisations have no power relations.

topics.title: Deterritorialization and becoming

topics.title: Disciplinary discourse

topics.title: Grand narratives
topics.core: Grand narratives are overarching accounts that legitimise knowledge or historical development.
topics.explanation: Lyotard characterises postmodernity through suspicion of such totalising accounts and attention to local narratives and heterogeneous language games.

topics.title: Intertextuality
topics.core: Intertextuality concerns how texts absorb, transform and relate to other texts and discourses.
topics.explanation: Kristeva's concept challenges the idea of a wholly self-contained original work. Relations can be explicit or implicit.
topics.example: Teaching illustration: A modern advertisement adapts the wording of a familiar proverb.

topics.title: Mimicry
topics.core: Bhabha's mimicry concerns colonial imitation that remains marked as different.
topics.explanation: The demand for similarity and continued exclusion creates ambivalence and can unsettle colonial authority, although resistance is not guaranteed.
topics.example: Teaching illustration: Colonial education invites imitation of the ruler's manners while withholding equal status.
topics.confusion: Mimicry is not always a consciously planned parody.

questions.prompt: Why can colonial mimicry threaten as well as support authority?

topics.title: Neocolonialism
topics.core: Neocolonialism describes indirect forms of domination after formal colonial rule.
topics.explanation: Economic, political and cultural dependencies can preserve unequal power without direct colonial administration.
topics.example: Teaching illustration: A formally independent country's choices are constrained by unequal financial and cultural relations.
topics.confusion: Political independence does not by itself establish equal power, but every foreign exchange is not domination.

topics.title: Culture
topics.core: Culture includes systems of meaning, creative practices and ways of life.
topics.explanation: Williams broadens attention beyond elite artistic achievements to ordinary lived practices, while definitions remain contested.
topics.example: Teaching illustration: Study food rituals or television viewing as meaningful cultural practices.
topics.confusion: A broad definition does not imply that every practice has identical value or power.

questions.prompt: What does cultural theory study?
questions.shortAnswer: Cultural theory investigates how practices, institutions and representations produce meaning and social identities.
questions.answer: Cultural theory investigates how practices, institutions and representations produce meaning and social identities. It studies everyday and prestigious forms, connecting culture with power, consumption and contested interpretation.

topics.title: Popular culture
topics.core: Popular culture concerns widely circulating or everyday cultural practices and products.
topics.explanation: The term can refer to mass consumption, culture made by people, or what is excluded from high-cultural canons. Audiences can actively interpret its meanings.
topics.example: Teaching illustration: Fans use a television character to express identities different from a producer's preferred message.
topics.confusion: Popularity does not automatically mean passive acceptance of a single message.

topics.title: Consumption
topics.core: Cultural consumption involves using and interpreting products as meaningful practices.
topics.explanation: Choices of clothing, media or commodities can communicate identity and status. Analysis connects audience agency with markets and social conditions.
topics.example: Teaching illustration: A music preference signals belonging to a peer group.
topics.confusion: Consumption is not merely purchasing, and consumers are not necessarily passive.

topics.title: Representation
topics.core: Hall treats representation as meaning production through concepts and signs.
topics.explanation: His constructionist approach emphasises shared codes and social practices rather than a simple mirror of things or private intention.
topics.example: Teaching illustration: Traffic-light colours acquire their significance through an established code.
topics.confusion: Meaning construction does not mean the material world does not exist.

topics.title: Sociolinguistics
topics.core: Sociolinguistics studies relationships between language and social life.
topics.explanation: It examines variation, interaction, identity, attitudes and institutions, asking how language both reflects and helps organise social relations.
topics.example: Teaching illustration: Compare how the same speaker addresses friends and a lecturer.
topics.confusion: Social influences do not make variation random or ruleless.

questions.shortAnswer: It helps teachers understand learners' varieties, identities and communicative contexts, and question prejudices that confuse linguistic difference with lack of ability.

topics.title: Scope and language attitudes
topics.core: The field includes language variation, contact, policy, identities and attitudes.
topics.explanation: Language attitudes are evaluations of languages, varieties or speakers; they can affect educational opportunity and linguistic choices.
topics.example: Teaching illustration: An accent is praised in one group and stigmatised in another.
topics.confusion: Judgments of a speaker's intelligence may reflect social stereotypes about an accent.

topics.title: Sociolinguistics and sociology of language
topics.core: The two fields overlap but differ in analytical emphasis.
topics.explanation: Sociolinguistics often starts with linguistic variation or use; sociology of language often starts with institutions, groups and the social distribution of languages.
topics.example: Teaching illustration: Compare a pronunciation variable across classes, or examine how official-language policy structures access.
topics.confusion: The distinction is an emphasis, not a rigid one-way society-to-language versus language-to-society split.

topics.title: Language and dialect
topics.core: A dialect is a systematic variety; language boundaries also involve social and political histories.
topics.explanation: Mutual intelligibility is useful but not decisive. Standard varieties are dialects too, and a dialect does not require a written tradition.
topics.example: Teaching illustration: Two closely related varieties may have separate institutional identities.
topics.confusion: Dialect does not mean defective language or only rural speech.

topics.title: Regional and social dialects
topics.core: Regional dialects correlate with place; sociolects correlate with social groups.
topics.explanation: Pronunciation, grammar and vocabulary can vary along several intersecting dimensions. A speaker is not reducible to one regional or social category.
topics.example: Teaching illustration: A regional pronunciation pattern coexists with a professional vocabulary.
topics.confusion: Regional and social variation can occur together.

topics.title: Accent, dialect and idiolect
topics.core: Accent concerns pronunciation; dialect includes grammar and vocabulary; idiolect concerns an individual's usage.
topics.explanation: These terms focus on different aspects of variation rather than marking degrees of linguistic sophistication.
topics.example: Teaching illustration: Two speakers share grammar but pronounce vowels differently.
topics.confusion: Everyone has an accent, including speakers of prestigious varieties.

topics.title: Register
topics.core: Register is language variation associated with situations, activities or uses.
topics.explanation: Specialised vocabulary and grammatical patterns can help realise a particular communicative task. The same person can use several registers.
topics.example: Teaching illustration: A doctor explains a diagnosis differently to a patient and to a specialist colleague.
topics.confusion: Register is not simply a speaker's social class or an individual language.

topics.title: Standard language
topics.core: A standard variety is socially selected, codified and institutionally supported.
topics.explanation: Its prestige and public functions arise through social history. Standardisation can aid shared communication while also producing hierarchies.
topics.example: Teaching illustration: A school adopts a codified spelling system for textbooks.
topics.confusion: Institutional prestige does not establish intrinsic linguistic superiority.

topics.title: Standardization
topics.core: Standardization develops shared norms through selection, codification, functional elaboration and acceptance.
topics.explanation: These processes can overlap and be contested. Codification records norms; elaboration extends their use into new domains.
topics.example: Teaching illustration: A selected variety receives dictionaries, technical terminology and educational support.
topics.confusion: Producing a dictionary does not automatically secure public acceptance.

topics.title: Pidgins and pidginization
topics.core: A pidgin is a contact variety conventionally used as an additional means of communication among groups.
topics.explanation: Pidginization concerns its development in contact settings. Pidgins have structured grammars; some expand across functions and persist over time.
topics.example: Teaching illustration: A contact variety develops for communication among speakers without a shared first language.
topics.confusion: Pidgins are not random broken speech, and not all are temporary.

topics.title: Creoles and creolization
topics.core: Creoles are established community languages that developed in particular language-contact histories.
topics.explanation: The textbook pidgin-to-native-language route is one account, but creole origins are diverse and debated. Creoles are fully systematic languages.
topics.example: Teaching illustration: A contact language serves everyday community life and is acquired by children.
topics.confusion: Not every creole is demonstrated to have passed through the same prior pidgin stage.

topics.confusion: The wave model complements rather than simply disproves genealogical classification.

topics.title: Bilingualism
topics.core: Bilingualism is the use or knowledge of two languages by individuals or communities.
topics.explanation: Competence varies across skills, domains and time. Balanced native-like proficiency in every domain is not necessary.
topics.example: Teaching illustration: A person reads academic material in one language and talks with family in another.
topics.confusion: Bilingual does not require equal proficiency or perfect translation ability.

topics.title: Simultaneous and sequential bilingualism
topics.core: Simultaneous bilingual development begins with two languages early together; sequential development adds another after initial first-language development.
topics.explanation: The timing distinction does not predict identical outcomes for all learners. Input, use and social conditions matter.
topics.example: Teaching illustration: A child hears two home languages from infancy, while another begins a new school language later.
topics.confusion: Sequential bilingualism is not automatically inferior development.

topics.title: Multilingualism and domains
topics.core: Multilingualism concerns the use or knowledge of multiple languages, at individual or societal levels.
topics.explanation: A society may distribute languages across home, education, work or worship without every member speaking every language.
topics.example: Teaching illustration: A city uses several languages across neighbourhoods and public institutions.
topics.confusion: Societal multilingualism does not imply that each resident is multilingual.

topics.title: Code-switching
topics.core: Code-switching alternates languages or varieties within an interaction or utterance.
topics.explanation: Switching may mark topic, audience, solidarity, stance or clarification. Linguistic competence and social purposes both matter.
topics.example: Teaching illustration: A bilingual speaker quotes someone in the language of the original exchange.
topics.confusion: Switching is not by itself evidence of low proficiency or confusion.

topics.title: Types of code-switching
topics.core: Inter-sentential switching occurs across sentence boundaries; intra-sentential switching occurs within a sentence.
topics.explanation: Tag-switching inserts a tag or discourse marker. Situational and metaphorical labels concern social motivation rather than sentence position.

topics.title: Code-mixing and the matrix language
topics.core: Code-mixing commonly refers to combining elements from different languages within an utterance.

topics.title: Borrowing
topics.core: Borrowing incorporates linguistic material into another language's conventional repertoire.
topics.explanation: Loanwords can become socially established and may undergo phonological or morphological adaptation. Speakers need not be bilingual to use established loans.

topics.title: Language planning

topics.title: Language policy and ideology
topics.core: Language policy includes decisions and practices shaping which codes are used, valued or learned.
topics.explanation: Ideologies can frame one language as unity, progress or authenticity while marginalising others. Examine both explicit rules and institutional practice.

topics.title: Behaviourist approaches to meaning

topics.title: Truth-conditional semantics

topics.title: Generative semantics
topics.core: Historical generative semantics explored a close derivational relationship between semantic representations and sentence structure.

topics.title: Metonymy
topics.core: Metonymy uses an expression to refer to something closely connected with what it denotes.

topics.title: Pragmatics

topics.title: Sentence and utterance

topics.title: Entailment

topics.title: Searle's speech-act categories
topics.core: Searle distinguishes representatives, directives, commissives, expressives and declarations.
topics.explanation: These concern commitments to truth, attempts to get action, future commitments, expressed attitudes and institutionally effective changes.
topics.example: Teaching example: An assertion represents; a request directs; a promise commits; thanks expresses; an authorised verdict declares.
topics.confusion: A declarative grammatical sentence need not perform a declaration.

questions.prompt: Why is 'The room is empty' not automatically a declaration in Searle's sense?
questions.shortAnswer: It normally represents a state of affairs rather than changing an institutional state through authorised utterance.

topics.title: Indirect speech acts
topics.core: An indirect speech act performs an action through a form conventionally associated with another action.
topics.explanation: Interpretation relies on context and familiar patterns, not only on literal sentence type.
topics.example: Teaching example: Can you pass the salt? is often a request rather than a genuine ability inquiry.
topics.confusion: Indirectness does not automatically mean greater politeness in every context.

questions.prompt: What makes 'Can you open the window?' an indirect request in an ordinary room?

questions.answer: Its literal form asks about ability, but the context makes a request for action the relevant interpretation. The hearer need not stop at answering yes.

topics.title: Politeness and context
topics.core: Politeness concerns how interaction attends to social relations and participants' expectations.
topics.explanation: Interpretation depends on relationship, activity, wording and context. Face-based theory is one influential account, not the only account.
topics.example: Teaching example: Please can soften a request, but an aggressive context may undermine it.
topics.confusion: Formality, indirectness and politeness are related but not equivalent.

questions.prompt: Does adding please guarantee that a request is polite?
questions.shortAnswer: No.

topics.title: Positive and negative face
topics.core: In Brown and Levinson's framework, positive face concerns approval and negative face concerns freedom from imposition.
topics.explanation: Face wants motivate ways of managing potentially threatening acts.
topics.example: Teaching example: A criticism can threaten approval; a demanding request can threaten freedom of action.
topics.confusion: Positive and negative do not mean good and bad personalities.

topics.title: Positive and negative politeness
topics.core: Positive politeness attends to approval or solidarity; negative politeness attends to non-imposition.
topics.explanation: Strategies can include common-ground appeals or respectful mitigation, depending on context.
topics.example: Teaching example: Could you possibly help, if you have time? acknowledges a potential imposition.

questions.prompt: How does offering an easy refusal help manage a request?

topics.title: Impoliteness
topics.core: Impoliteness involves behaviour interpreted as damaging or attacking social relations or face in context.
topics.explanation: Insults, exclusion and dismissive wording can contribute, but interpretation depends on the activity and participants.
topics.example: Teaching example: Go away, nobody wants you here can explicitly exclude a participant.
topics.confusion: Directness alone is not proof of impoliteness.

questions.prompt: Why might the same direct command be acceptable in an emergency but offensive in ordinary conversation?
questions.shortAnswer: Urgency and shared activity change expectations and entitlement.
questions.answer: Urgency and shared activity change expectations and entitlement. Its social meaning depends on the situation rather than sentence form alone.

topics.title: Topic management
topics.core: Conversation participants establish, maintain, shift and negotiate what their talk is about.
topics.explanation: Topic conflict can arise when speakers pursue incompatible agendas or resist each other's proposed direction.
topics.example: Teaching example: An evasive weather comment can redirect a sensitive discussion.
topics.confusion: A topic shift can still belong to an orderly conversational sequence.

questions.prompt: Why should a change of subject not automatically be labelled incoherent?
questions.shortAnswer: A shift may be understood as avoidance, a new proposal or part of a sequence.
questions.answer: A shift may be understood as avoidance, a new proposal or part of a sequence. Participants can make sense of it through its interactional position and context.
keyPoints: A shift may be understood as avoidance, a new proposal or part of a sequence.

topics.title: Repair
topics.core: Repair addresses problems in speaking, hearing or understanding.
topics.explanation: Distinguish who initiates repair from who supplies the solution.
topics.example: Teaching example: A says Tuesday—sorry, Thursday: the speaker initiates and completes self-repair.
topics.confusion: Repair is broader than correcting grammar mistakes.

questions.prompt: In 'A: Tuesday. B: Tuesday? A: Thursday, sorry', who initiates and who repairs?

topics.title: Insertion sequences
topics.core: An insertion sequence occurs between the parts of a base adjacency pair.
topics.explanation: The inserted exchange can resolve something needed before the pending response.
topics.example: Teaching example: A: Can I borrow it? B: When? A: Tonight. B: Yes.
topics.confusion: The inserted turns delay, rather than necessarily abandon, the original response.

topics.title: Adjacency pairs
topics.core: An adjacency pair links a first action with a relevant responsive action by another speaker.
topics.explanation: A first pair part makes a limited range of second actions relevant, such as a greeting and return greeting.
topics.example: Teaching example: A question makes an answer relevant, though an insertion may intervene.
topics.confusion: Adjacency is an organisational relation, not a claim that the turns must always be physically next to each other.

topics.title: The semantics–pragmatics interface
topics.core: Semantics and pragmatics distinguish conventional linguistic contributions from context-sensitive use and inference, while interacting in interpretation.
topics.explanation: Deictic reference and implied messages show why the boundary is analytically useful but theoretically debated.
topics.example: Teaching example: The conventional meaning of I identifies a speaker role; context determines its referent.
topics.confusion: Semantics is not wholly unrelated to context, and pragmatics is not unrestricted guesswork.

questions.shortAnswer: Expressions such as pronouns and indexicals require contextual values even when their conventional meaning supplies a rule.

topics.title: Cohesion
topics.core: Cohesion consists of identifiable linguistic ties connecting parts of a text.
topics.explanation: Reference, substitution, ellipsis, lexical relations and conjunction can link clauses or turns.
topics.example: Teaching example: A student arrived. She sat down uses an anaphoric reference tie.

questions.prompt: Can a passage contain many connectives yet remain incoherent?

topics.title: Reference ties
topics.core: Reference ties connect an expression with an entity interpreted through text or situation.
topics.explanation: Anaphora points back; cataphora points forward. Endophoric reference is text-internal, while exophoric reference depends on the situation.

questions.prompt: How do anaphora and deixis differ?

topics.title: Substitution and ellipsis
topics.core: Substitution replaces material with a grammatical substitute; ellipsis leaves recoverable material unspoken.

topics.title: Lexical cohesion
topics.core: Lexical cohesion connects a text through vocabulary relations and associations.

topics.title: Conjunction in discourse
topics.core: Conjunction marks relations such as addition, contrast, cause or sequence between discourse parts.

topics.title: Coherence
topics.core: Coherence is the meaningful connectedness that makes discourse interpretable as a whole.

topics.title: Phonetics
topics.core: Phonetics studies the production, transmission and perception of speech sounds.
topics.explanation: It describes physical speech events, including articulatory movements, acoustic properties and auditory processing.
topics.example: Teaching example: The aspiration after [p] in pin can be measured as a physical feature.
topics.confusion: Phonetics is not restricted to spelling or to sounds that distinguish words.

topics.title: Branches of phonetics

topics.title: Phone and phoneme

topics.title: Allophones

topics.title: Strong and weak forms

topics.title: Contractions

topics.title: Elision
topics.core: Elision is the absence of a sound that may occur in a fuller pronunciation.
topics.explanation: It often affects consonant clusters or unstressed material and varies with style and context.

topics.title: Regressive assimilation
topics.core: Regressive assimilation occurs when a following sound influences an earlier one.

topics.title: Progressive and coalescent assimilation
topics.core: Progressive assimilation reflects an earlier sound's influence; coalescence combines neighbouring segments into a new outcome.

topics.title: Stress and prominence
topics.core: Stress is the relative prominence of a syllable within a word or larger utterance.
topics.explanation: Prominence can involve pitch, duration, intensity and vowel quality, with their relative contribution varying.

topics.title: Primary, secondary and word stress

topics.title: Stress placement and suffixes
topics.core: English word stress is influenced by syllable structure, word class, morphology and lexical history.

topics.title: Compound and contrastive stress

topics.title: Chunking speech

topics.title: Tone-unit structure

topics.title: Compounding and headedness
topics.core: Compounding forms a word from two or more bases.
topics.explanation: An endocentric compound has an internal head defining its type; an exocentric compound lacks that straightforward internal semantic head.
topics.example: Teaching example: A blackboard is a kind of board; a pickpocket is a person, not a kind of pocket.
topics.confusion: Compound stress is a useful tendency, not an exception-free rule.

questions.prompt: Explain compounding and headedness briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Compounding forms a word from two or more bases.
questions.answer: Compounding forms a word from two or more bases. An endocentric compound has an internal head defining its type; an exocentric compound lacks that straightforward internal semantic head.
keyPoints: Compounding forms a word from two or more bases.

questions.prompt: What makes blackboard endocentric and pickpocket exocentric?
questions.shortAnswer: Blackboard names a type of board, so board is its semantic head.
questions.answer: Blackboard names a type of board, so board is its semantic head. Pickpocket names a person rather than a type of pocket or picking.
keyPoints: Blackboard names a type of board, so board is its semantic head.
Pickpocket names a person rather than a type of pocket or picking.

topics.title: Conversion
topics.core: Conversion creates a new word-class use without an overt derivational affix.
topics.explanation: It is also called zero derivation, though analyses differ on whether a silent affix should be posited.
topics.example: Teaching example: Email functions as a noun in an email and as a verb in email me.
topics.confusion: Conversion concerns lexical category change, not ordinary inflection.

questions.prompt: What is conversion?
questions.shortAnswer: Conversion creates a new word-class use without an overt derivational affix.
questions.answer: Conversion creates a new word-class use without an overt derivational affix. It is also called zero derivation, though analyses differ on whether a silent affix should be posited.
keyPoints: Conversion creates a new word-class use without an overt derivational affix.

questions.prompt: What process turns bottle into a verb in bottle the juice?
questions.shortAnswer: Conversion: a noun base is used as a verb without an overt category-changing suffix.
questions.answer: Conversion: a noun base is used as a verb without an overt category-changing suffix.

topics.title: Clipping and blending
topics.core: Clipping shortens a word; blending combines parts of words into a new form.
topics.explanation: The new forms preserve enough source material for their origin to be recognised, but the processes differ.
topics.example: Teaching example: Lab clips laboratory; brunch blends breakfast and lunch.
topics.confusion: A blend does not simply concatenate two complete bases.

questions.prompt: Explain clipping and blending briefly.

keyPoints: Clipping shortens a word; blending combines parts of words into a new form.

questions.shortAnswer: Lab is a shortened form of one source word.
questions.answer: Lab is a shortened form of one source word. Brunch merges portions of two source words into a new word.

topics.title: Acronyms and initialisms
topics.core: Acronyms and initialisms use initial letters of longer expressions.
topics.explanation: Acronyms are pronounced as words, whereas initialisms are pronounced as letter names under a common terminology.

questions.prompt: How would you distinguish NATO from BBC as word-formation examples?
questions.shortAnswer: Both originate from initials, but NATO is a word-pronounced acronym and BBC a letter-pronounced initialism in the narrower distinction.

topics.title: Back-formation
topics.core: Back-formation creates a new word by removing a part interpreted as an affix.
topics.explanation: The historical direction matters: apparent morphological simplicity does not prove which form came first.

topics.confusion: Back-formation is not the same as clipping a word casually.

questions.prompt: What is back-formation?

questions.prompt: Why is edit from editor back-formation rather than ordinary suffixation?
questions.shortAnswer: The longer noun existed first; speakers interpreted its ending as removable and created the verb.

topics.title: Borrowing and reduplication
topics.core: Borrowing adopts linguistic material from another language; reduplication repeats all or part of a form.
topics.explanation: Borrowed forms may become adapted to the receiving language. Reduplication can serve grammatical or expressive functions, depending on the language.

questions.prompt: Can a borrowed word later take English affixes?
questions.shortAnswer: Yes.

topics.title: Words and phrases
topics.core: Words show internal cohesion; phrases are syntactic combinations whose parts can often be independently modified.
topics.explanation: Stress, meaning, inflection and insertion provide relevant evidence, but compound–phrase boundaries can be difficult.
topics.example: Teaching example: A greenhouse is a building for plants; a green house is a house described as green.
topics.confusion: Idiomatic meaning or initial stress alone does not provide a universal test.

questions.prompt: Explain words and phrases briefly.

questions.answer: Words show internal cohesion; phrases are syntactic combinations whose parts can often be independently modified. Stress, meaning, inflection and insertion provide relevant evidence, but compound–phrase boundaries can be difficult.
keyPoints: Words show internal cohesion; phrases are syntactic combinations whose parts can often be independently modified.

questions.prompt: Why can greenhouse and green house differ despite sharing the same bases?

topics.title: Morphological segmentation
topics.core: Morphological analysis identifies meaningful components and their structural relationships.
topics.explanation: Use recurring form–meaning correspondences and category information rather than splitting wherever letters happen to repeat.
topics.example: Teaching example: Teachers can be segmented teach-er-s; corner is not ordinarily corn-er.
topics.confusion: A recurring letter sequence is not sufficient evidence for a morpheme.

questions.prompt: What is morphological segmentation?
questions.shortAnswer: Morphological analysis identifies meaningful components and their structural relationships.

keyPoints: Morphological analysis identifies meaningful components and their structural relationships.

questions.shortAnswer: The supposed parts do not contribute the relevant meanings or productive category relation.

topics.title: Morphological rules
topics.core: A morphological rule states a pattern relating bases and formed words, including meaning and category.
topics.explanation: For example, agentive -er commonly attaches to verbs to create nouns; productivity is restricted and exceptions matter.
topics.example: Teaching example: Teach plus -er gives teacher, a person associated with teaching.
topics.confusion: A rule describes productive patterns without claiming every possible formation is conventional.

questions.prompt: Explain morphological rules briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: A morphological rule states a pattern relating bases and formed words, including meaning and category.

questions.shortAnswer: Morphological productivity has lexical and conventional limits.

topics.title: Morphological trees and ambiguity
topics.core: Morphological trees show hierarchical grouping and the order in which bases and affixes combine.
