topics.title: Syntagmatic and paradigmatic relations
topics.core: Syntagmatic relations concern combination; paradigmatic relations concern alternatives in a structural position.
topics.explanation: In morphology, affixes combine with bases while related forms contrast within a paradigm or word family.
topics.example: Teaching example: Teach-er-s illustrates combination; cat/cats illustrates a number contrast.
topics.confusion: Paradigmatic alternatives need not occur next to each other in the same utterance.

topics.title: Morpheme, morph and allomorph
topics.core: A morpheme is an abstract meaningful unit; a morph is a realisation; allomorphs are alternative realisations of a morpheme.
topics.explanation: Allomorphic choice can be conditioned by sound environment, grammatical context or particular lexical items.

topics.title: Prosodic morphology
topics.core: Prosodic morphology studies how morphological patterns interact with units such as syllables, feet and stress.
topics.explanation: Morphological contrasts can involve changes in prosody rather than the addition of a straightforward segmental suffix.

topics.title: Zero morph
topics.core: A zero morph is a posited absence of overt form representing a grammatical contrast in an analysis.
topics.explanation: A zero analysis preserves a distinction such as plural even when no segment is added; alternative morphological frameworks may represent it differently.

topics.title: Morphophonology

questions.prompt: Explain noun phrases briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: A noun phrase is a constituent organised around a nominal head in the course's analysis.
questions.answer: A noun phrase is a constituent organised around a nominal head in the course's analysis. It may include determiners, modifiers and complements, and can function in different clause positions.
keyPoints: A noun phrase is a constituent organised around a nominal head in the course's analysis.

questions.prompt: Identify the head in those very useful books on syntax.
questions.shortAnswer: Books is the nominal head; those is a determiner, useful is an adjective modifier, and on syntax supplies further information about the books.
questions.answer: Books is the nominal head; those is a determiner, useful is an adjective modifier, and on syntax supplies further information about the books.
keyPoints: Books is the nominal head; those is a determiner, useful is an adjective modifier, and on syntax supplies further information about the books.

topics.title: Verb phrases
topics.core: A verb phrase is a constituent headed by a verb, with dependents permitted by that verb and the analysis.
topics.explanation: Objects and other complements combine with verbs, and adjuncts may add information about the event.
topics.example: Teaching example: Read the book carefully contains a verbal head, an object NP and a manner adjunct.
topics.confusion: A VP should not be identified simply as all words after the subject without structural analysis.

questions.prompt: Explain verb phrases briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: A verb phrase is a constituent headed by a verb, with dependents permitted by that verb and the analysis.
questions.answer: A verb phrase is a constituent headed by a verb, with dependents permitted by that verb and the analysis. Objects and other complements combine with verbs, and adjuncts may add information about the event.
keyPoints: A verb phrase is a constituent headed by a verb, with dependents permitted by that verb and the analysis.

questions.prompt: In read the book carefully, what roles do the book and carefully play?
questions.shortAnswer: The book is the object licensed by read.
questions.answer: The book is the object licensed by read. Carefully is a manner adjunct modifying the reading event.
keyPoints: The book is the object licensed by read.
Carefully is a manner adjunct modifying the reading event.

topics.title: Adjective and adverb phrases
topics.core: Adjective phrases are headed by adjectives; adverb phrases are headed by adverbs.
topics.explanation: Degree modifiers may expand them, while complements depend on the head's grammatical possibilities.
topics.example: Teaching example: Very proud of her work is an AdjP; quite slowly is an AdvP.
topics.confusion: The first word is not necessarily a phrase's head.

questions.prompt: Explain adjective and adverb phrases briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Adjective phrases are headed by adjectives; adverb phrases are headed by adverbs.
questions.answer: Adjective phrases are headed by adjectives; adverb phrases are headed by adverbs. Degree modifiers may expand them, while complements depend on the head's grammatical possibilities.
keyPoints: Adjective phrases are headed by adjectives; adverb phrases are headed by adverbs.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes very happy from very happily structurally?
questions.shortAnswer: Happy is an adjective head, so the first is an adjective phrase.
questions.answer: Happy is an adjective head, so the first is an adjective phrase. Happily is an adverb head, so the second is an adverb phrase.
keyPoints: Happy is an adjective head, so the first is an adjective phrase.
Happily is an adverb head, so the second is an adverb phrase.

topics.title: Prepositional phrases
topics.core: A prepositional phrase is headed by a preposition and includes any dependents it licenses.
topics.explanation: PPs can function within clauses or inside other phrases, depending on their attachment and context.
topics.example: Teaching example: On the table modifies book in the book on the table, or supplies location in she waited on the table in an appropriate reading.
topics.confusion: Phrase category and grammatical function should be stated separately.

questions.prompt: Explain prepositional phrases briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: A prepositional phrase is headed by a preposition and includes any dependents it licenses.
questions.answer: A prepositional phrase is headed by a preposition and includes any dependents it licenses. PPs can function within clauses or inside other phrases, depending on their attachment and context.
keyPoints: A prepositional phrase is headed by a preposition and includes any dependents it licenses.

questions.prompt: In the book on the shelf, does on the shelf form part of the NP?
questions.shortAnswer: In the ordinary reading it is a PP modifying book inside the larger noun phrase.
questions.answer: In the ordinary reading it is a PP modifying book inside the larger noun phrase. The nested categories differ from their functions.
keyPoints: In the ordinary reading it is a PP modifying book inside the larger noun phrase.
The nested categories differ from their functions.

topics.title: Complements and adjuncts
topics.core: Complements are licensed by a head's grammatical properties; adjuncts add relatively independent modification.
topics.explanation: Obligatoriness is a useful clue but is not a complete test: some complements can be omitted in context, and some required dependents are classified differently across frameworks.
topics.example: Teaching example: In she put it on the desk, the location is selected by this use of put; yesterday adds temporal modification.
topics.confusion: Complement does not always mean an overtly obligatory expression.

questions.prompt: Explain complements and adjuncts briefly.

Obligatoriness is a useful clue but is not a complete test: some complements can be omitted in context, and some required dependents are classified differently across frameworks.
keyPoints: Complements are licensed by a head's grammatical properties; adjuncts add relatively independent modification.

questions.prompt: Why is optionality alone an unreliable complement test?
questions.shortAnswer: Some heads permit their complements to be unexpressed, as in she ate.
questions.answer: Some heads permit their complements to be unexpressed, as in she ate. Classification also depends on the head's selection and the construction, not just whether omission is possible.

topics.title: Immediate constituents
topics.core: Immediate constituent analysis divides a larger unit into its directly contained structural parts.
topics.explanation: Successive divisions distinguish larger groupings from ultimate constituents. The analysis makes hierarchy explicit.
topics.example: Teaching example: Poor John ran away can first be grouped into subject NP and predicate VP.
topics.confusion: Immediate means directly contained, not merely adjacent in a word string.

questions.prompt: Explain immediate constituents briefly.

questions.answer: Immediate constituent analysis divides a larger unit into its directly contained structural parts. Successive divisions distinguish larger groupings from ultimate constituents. The analysis makes hierarchy explicit.
keyPoints: Immediate constituent analysis divides a larger unit into its directly contained structural parts.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between immediate and ultimate constituents?
questions.shortAnswer: Immediate constituents are the next structural parts of a given unit; ultimate constituents are the smallest units reached in the chosen analysis.
questions.answer: Immediate constituents are the next structural parts of a given unit; ultimate constituents are the smallest units reached in the chosen analysis.
keyPoints: Immediate constituents are the next structural parts of a given unit; ultimate constituents are the smallest units reached in the chosen analysis.

topics.title: Constituency and attachment ambiguity
topics.core: Constituency tests provide evidence that words form a unit; different attachments can produce different readings.
topics.explanation: Substitution, movement and coordination offer diagnostics with limits. A structural analysis should connect grouping with interpretation.
topics.example: Teaching example: The man with a telescope can form an NP, or with a telescope can modify the seeing event.
topics.confusion: No single constituency test is mechanically decisive in every construction.

questions.prompt: Explain constituency and attachment ambiguity briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Constituency tests provide evidence that words form a unit; different attachments can produce different readings.
questions.answer: Constituency tests provide evidence that words form a unit; different attachments can produce different readings. Substitution, movement and coordination offer diagnostics with limits. A structural analysis should connect grouping with interpretation.
keyPoints: Constituency tests provide evidence that words form a unit; different attachments can produce different readings.

questions.prompt: Give two readings of I saw the man with a telescope.
questions.shortAnswer: The telescope may be my instrument for seeing, attached to the VP, or it may describe the man I saw, attached within the NP.
questions.answer: The telescope may be my instrument for seeing, attached to the VP, or it may describe the man I saw, attached within the NP.
keyPoints: The telescope may be my instrument for seeing, attached to the VP, or it may describe the man I saw, attached within the NP.

topics.title: Phrase structure rules
topics.core: Phrase structure rules state how a constituent can be expanded into smaller constituents.
topics.explanation: They represent hierarchical structure and can include recursive possibilities. The exact rules depend on the grammar model.
topics.example: Teaching example: A simple teaching rule is S → NP VP; PP → P NP.
topics.confusion: A rewrite rule is a model of structure, not a prescription for how people must speak.

questions.prompt: Explain phrase structure rules briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Phrase structure rules state how a constituent can be expanded into smaller constituents.
questions.answer: Phrase structure rules state how a constituent can be expanded into smaller constituents. They represent hierarchical structure and can include recursive possibilities. The exact rules depend on the grammar model.
keyPoints: Phrase structure rules state how a constituent can be expanded into smaller constituents.

questions.prompt: How can phrase structure rules represent an indefinitely expandable NP?
questions.shortAnswer: A recursive rule can allow an NP to contain a modifier that itself contains an NP, such as the book on the shelf near the window.
questions.answer: A recursive rule can allow an NP to contain a modifier that itself contains an NP, such as the book on the shelf near the window.
keyPoints: A recursive rule can allow an NP to contain a modifier that itself contains an NP, such as the book on the shelf near the window.

topics.title: Transformational rules
topics.core: Transformational rules relate structural configurations, often through movement, in transformational grammars.
topics.explanation: Historical versions distinguish underlying and surface representations; later theories organise these relationships differently.
topics.example: Teaching example: Subject–auxiliary inversion relates she can swim and can she swim in an elementary analysis.
topics.confusion: Deep and surface structure are framework-specific terms rather than universal facts of all syntactic theories.

questions.prompt: Explain transformational rules briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Transformational rules relate structural configurations, often through movement, in transformational grammars.
questions.answer: Transformational rules relate structural configurations, often through movement, in transformational grammars. Historical versions distinguish underlying and surface representations; later theories organise these relationships differently.
keyPoints: Transformational rules relate structural configurations, often through movement, in transformational grammars.

questions.prompt: What does subject–auxiliary inversion change in Can she swim?
questions.shortAnswer: It places the auxiliary before the subject in this interrogative construction, while preserving relevant grammatical relationships.
questions.answer: It places the auxiliary before the subject in this interrogative construction, while preserving relevant grammatical relationships.
keyPoints: It places the auxiliary before the subject in this interrogative construction, while preserving relevant grammatical relationships.

topics.title: Projection
topics.core: Projection relates a head to larger structures that share its grammatical category in an analysis.
topics.explanation: In X-bar approaches, a head X projects intermediate and maximal levels, with positions for complements and modifiers.
topics.example: Teaching example: A noun head projects a nominal phrase containing its dependents.
topics.confusion: The labels and number of levels vary among frameworks.

questions.prompt: What is projection?
questions.shortAnswer: Projection relates a head to larger structures that share its grammatical category in an analysis.
questions.answer: Projection relates a head to larger structures that share its grammatical category in an analysis. In X-bar approaches, a head X projects intermediate and maximal levels, with positions for complements and modifiers.
keyPoints: Projection relates a head to larger structures that share its grammatical category in an analysis.

questions.prompt: Why is an NP called a projection of its head noun in X-bar analysis?
questions.shortAnswer: The noun determines key category properties of the larger structure; the phrase expands that head with licensed dependents and modifiers.
questions.answer: The noun determines key category properties of the larger structure; the phrase expands that head with licensed dependents and modifiers.
keyPoints: The noun determines key category properties of the larger structure; the phrase expands that head with licensed dependents and modifiers.

topics.title: Merge
topics.core: Merge combines syntactic objects into a larger object in minimalist syntax.
topics.explanation: It builds hierarchical structure recursively. Describing it as a formal operation does not mean speakers consciously apply textbook rules.
topics.example: Teaching example: Combining a verb with an object forms a larger syntactic unit.
topics.confusion: Merge is not merely placing two words next to each other.

questions.prompt: What is merge?
questions.shortAnswer: Merge combines syntactic objects into a larger object in minimalist syntax.
questions.answer: Merge combines syntactic objects into a larger object in minimalist syntax. It builds hierarchical structure recursively. Describing it as a formal operation does not mean speakers consciously apply textbook rules.
keyPoints: Merge combines syntactic objects into a larger object in minimalist syntax.

questions.prompt: How does Merge differ from a simple list of words?
questions.shortAnswer: Merge creates a hierarchical object with structural relations, whereas a list supplies only a linear sequence and does not by itself specify constituency.
questions.answer: Merge creates a hierarchical object with structural relations, whereas a list supplies only a linear sequence and does not by itself specify constituency.
keyPoints: Merge creates a hierarchical object with structural relations, whereas a list supplies only a linear sequence and does not by itself specify constituency.

topics.title: Adjunction
topics.core: Adjunction attaches a modifying constituent to a larger structure within a syntactic analysis.
topics.explanation: The resulting structure generally retains the relevant category of the host. Analyses specify how modifiers relate to complements and heads.
topics.example: Teaching example: A time modifier such as yesterday can adjoin to a clause or verbal projection in a chosen model.
topics.confusion: Adjunction and complement combination have different structural relations in many frameworks.

questions.prompt: What is adjunction?

keyPoints: Adjunction attaches a modifying constituent to a larger structure within a syntactic analysis.

questions.prompt: What changes when quietly is added to a simple reading clause as an adjunct?
questions.shortAnswer: It adds manner information about the reading event without changing the core argument relation between the verb and its object.
questions.answer: It adds manner information about the reading event without changing the core argument relation between the verb and its object.

topics.title: Clause types
topics.core: Clauses can be classified by dependence, finiteness and communicative form.
topics.explanation: Main and subordinate, finite and non-finite, declarative and interrogative describe different classification dimensions.
topics.example: Teaching example: Because she left is a finite subordinate clause; to leave can form a non-finite clause.
topics.confusion: Subordinate does not mean non-finite.

questions.prompt: Explain clause types briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Clauses can be classified by dependence, finiteness and communicative form.
questions.answer: Clauses can be classified by dependence, finiteness and communicative form. Main and subordinate, finite and non-finite, declarative and interrogative describe different classification dimensions.
keyPoints: Clauses can be classified by dependence, finiteness and communicative form.

questions.prompt: Can a subordinate clause be finite?
questions.shortAnswer: Yes.
questions.answer: Yes. In I know that she left, that she left is subordinate but contains a finite past-tense verb.
keyPoints: Yes.

topics.title: Clause functions and patterns
topics.core: Clause analysis identifies functions such as subject, verb, object, complement and adverbial.
topics.explanation: The course uses patterns such as SV, SVO, SVC, SVA, SVOO, SVOC and SVOA. Identify functions from the construction rather than word order alone.
topics.example: Teaching example: She gave him a book is SVOO; they elected her chair is SVOC.
topics.confusion: An object complement describes or identifies an object; it is not a second object.

questions.prompt: In They elected her chair, why is chair an object complement?
questions.shortAnswer: Chair identifies the role assigned to her.

topics.title: Sentence types and embedded clauses
topics.core: Simple, compound, complex and compound-complex sentences distinguish patterns of clause combination.
topics.explanation: Coordination joins units of comparable status; subordination embeds or depends one clause within another construction.
topics.example: Teaching example: She left and he stayed is compound; she left because she was tired is complex.
topics.confusion: The number of words does not determine whether a sentence is complex.

questions.prompt: Explain sentence types and embedded clauses briefly.

questions.prompt: Can a long sentence still be structurally simple?
questions.shortAnswer: Yes.
questions.answer: Yes. A single clause can contain many phrases and modifiers. Complexity in this classification concerns clause organisation, not length alone.
keyPoints: Yes.

topics.title: Tense
topics.core: Tense grammatically locates a situation relative to a temporal reference point.
topics.explanation: English is commonly analysed as contrasting present and past inflection; future reference can use auxiliaries and other constructions. Pedagogical tense labels often combine tense and aspect.
topics.example: Teaching example: She walked has past inflection; she will walk uses an auxiliary construction for future reference.
topics.confusion: Time and grammatical tense do not map one to one.

questions.prompt: What is tense?
questions.shortAnswer: Tense grammatically locates a situation relative to a temporal reference point.
questions.answer: Tense grammatically locates a situation relative to a temporal reference point. English is commonly analysed as contrasting present and past inflection; future reference can use auxiliaries and other constructions. Pedagogical tense labels often combine tense and aspect.
keyPoints: Tense grammatically locates a situation relative to a temporal reference point.

questions.prompt: Why can The train leaves tomorrow use a present form for future time?
questions.shortAnswer: Grammatical tense interacts with context and construction.
questions.answer: Grammatical tense interacts with context and construction. A present-tense form can describe a scheduled future event without becoming a distinct future inflection.
keyPoints: Grammatical tense interacts with context and construction.

topics.title: Aspect
topics.core: Aspect presents how a situation unfolds or relates to another time, such as progressive or perfect viewpoint.
topics.explanation: Progressive typically presents an event as ongoing around a reference time. Perfect relates a prior situation to a later reference point; interpretations vary with context.
topics.example: Teaching example: Was reading combines past tense with progressive aspect.
topics.confusion: Perfect does not simply mean finished action in every use.

questions.prompt: What is aspect?

keyPoints: Aspect presents how a situation unfolds or relates to another time, such as progressive or perfect viewpoint.

questions.prompt: In She was reading, what do tense and aspect each contribute?
questions.shortAnswer: Past tense locates the reference in the past; progressive aspect presents the reading as in progress around that reference time.
questions.answer: Past tense locates the reference in the past; progressive aspect presents the reading as in progress around that reference time.
keyPoints: Past tense locates the reference in the past; progressive aspect presents the reading as in progress around that reference time.

topics.title: Voice
topics.core: Voice concerns how participant roles map onto grammatical functions, especially in active and passive constructions.
topics.explanation: A passive can promote an affected participant to subject while the agent is expressed in a by-phrase or left unexpressed.
topics.example: Teaching example: The committee approved it and it was approved by the committee organise the same event differently.
topics.confusion: An omitted agent does not mean the event has no agent.

questions.prompt: What is voice?

questions.shortAnswer: The passive foregrounds the results and leaves the checker unexpressed when irrelevant, unknown or already understood.

topics.title: Mood and modality
topics.core: Mood and modality express distinctions involving factuality, possibility, necessity, wishes and related meanings.
topics.explanation: Mood is a grammatical category; modality can be expressed through auxiliaries, adverbs and other devices. The relationship between the terms varies by framework.
topics.example: Teaching example: Might signals possibility; must can express obligation or inference.
topics.confusion: The same modal form can have different meanings in context.

questions.shortAnswer: The first commonly expresses obligation.

topics.title: Relational Grammar
topics.core: Relational Grammar analyses grammatical relations such as subject and object as central primitives.
topics.explanation: It models changes in relations across grammatical structures rather than reducing all descriptions to word order alone.
topics.example: Teaching example: A passive can be described in terms of changes in the status of arguments.
topics.confusion: Grammatical relations are not identical to semantic roles.

questions.prompt: How would Relational Grammar's focus differ from a phrase-label-only description of a passive?
questions.shortAnswer: It would emphasise changes in relations such as subject and object, while a phrase-label description primarily displays constituent categories and hierarchy.

topics.title: Lexical-Functional Grammar
topics.core: Lexical-Functional Grammar represents constituent structure and grammatical functions in parallel structures.
topics.explanation: C-structure represents constituent organisation; f-structure represents functions such as subject and object, linked by correspondence principles.
topics.example: Teaching example: Different word orders can correspond to comparable functional relationships.
topics.confusion: LFG does not simply use one phrase tree as its complete grammatical representation.

questions.prompt: What is lexical-functional grammar?
questions.shortAnswer: Lexical-Functional Grammar represents constituent structure and grammatical functions in parallel structures.

questions.prompt: What is the distinction between c-structure and f-structure in LFG?
questions.shortAnswer: C-structure represents phrase organisation and order; f-structure represents grammatical functions and associated features.

topics.title: Government and Binding
topics.core: Government and Binding is a principles-and-parameters model of generative syntax with interacting modules.
topics.explanation: Case, theta roles, binding and movement constraints help explain dependencies. Its historical terminology should be distinguished from later minimalist formulations.
topics.example: Teaching example: Binding principles constrain interpretations of pronouns and reflexives.
topics.confusion: Government in this technical theory does not mean social or political authority.

topics.title: Role and Reference Grammar
topics.core: Role and Reference Grammar links syntactic organisation with semantics and communicative functions.
topics.explanation: Its layered clause representation distinguishes nucleus, core and periphery; semantic roles and linking principles connect predicates with arguments.
topics.example: Teaching example: The verb forms the nucleus; its arguments belong to the core; some modifiers occur in the periphery.
topics.confusion: RRG is not simply a different set of phrase-structure labels for the same transformational analysis.

topics.title: Psycholinguistics
topics.core: Psycholinguistics studies the mental knowledge and processes involved in acquiring, understanding and producing language.
topics.explanation: It examines how linguistic representations interact with attention, memory and other cognitive processes; mental processes are inferred from evidence rather than directly read from behaviour.
topics.example: Teaching example: A listener rapidly combines word meanings with sentence structure to understand a spoken question.
topics.confusion: Knowing grammatical rules explicitly is different from using tacit linguistic knowledge.

questions.shortAnswer: Psycholinguistics studies the mental knowledge and processes involved in acquiring, understanding and producing language.

questions.prompt: Why can fluent speakers use a grammatical pattern without explaining its rule?
questions.shortAnswer: Much linguistic knowledge is tacit.
questions.answer: Much linguistic knowledge is tacit. Psycholinguistics distinguishes the representations that support use from a person's ability to state those representations consciously.
keyPoints: Much linguistic knowledge is tacit.

topics.title: History of psycholinguistics
topics.core: Psycholinguistics developed through exchanges between psychology and linguistics, with a major mid-twentieth-century revival.
topics.explanation: Early work examined language and thought; behaviourist approaches stressed learning histories, while cognitive and generative work renewed interest in internal representations.
topics.example: Teaching example: The contrast between Skinner's account and Chomsky's critique helped shape debates about language learning.
topics.confusion: The field did not begin with one person or a single experiment.

questions.prompt: Why was the cognitive turn important for psycholinguistics?
questions.shortAnswer: It made internal representations and mental processes legitimate targets of explanation, encouraging experimental models of comprehension, production and acquisition beyond observable stimulus–response descriptions.
questions.answer: It made internal representations and mental processes legitimate targets of explanation, encouraging experimental models of comprehension, production and acquisition beyond observable stimulus–response descriptions.
keyPoints: It made internal representations and mental processes legitimate targets of explanation, encouraging experimental models of comprehension, production and acquisition beyond observable stimulus–response descriptions.

topics.title: Branches of psycholinguistics
topics.core: Psycholinguistic branches include experimental, developmental and neurolinguistic approaches to language.
topics.explanation: Experimental work studies processing through tasks; developmental work studies acquisition and change; neurolinguistics relates language to brain organisation.
topics.example: Teaching example: A child-language recording and an adult reaction-time experiment investigate different dimensions of language processing.
topics.confusion: The branches overlap rather than forming sealed disciplines.

questions.prompt: Explain branches of psycholinguistics briefly.

questions.prompt: How can one study be both developmental and experimental?

topics.title: Speech production
topics.core: Speech production transforms a communicative intention into a planned and articulated utterance.
topics.explanation: A useful model distinguishes conceptualisation, formulation and articulation, with monitoring of the output. Real-time coordination is complex and partly automatic.
topics.example: Teaching example: A speaker chooses a message, selects words and grammatical patterns, then produces their sounds.
topics.confusion: An occasional speech error does not mean the speaker lacks the relevant grammar.

questions.prompt: What is speech production?

questions.prompt: What can a slip of the tongue reveal about production?
questions.shortAnswer: A systematic slip can show that speakers plan and organise linguistic units before articulation.

topics.title: Comprehension and context
topics.core: Comprehension builds an interpretation from linguistic input using knowledge and context.
topics.explanation: Listeners and readers identify forms, assemble structure and integrate meanings. Bottom-up input and top-down expectations can interact.
topics.example: Teaching example: The context of a river helps select the intended meaning of bank.
topics.confusion: Context can guide interpretation but does not make the acoustic or written input irrelevant.

questions.prompt: Why can the same word be recognised differently in different contexts?
questions.shortAnswer: Context activates different expectations and meanings, which interact with the incoming form.

topics.title: Pre-linguistic development
topics.core: Pre-linguistic development includes early perception, vocalisation and communicative behaviour before stable words.
topics.explanation: Infants attend to speech, participate in interaction and gradually tune perception to the languages around them. These abilities develop at varying rates.
topics.example: Teaching example: A baby alternates gaze and vocalisation with a caregiver before producing recognisable words.
topics.confusion: The absence of spoken words does not imply the absence of communicative learning.

topics.title: Babbling
topics.core: Babbling is early production of speech-like syllabic patterns before stable meaningful words.
topics.explanation: Repeated and varied consonant–vowel sequences provide experience with articulation and interact with the ambient language. Babbling and later words show continuities and changes.
topics.example: Teaching example: Repeated ba-ba or varied ba-da are possible babbling patterns.
topics.confusion: A repeated sound becomes a word only when it has a sufficiently stable meaningful use.

questions.shortAnswer: It may be a babbled sound sequence without a consistent referential or communicative meaning.

topics.title: Sensori-motor development
topics.core: In Piaget's account, sensori-motor development concerns learning through perception and action during early life.
topics.explanation: Object permanence, intentional action and symbolic capacities provide a cognitive context for language development. Cognitive stages should not be treated as exact universal language timetables.
topics.example: Teaching example: A child searching for a hidden object shows an understanding relevant to representing absent things.
topics.confusion: Sensori-motor stage is a cognitive-development label, not a specific grammatical stage.

questions.prompt: How might object permanence support later language use?
questions.shortAnswer: Representing objects that are out of sight helps support reference beyond the immediate scene, though it does not by itself explain the acquisition of grammar.

topics.title: Holophrastic stage
topics.core: At the holophrastic stage, a single word can perform a communicative act that adults express more fully.
topics.explanation: Context, gesture and intonation help an adult interpret the intention; an adult paraphrase does not prove that the child represents a complete adult sentence internally.
topics.example: Teaching example: Milk may function as a request for milk, depending on the setting.
topics.confusion: One-word speech need not correspond to one fixed sentence meaning.

topics.title: Two-word combinations
topics.core: Two-word speech combines lexical items to express relationships such as agent–action or possession.
topics.explanation: Early combinations show emerging organisation, often without the full set of adult function words and inflections.
topics.example: Teaching example: Mummy go can link an agent with an action; daddy shoe can signal possession.
topics.confusion: Two adjacent words are not necessarily evidence of complete adult-like syntax.

questions.prompt: How can two-word speech reveal more than vocabulary growth?
questions.shortAnswer: The child combines words into meaningful relations and often uses language-appropriate ordering patterns, showing emerging structural knowledge rather than isolated naming alone.

topics.title: Telegraphic speech
topics.core: Telegraphic speech uses short multiword combinations with many content words but fewer function words or inflections.
topics.explanation: It can express increasingly varied meanings while grammatical detail continues to develop. The term describes a broad pattern, with substantial individual variation.
topics.example: Teaching example: Mummy give ball communicates an event while omitting several adult grammatical elements.
topics.confusion: Missing function words do not imply that the utterance lacks organisation.

topics.title: Overgeneralisation and the Wug test
topics.core: Overgeneralisation applies a learned pattern beyond its conventional range; novel-word tasks test productive knowledge.
topics.explanation: Children can use inflections on unfamiliar forms, supporting the idea that they generalise patterns rather than merely memorise all complete words.
topics.example: Teaching example: A child who says goed applies a regular past-tense pattern to an irregular verb.
topics.confusion: A developmental error can provide evidence of learning, not just failure.

questions.shortAnswer: Successful pluralisation of a novel noun indicates that children can generalise a morphological pattern beyond familiar memorised words.

topics.title: Caretaker speech
topics.core: Caretaker or child-directed speech is speech adapted to interaction with a child.
topics.explanation: It may involve exaggerated prosody, repetition, shorter utterances and responsive interaction, but its forms vary across cultures and contexts.
topics.example: Teaching example: A caregiver repeats a label while following the child's attention to an object.
topics.confusion: One culturally familiar style of baby talk is not a universal prerequisite for acquisition.

questions.prompt: Why should child-directed speech not be defined as universally ungrammatical baby talk?
questions.shortAnswer: Much child-directed speech is grammatical, and caregiver styles vary.

topics.title: Critical and sensitive periods
topics.core: A critical-period hypothesis proposes age-related constraints on language acquisition; sensitive-period accounts allow more gradual changes.
topics.explanation: Different language abilities may show different age patterns. Age-related outcomes interact with experience and learning opportunities, so a single rigid cutoff is too simple.
topics.example: Teaching example: Early and late learners may differ in ultimate pronunciation even when older beginners initially progress quickly.
topics.confusion: A decline in average attainment does not mean adults cannot learn a language successfully.

topics.title: Deprivation evidence
topics.core: Language-deprivation cases inform age questions but contain major confounds.
topics.explanation: Severe isolation often involves trauma, poor care and uncertain developmental histories. Such cases cannot cleanly isolate age from every other influence.
topics.example: Teaching example: A late first-language learner's difficulties may reflect both timing and broader deprivation.
topics.confusion: One unusual case cannot by itself prove a universal biological cutoff.

topics.title: Behaviourist acquisition theory
topics.core: Behaviourist accounts explain language learning through environmental associations, imitation and reinforcement.
topics.explanation: Skinner's operant account emphasises consequences that shape verbal behaviour. It highlights input and learning history, while simple imitation struggles to explain productive novelty.
topics.example: Teaching example: A caregiver's response can reinforce a useful request, yet the child also creates unfamiliar utterances.
topics.confusion: Negative reinforcement removes an aversive condition; it is not the same as punishment.

topics.title: Mentalist and innatist theory
topics.core: Mentalist or innatist approaches propose that language learning depends partly on inborn linguistic capacities.
topics.explanation: Chomskyan accounts connect acquisition with Universal Grammar and the problem of explaining abstract knowledge from limited evidence. Particular formulations and empirical claims remain debated.
topics.example: Teaching example: Children learn structural dependencies that are not taught as explicit rules.
topics.confusion: Innateness does not mean learning occurs without linguistic experience.

questions.shortAnswer: It argues that some acquired knowledge exceeds what input alone straightforwardly explains, motivating innate constraints.

topics.title: Biological theory
topics.core: Biological accounts relate language acquisition to species-specific capacities, maturation and brain development.
topics.explanation: Lenneberg connected language development with biological timing. Modern interpretation requires attention to plasticity, distributed networks and continuing learning rather than an all-or-nothing developmental switch.
topics.example: Teaching example: Children's capacity to acquire accessible spoken or signed language shows biological preparedness interacting with experience.
topics.confusion: Biological contribution does not exclude social or cognitive explanation.

topics.title: Cognitive acquisition theory
topics.core: Cognitive approaches connect language development with general processes such as categorisation, memory and pattern learning.
topics.explanation: Piagetian accounts emphasise links with conceptual development; other cognitive learning views focus on meaningful learning and information processing.

topics.title: Social interactionist theory

topics.title: Nature and nurture

topics.title: Krashen's Monitor Model
topics.core: Krashen's Monitor Model proposes five hypotheses concerning acquisition, learning, monitoring, natural order, input and affect.
topics.explanation: The model distinguishes acquired competence from conscious learning and stresses comprehensible input. Its strong separation of learning and acquisition and the testability of its concepts have been criticised.

topics.title: Interlanguage
topics.core: Interlanguage is a learner's developing linguistic system, with patterns distinct from both the first language and target norms.

questions.shortAnswer: Interlanguage is a learner's developing linguistic system, with patterns distinct from both the first language and target norms.
questions.answer: Interlanguage is a learner's developing linguistic system, with patterns distinct from both the first language and target norms. It can be systematic, changing and variable across contexts. Selinker related its development to transfer, training, strategies, communication and overgeneralisation.

questions.prompt: Why does a repeated learner error sometimes support an interlanguage analysis?
questions.shortAnswer: A regular pattern suggests a developing rule or representation.
questions.answer: A regular pattern suggests a developing rule or representation. Analyse where the form occurs and how it changes rather than treating each instance as unrelated failure.

topics.title: Linguistic universals
topics.core: Linguistic universals are proposed cross-linguistic properties or constraints, studied through typology and theories such as Universal Grammar.
topics.explanation: Typological approaches examine language samples and implicational patterns; generative approaches investigate constraints on possible grammars. L2 access to UG is a debated issue.
topics.example: Teaching example: A typological implication predicts that one structural property is associated with another across languages.
topics.confusion: A frequent cross-linguistic tendency is not automatically an exceptionless universal.

questions.prompt: Explain linguistic universals briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Linguistic universals are proposed cross-linguistic properties or constraints, studied through typology and theories such as Universal Grammar.

keyPoints: Linguistic universals are proposed cross-linguistic properties or constraints, studied through typology and theories such as Universal Grammar.

questions.prompt: How do typological universals and Universal Grammar differ as approaches?
questions.shortAnswer: Typology infers patterns from comparisons of languages.
questions.answer: Typology infers patterns from comparisons of languages. Universal Grammar proposes constraints or principles of the language faculty; their explanations and methods differ.
keyPoints: Typology infers patterns from comparisons of languages.
Universal Grammar proposes constraints or principles of the language faculty; their explanations and methods differ.

topics.title: Acculturation theory
topics.core: Schumann's acculturation account links aspects of second-language development to social and psychological relations with the target-language community.
topics.explanation: Social distance, attitudes and opportunities for contact can constrain learning. The theory offers a contextual perspective but does not fully explain cognitive mechanisms or every classroom setting.
topics.example: Teaching example: A learner may have extensive residence but limited access to interaction with target-language users.
topics.confusion: Residence length does not automatically measure meaningful contact or social inclusion.

questions.prompt: What is acculturation theory?

questions.prompt: Why might years in an L2 environment fail to predict high proficiency?
questions.shortAnswer: Access, social distance, identity, work patterns and interaction opportunities differ.
questions.answer: Access, social distance, identity, work patterns and interaction opportunities differ. Time alone does not reveal the quality or range of language experience.
keyPoints: Access, social distance, identity, work patterns and interaction opportunities differ.
Time alone does not reveal the quality or range of language experience.

topics.title: McLaughlin's cognitive theory
topics.core: McLaughlin treats L2 learning as complex skill development involving controlled and increasingly automatic processing.
topics.explanation: Practice can reorganise knowledge and processing; restructuring can produce temporary performance changes. Attention is limited, so fluency involves efficient access rather than simply more explicit rules.
topics.example: Teaching example: An initially effortful pattern becomes easier to retrieve in a familiar communicative task.
topics.confusion: Automaticity is not identical to perfect accuracy or absence of meaning.

questions.answer: McLaughlin treats L2 learning as complex skill development involving controlled and increasingly automatic processing. Practice can reorganise knowledge and processing; restructuring can produce temporary performance changes. keyPoints: McLaughlin treats L2 learning as complex skill development involving controlled and increasingly automatic processing.

questions.prompt: How can a temporary performance decline occur during learning?
questions.shortAnswer: Restructuring can change an earlier system and temporarily disrupt performance.
questions.answer: Restructuring can change an earlier system and temporarily disrupt performance. A brief decline need not mean that no learning is taking place.
keyPoints: Restructuring can change an earlier system and temporarily disrupt performance.
A brief decline need not mean that no learning is taking place.

topics.title: Sociocultural theory and ZPD
topics.core: Sociocultural theory explains development through mediation and participation in social activity.
topics.explanation: The zone of proximal development concerns what learners can achieve with appropriate support beyond independent performance. Scaffolding should respond to need and be adjusted over time.
topics.example: Teaching example: A partner's prompt helps a learner complete an explanation they cannot yet produce alone.
topics.confusion: ZPD is not simply every task that is difficult.

questions.prompt: Explain sociocultural theory and zpd briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Sociocultural theory explains development through mediation and participation in social activity.
questions.answer: Sociocultural theory explains development through mediation and participation in social activity. keyPoints: Sociocultural theory explains development through mediation and participation in social activity.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes scaffolding from giving a learner the full answer?
questions.shortAnswer: Scaffolding supports the learner's own activity with contingent prompts or tools and can be reduced as independence grows.
questions.answer: Scaffolding supports the learner's own activity with contingent prompts or tools and can be reduced as independence grows. Supplying the answer may leave the learner's processing unchanged.
keyPoints: Scaffolding supports the learner's own activity with contingent prompts or tools and can be reduced as independence grows.
Supplying the answer may leave the learner's processing unchanged.

topics.title: Age and ultimate attainment
topics.core: Age can relate differently to initial learning rate and ultimate attainment.
topics.explanation: Older beginners may progress quickly in some instructed tasks, while earlier sustained exposure can favour later attainment in some domains. Experience, skill and context shape the pattern.
topics.example: Teaching example: An adult may learn classroom vocabulary faster initially while a child develops more target-like pronunciation over time.
topics.confusion: Younger is not automatically better on every measure at every stage.

questions.prompt: Explain age and ultimate attainment briefly.

questions.answer: Age can relate differently to initial learning rate and ultimate attainment. Older beginners may progress quickly in some instructed tasks, while earlier sustained exposure can favour later attainment in some domains. Experience, skill and context shape the pattern.
keyPoints: Age can relate differently to initial learning rate and ultimate attainment.

questions.prompt: Why distinguish rate from ultimate attainment when comparing child and adult learners?
questions.shortAnswer: A group can learn faster initially yet reach a different long-term outcome.
questions.answer: A group can learn faster initially yet reach a different long-term outcome. A short course and many years of exposure answer different age-related questions.
keyPoints: A group can learn faster initially yet reach a different long-term outcome.
A short course and many years of exposure answer different age-related questions.

topics.title: Language aptitude
topics.core: Language aptitude refers to abilities that help explain differences in the ease or rate of language learning.
topics.explanation: Classic components include phonetic coding, grammatical sensitivity, inductive learning and associative memory. Aptitude interacts with tasks and instruction.
topics.example: Teaching example: One learner quickly detects an unfamiliar grammatical pattern; another excels at remembering sound–word associations.
topics.confusion: Aptitude is not a total measure of a person's worth or a fixed guarantee of success.

questions.prompt: What is language aptitude?
questions.shortAnswer: Language aptitude refers to abilities that help explain differences in the ease or rate of language learning.
questions.answer: Language aptitude refers to abilities that help explain differences in the ease or rate of language learning. Classic components include phonetic coding, grammatical sensitivity, inductive learning and associative memory. Aptitude interacts with tasks and instruction.
keyPoints: Language aptitude refers to abilities that help explain differences in the ease or rate of language learning.

questions.prompt: How does aptitude differ from motivation?
questions.shortAnswer: Aptitude concerns abilities relevant to learning; motivation concerns goals, effort and persistence.
questions.answer: Aptitude concerns abilities relevant to learning; motivation concerns goals, effort and persistence. They can interact, but they are different constructs.
keyPoints: Aptitude concerns abilities relevant to learning; motivation concerns goals, effort and persistence.
They can interact, but they are different constructs.

topics.title: Attitude
topics.core: Attitude is an evaluative orientation toward a language, its users or the learning situation.
topics.explanation: Attitudes can influence engagement and be reshaped by experience and social context. Associations with success need careful causal interpretation.
topics.example: Teaching example: A learner's positive view of a classroom community may encourage participation.
topics.confusion: An attitude is not identical to proficiency or an observable amount of effort.

questions.prompt: What is attitude?

questions.answer: Attitude is an evaluative orientation toward a language, its users or the learning situation. Attitudes can influence engagement and be reshaped by experience and social context. Associations with success need careful causal interpretation.
keyPoints: Attitude is an evaluative orientation toward a language, its users or the learning situation.

questions.prompt: Can successful learning change attitude as well as attitude influencing learning?
questions.shortAnswer: Yes.
questions.answer: Yes. The relationship can be reciprocal: experience and achievement may strengthen positive attitudes, while attitudes can affect engagement.
keyPoints: Yes.
The relationship can be reciprocal: experience and achievement may strengthen positive attitudes, while attitudes can affect engagement.

topics.title: Motivation
topics.core: Motivation concerns the direction, intensity and persistence of effort toward language-learning goals.
topics.explanation: Instrumental and integrative orientations concern reasons for learning; intrinsic and extrinsic distinctions concern the source or character of engagement. Motivation changes over time.
topics.example: Teaching example: A learner studies for employment and also enjoys communicating in the language.
topics.confusion: Instrumental reasons do not automatically produce weak learning.

questions.prompt: What is motivation?

questions.answer: Motivation concerns the direction, intensity and persistence of effort toward language-learning goals. Instrumental and integrative orientations concern reasons for learning; intrinsic and extrinsic distinctions concern the source or character of engagement. Motivation changes over time.

questions.prompt: Can instrumental and intrinsic motivation coexist?
questions.shortAnswer: Yes.
questions.answer: Yes. A learner may want a qualification and also enjoy the activity itself. Motivational orientations can overlap and change with experience.
keyPoints: Yes.
A learner may want a qualification and also enjoy the activity itself.
Motivational orientations can overlap and change with experience.

topics.title: Personality, anxiety and willingness to communicate
topics.core: Personality-related factors and anxiety can affect participation and learning opportunities, with effects depending on task and setting.
topics.explanation: Extraversion may support some interaction, while introverted learners may succeed in other tasks. Willingness to communicate changes by topic, partner and perceived safety.
topics.example: Teaching example: A learner speaks freely with a friend but stays silent before an examiner.
topics.confusion: A quiet learner is not necessarily unmotivated or less capable.

questions.prompt: Explain personality, anxiety and willingness to communicate briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Personality-related factors and anxiety can affect participation and learning opportunities, with effects depending on task and setting.

questions.prompt: Why should an examiner-facing silence not be treated as proof of poor language knowledge?
questions.shortAnswer: Anxiety, processing pressure and the social setting can limit access or willingness to speak.
questions.answer: Anxiety, processing pressure and the social setting can limit access or willingness to speak. Performance reflects more than underlying knowledge alone.
keyPoints: Anxiety, processing pressure and the social setting can limit access or willingness to speak.
Performance reflects more than underlying knowledge alone.

topics.title: Cognitive style and learning-style claims
topics.core: Cognitive style describes habitual approaches to processing information; preferences do not establish that matching instruction to a style improves learning.
topics.explanation: Field dependence and independence are classic constructs in the guide. Measures overlap with other abilities, and style categories should not be treated as fixed prescriptions.
topics.example: Teaching example: A learner may prefer diagrams while still benefiting from explanations suited to the subject matter.
topics.confusion: Preference and demonstrated instructional effectiveness are different kinds of evidence.

questions.prompt: Explain cognitive style and learning-style claims briefly.

questions.shortAnswer: It would require a credible interaction showing that learners with different assessed styles benefit from different matched methods.

topics.title: Memory and working memory
topics.core: Memory supports storage and retrieval of language; working memory maintains and manipulates information during ongoing activity.
topics.explanation: Phonological memory can support unfamiliar word forms, while meaningful connections and retrieval affect longer-term access. Capacity is task-dependent rather than a single explanation of success.
topics.example: Teaching example: A learner holds earlier words in mind while interpreting the end of a long sentence.
topics.confusion: Remembering a rule explicitly is not the same as accessing it efficiently in conversation.

questions.prompt: Explain memory and working memory briefly.

questions.prompt: Why can a long sentence be difficult despite containing familiar words?
questions.shortAnswer: Maintaining and integrating its parts places processing demands on working memory and structural interpretation.
questions.answer: Maintaining and integrating its parts places processing demands on working memory and structural interpretation. Vocabulary familiarity alone does not remove those demands.

topics.title: Transfer and transfer of training
topics.core: Transfer uses prior knowledge in new learning; transfer of training concerns influences of previous teaching or practice.
topics.explanation: Similarity can support performance, while differences or learned routines can encourage non-target patterns. Not every learner error originates in L1.
topics.example: Teaching example: A repeatedly drilled answer format may be overused in conversation even where it is unnatural.
topics.confusion: L1 transfer and transfer of training have different sources.

topics.title: Intelligence and language learning
topics.core: Intelligence measures can relate to some language-learning tasks, especially academic and analytical ones, without explaining all communicative development.
topics.explanation: Different abilities and opportunities contribute to outcomes. Multiple-intelligences proposals should not be treated as proof that matching fixed learner types improves instruction.
topics.example: Teaching example: An analytic test score may relate to grammar study more directly than to comfortable conversation.
topics.confusion: A low score on one intelligence test does not imply inability to acquire or use language.

questions.prompt: Explain intelligence and language learning briefly.

topics.title: Fossilization and stabilisation
topics.core: Fossilization describes persistent stabilisation of interlanguage features despite opportunities for further development.
topics.explanation: Permanence is difficult to establish; a long-lasting pattern may change with new conditions. Distinguish a short plateau from stronger claims of fossilization.
topics.example: Teaching example: A learner persistently omits an inflection over many contexts and years.
topics.confusion: One repeated error or brief learning plateau is insufficient evidence of permanent cessation.

questions.prompt: Why is fossilization difficult to prove empirically?
questions.shortAnswer: It requires a strong claim about persistence, yet researchers cannot observe all future development.

topics.title: Identity, investment and learner strategies
topics.core: Learner identity and access to valued activities shape how motivation can be put into practice.
topics.explanation: Investment relates participation to social identities and resources. Strategies include deliberate ways of organising learning or communication, whose effectiveness depends on task and context.
topics.example: Teaching example: An interested learner may speak little because peers exclude their contributions.
topics.confusion: Low participation is not always an individual motivational failure.

questions.prompt: How can a learner be motivated but have little chance to improve through interaction?
questions.shortAnswer: Social exclusion or unequal access can restrict participation despite strong desire.

topics.title: Neurolinguistics and lateralisation
topics.core: Neurolinguistics investigates relationships between language processes and brain organisation.
topics.explanation: Language is often left-lateralised, but multiple regions and pathways contribute; right-hemisphere processes can support prosody and discourse. Individual patterns vary.
topics.example: Teaching example: A language task can involve a network rather than one isolated point in the brain.
topics.confusion: Lateralisation does not mean one hemisphere performs all language alone.

questions.prompt: Explain neurolinguistics and lateralisation briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Neurolinguistics investigates relationships between language processes and brain organisation.

questions.prompt: Why is left-lateralised language not equivalent to saying the right hemisphere has no role?
questions.shortAnswer: Lateralisation describes relative specialisation, not exclusive control.
questions.answer: Lateralisation describes relative specialisation, not exclusive control. Language activity involves interacting systems, including functions often associated with the right hemisphere.

topics.title: Aphasia
topics.core: Aphasia is an acquired language disorder associated with brain damage that can affect speaking, comprehension, reading or writing.
topics.explanation: Profiles vary with the affected network and individual history. Language impairment should not be equated with global loss of intelligence.
topics.example: Teaching example: A person may struggle to retrieve words after a stroke while retaining many other abilities.
topics.confusion: Aphasia is not simply a disorder of the speech muscles.

questions.prompt: What is aphasia?
questions.shortAnswer: Aphasia is an acquired language disorder associated with brain damage that can affect speaking, comprehension, reading or writing.

questions.prompt: How can aphasia affect a person who can still move the speech organs?
questions.shortAnswer: The impairment concerns language representations or processing, such as word retrieval or comprehension, rather than only the motor ability to produce sound.

topics.title: Broca-type and Wernicke-type profiles
topics.core: Classic Broca-type aphasia often involves effortful nonfluent production; Wernicke-type profiles often involve fluent but impaired meaningful communication and comprehension.
topics.explanation: These are useful historical clinical patterns, not perfectly separate language boxes. Symptoms and lesion locations do not map one to one in every individual.

topics.title: Dyslexia
topics.core: Dyslexia involves persistent difficulty with accurate or fluent word reading and related literacy processes.
topics.explanation: Developmental and acquired reading difficulties should be distinguished. Phonological processing often matters, while profiles vary; intelligence alone does not define reading skill.
topics.example: Teaching example: A learner may understand spoken explanations well but struggle to decode unfamiliar written words.

topics.title: Language therapy
topics.core: Language therapy aims to support communication by restoring skills where possible and developing compensatory strategies.
topics.explanation: Intervention follows assessment of the individual's needs and goals and may involve family, educational or clinical support. Outcomes vary and improvement can continue beyond an early recovery phase.
topics.example: Teaching example: Practising word retrieval and using communication aids can address different functional needs.
topics.confusion: Language therapy is not one universal drill for every language difficulty.

topics.title: Plasticity and modularity
topics.core: Plasticity concerns change in brain organisation; modularity concerns the degree to which language processes are specialised.

topics.title: Research and its quality
topics.core: Research is systematic inquiry using evidence to answer questions or develop knowledge.
topics.explanation: Good research is systematic, rigorous, empirical, critical, and sufficiently transparent to be checked. Appropriate control and valid measurement strengthen claims; perfect control is rarely possible in human settings.
topics.example: Record classroom participation using defined rules, then analyse the pattern rather than relying on a teacher's impression.
topics.confusion: Following steps neatly does not make a weak measurement valid.

questions.prompt: Explain research and its quality briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Research is systematic inquiry using evidence to answer questions or develop knowledge.
questions.answer: Research is systematic inquiry using evidence to answer questions or develop knowledge. Good research is systematic, rigorous, empirical, critical, and sufficiently transparent to be checked.
keyPoints: Research is systematic inquiry using evidence to answer questions or develop knowledge.

questions.prompt: A teacher says students seem more fluent. What would turn that impression into research?
questions.shortAnswer: Define fluency, formulate a focused question, collect suitable performance evidence, analyse it systematically and acknowledge alternative explanations.
questions.answer: Define fluency, formulate a focused question, collect suitable performance evidence, analyse it systematically and acknowledge alternative explanations.
keyPoints: Define fluency, formulate a focused question, collect suitable performance evidence, analyse it systematically and acknowledge alternative explanations.

topics.title: Qualitative research
topics.core: Qualitative research interprets meanings, experiences and practices in context.
topics.explanation: It commonly works with interviews, observations and texts. The researcher explains how evidence supports an interpretation, including cases that challenge it.
topics.example: Interview quiet learners to understand how they experience speaking in class.
topics.confusion: Qualitative does not mean unsystematic or simply non-numerical description.

questions.prompt: What is qualitative research?
questions.shortAnswer: Qualitative research interprets meanings, experiences and practices in context.
questions.answer: Qualitative research interprets meanings, experiences and practices in context. It commonly works with interviews, observations and texts.
keyPoints: Qualitative research interprets meanings, experiences and practices in context.

questions.prompt: Why might interviews help explain classroom silence better than a score alone?
questions.shortAnswer: Interviews can reveal meanings such as fear of peer judgment that a score does not capture.
questions.answer: Interviews can reveal meanings such as fear of peer judgment that a score does not capture. Accounts still need contextual analysis and do not directly prove actual behaviour.
keyPoints: Interviews can reveal meanings such as fear of peer judgment that a score does not capture.
Accounts still need contextual analysis and do not directly prove actual behaviour.

topics.title: Quantitative research
topics.core: Quantitative research measures variables and analyses numerical patterns, differences or relationships.
topics.explanation: Specify what is measured, how scores are produced, and what comparison answers the question. Numerical precision does not compensate for a poor construct measure.
topics.example: Compare fluency scores before and after a teaching intervention.
topics.confusion: A quantitative study need not be an experiment.

questions.prompt: What is quantitative research?
questions.shortAnswer: Quantitative research measures variables and analyses numerical patterns, differences or relationships.
questions.answer: Quantitative research measures variables and analyses numerical patterns, differences or relationships. Specify what is measured, how scores are produced, and what comparison answers the question.
keyPoints: Quantitative research measures variables and analyses numerical patterns, differences or relationships.

questions.prompt: Is counting the number of English words in student essays quantitative research?
questions.shortAnswer: It can be quantitative if the counts answer a clear question through systematic sampling and analysis.
questions.answer: It can be quantitative if the counts answer a clear question through systematic sampling and analysis. Counting alone is insufficient without a reasoned design and interpretation.
keyPoints: It can be quantitative if the counts answer a clear question through systematic sampling and analysis.
Counting alone is insufficient without a reasoned design and interpretation.

topics.title: Mixed methods
topics.core: Mixed methods integrates qualitative and quantitative evidence in one investigation.
topics.explanation: The strands may be sequential, concurrent, embedded or multiphase. Explain where they connect: design, sampling, analysis or interpretation.
topics.example: Compare speaking scores, then interview learners to explain contrasting gains.
topics.confusion: A questionnaire with an open comment box is not automatically a mixed-methods study.

questions.prompt: Explain mixed methods briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Mixed methods integrates qualitative and quantitative evidence in one investigation.
questions.answer: Mixed methods integrates qualitative and quantitative evidence in one investigation. The strands may be sequential, concurrent, embedded or multiphase.
keyPoints: Mixed methods integrates qualitative and quantitative evidence in one investigation.

questions.prompt: You collect test scores and interviews but discuss them separately. What is missing?
questions.shortAnswer: A clear integration of the two strands.
questions.answer: A clear integration of the two strands. Explain how interview findings help interpret, challenge or extend the numerical results.
keyPoints: A clear integration of the two strands.
Explain how interview findings help interpret, challenge or extend the numerical results.

topics.title: Research classifications
topics.core: A study can receive different labels according to its purpose, objective, evidence, timing and design.
topics.explanation: Basic research primarily develops knowledge; applied research addresses a practical problem. Exploratory, descriptive, correlational and explanatory labels concern the aim. These classifications can overlap.
topics.example: A classroom experiment may be applied, quantitative, explanatory and longitudinal.
topics.confusion: Basic research can have practical consequences; applied research can develop theory.

questions.prompt: Explain research classifications briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: A study can receive different labels according to its purpose, objective, evidence, timing and design.
questions.answer: A study can receive different labels according to its purpose, objective, evidence, timing and design. Basic research primarily develops knowledge; applied research addresses a practical problem.
keyPoints: A study can receive different labels according to its purpose, objective, evidence, timing and design.

questions.prompt: Can a study be both applied and qualitative?
questions.shortAnswer: Yes.
questions.answer: Yes. Applied describes its practical purpose, while qualitative describes its approach to evidence and interpretation. They classify different aspects of the study.
keyPoints: Yes.
Applied describes its practical purpose, while qualitative describes its approach to evidence and interpretation.
They classify different aspects of the study.

topics.title: Induction and deduction
topics.core: Induction develops explanations from observations; deduction tests implications of existing explanations.
topics.explanation: Inductive reasoning moves from cases to patterns. Deductive reasoning moves from theory through a prediction to evidence. Studies may alternate between them.
topics.example: Develop a model of speaking anxiety from interviews, then test its predictions in another group.
topics.confusion: A supported prediction does not prove a theory universally.

questions.prompt: Explain induction and deduction briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Induction develops explanations from observations; deduction tests implications of existing explanations.
questions.answer: Induction develops explanations from observations; deduction tests implications of existing explanations. Inductive reasoning moves from cases to patterns.
keyPoints: Induction develops explanations from observations; deduction tests implications of existing explanations.

questions.prompt: You start with a theory and predict higher fluency after practice. Which reasoning is this?
questions.shortAnswer: Deductive reasoning: the prediction follows from an existing explanation and is checked against data.
questions.answer: Deductive reasoning: the prediction follows from an existing explanation and is checked against data. Unexpected results may prompt inductive revision.
keyPoints: Deductive reasoning: the prediction follows from an existing explanation and is checked against data.
Unexpected results may prompt inductive revision.

topics.title: Longitudinal and cross-sectional designs
topics.core: Longitudinal designs collect evidence over time; cross-sectional designs examine a population or groups at one time.
topics.explanation: Panel designs repeatedly study the same individuals. Trend designs can use different samples from the same population; cohort designs focus on a group sharing a starting feature. Timing is separate from whether a study is experimental.
topics.example: Follow the same learners across semesters to track vocabulary development, or compare year groups at one time for a cross-sectional snapshot.
topics.confusion: A difference between year groups does not directly measure change within the same individuals.

questions.prompt: Explain longitudinal and cross-sectional designs briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Longitudinal designs collect evidence over time; cross-sectional designs examine a population or groups at one time.
questions.answer: Longitudinal designs collect evidence over time; cross-sectional designs examine a population or groups at one time. Panel designs repeatedly study the same individuals.
keyPoints: Longitudinal designs collect evidence over time; cross-sectional designs examine a population or groups at one time.

questions.prompt: Why might a panel design help investigate language development?
questions.shortAnswer: Repeated observations of the same learners can show individual change over time.
questions.answer: Repeated observations of the same learners can show individual change over time. Comparable measures and attention to attrition are needed; observed change does not by itself establish its cause.
keyPoints: Repeated observations of the same learners can show individual change over time.
Comparable measures and attention to attrition are needed; observed change does not by itself establish its cause.

topics.title: Narrative inquiry
topics.core: Narrative inquiry studies how people organise and interpret experience through stories.
topics.explanation: Attend to sequence, turning points, identity and the setting in which a story is told. A story is a situated account rather than a transparent record of every event.
topics.example: Ask a teacher to narrate becoming an English teacher and analyse how key events shape professional identity.
topics.confusion: Narrative inquiry focuses on story construction, not merely extracting isolated themes.

questions.prompt: What is narrative inquiry?
questions.shortAnswer: Narrative inquiry studies how people organise and interpret experience through stories.
questions.answer: Narrative inquiry studies how people organise and interpret experience through stories. Attend to sequence, turning points, identity and the setting in which a story is told.
keyPoints: Narrative inquiry studies how people organise and interpret experience through stories.

questions.prompt: How would you investigate a learner's changing relationship with English through narrative inquiry?
questions.shortAnswer: Invite a learning-history account, examine turning points and identity positions, and relate the telling to its social context.
questions.answer: Invite a learning-history account, examine turning points and identity positions, and relate the telling to its social context. Preserve the sequence and the learner's meaning-making.
keyPoints: Invite a learning-history account, examine turning points and identity positions, and relate the telling to its social context.
Preserve the sequence and the learner's meaning-making.

topics.title: Case study
topics.core: A case study examines a bounded case in depth within its real context.
topics.explanation: A case may be a person, class, programme or institution. Define boundaries of place, time and activity and use suitable evidence such as interviews, observations and documents.
topics.example: Study one Grade 8 class's group work during one academic year.
topics.confusion: A case is a bounded unit; it is not automatically a representative sample.

questions.prompt: What is case study?
questions.shortAnswer: A case study examines a bounded case in depth within its real context.
questions.answer: A case study examines a bounded case in depth within its real context. A case may be a person, class, programme or institution.
keyPoints: A case study examines a bounded case in depth within its real context.

questions.prompt: Why is 'students in Bangladesh' too vague as a case-study boundary?
questions.shortAnswer: It does not identify a specific bounded case.
questions.answer: It does not identify a specific bounded case. Specify a class, institution, group or programme and define its time, place and activity boundaries.
keyPoints: It does not identify a specific bounded case.
Specify a class, institution, group or programme and define its time, place and activity boundaries.

topics.title: Case-study types
topics.core: Intrinsic studies examine a case for its own interest; instrumental studies use it to understand a wider issue.
topics.explanation: Collective studies compare cases. Embedded studies examine subunits; holistic studies treat the case as one unit. Longitudinal refers to time and can combine with the other labels.
topics.example: One school may be an instrumental case with three embedded classroom units.
topics.confusion: These labels are based on different dimensions and are not mutually exclusive.

questions.prompt: Explain case-study types briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Intrinsic studies examine a case for its own interest; instrumental studies use it to understand a wider issue.
questions.answer: Intrinsic studies examine a case for its own interest; instrumental studies use it to understand a wider issue. Collective studies compare cases.
