questions.shortAnswer: A post-creole continuum is a range of socially related varieties between more creole-like and more lexifier-like forms.
questions.answer: A post-creole continuum is a range of socially related varieties between more creole-like and more lexifier-like forms. Basilect, mesolect and acrolect name relative positions in such a continuum. Speakers may vary by situation and access.
keyPoints: A post-creole continuum is a range of socially related varieties between more creole-like and more lexifier-like forms.
Basilect, mesolect and acrolect name relative positions in such a continuum. Speakers may vary by situation and access.

questions.prompt: How do basilect, mesolect and acrolect differ?
questions.shortAnswer: They identify varieties relatively furthest from, intermediate to and closest to the socially prestigious lexifier-associated variety, in a particular continuum.
questions.answer: They identify varieties relatively furthest from, intermediate to and closest to the socially prestigious lexifier-associated variety, in a particular continuum.
keyPoints: They identify varieties relatively furthest from, intermediate to and closest to the socially prestigious lexifier-associated variety, in a particular continuum.

questions.prompt: Explain lexifier and decreolization briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: A lexifier supplies much of a contact language's vocabulary; decreolization refers to convergence toward a lexifier-associated prestigious variety.
questions.answer: A lexifier supplies much of a contact language's vocabulary; decreolization refers to convergence toward a lexifier-associated prestigious variety. The contribution of vocabulary does not make the resulting language merely a corrupt form of its lexifier. Social conditions shape convergence and maintenance.
keyPoints: A lexifier supplies much of a contact language's vocabulary; decreolization refers to convergence toward a lexifier-associated prestigious variety.
The contribution of vocabulary does not make the resulting language merely a corrupt form of its lexifier. Social conditions shape convergence and maintenance.

questions.prompt: Why does having English-derived vocabulary not make a creole simply English with errors?
questions.shortAnswer: The creole has its own systematic grammatical and social history; vocabulary source alone does not determine the identity or rules of a language.
questions.answer: The creole has its own systematic grammatical and social history; vocabulary source alone does not determine the identity or rules of a language.
keyPoints: The creole has its own systematic grammatical and social history; vocabulary source alone does not determine the identity or rules of a language.

questions.prompt: Explain tree and wave models briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: A tree represents genealogical branching; a wave represents diffusion of innovations across communities.
questions.answer: A tree represents genealogical branching; a wave represents diffusion of innovations across communities. The models emphasise inheritance and contact respectively. Contact can cross genealogical boundaries, so neither model alone captures every relation.
keyPoints: A tree represents genealogical branching; a wave represents diffusion of innovations across communities.
The models emphasise inheritance and contact respectively. Contact can cross genealogical boundaries, so neither model alone captures every relation.

questions.prompt: What kind of evidence is a wave model better placed to represent than a simple family tree?
questions.shortAnswer: Overlapping innovations spreading through contact across dialect areas, rather than only clean splits into separate descendant branches.
questions.answer: Overlapping innovations spreading through contact across dialect areas, rather than only clean splits into separate descendant branches.
keyPoints: Overlapping innovations spreading through contact across dialect areas, rather than only clean splits into separate descendant branches.

questions.prompt: Explain isogloss briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: An isogloss maps the geographical distribution boundary of a linguistic feature.
questions.answer: An isogloss maps the geographical distribution boundary of a linguistic feature. Several isoglosses may cluster into a bundle, helping identify dialect areas. Different features need not have identical boundaries.
keyPoints: An isogloss maps the geographical distribution boundary of a linguistic feature.
Several isoglosses may cluster into a bundle, helping identify dialect areas. Different features need not have identical boundaries.

questions.prompt: Why are bundles of isoglosses more informative than a single line?
questions.shortAnswer: Several shared feature distributions can support a broader dialect pattern, whereas one feature may have a distinctive local history.
questions.answer: Several shared feature distributions can support a broader dialect pattern, whereas one feature may have a distinctive local history.
keyPoints: Several shared feature distributions can support a broader dialect pattern, whereas one feature may have a distinctive local history.

questions.prompt: Explain diffusion and social networks briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Diffusion is the spread of linguistic innovations through contact and social relations.
questions.answer: Diffusion is the spread of linguistic innovations through contact and social relations. Access, prestige, identity and networks affect adoption. Spread need not be uniform or form perfectly circular waves.
keyPoints: Diffusion is the spread of linguistic innovations through contact and social relations.
Access, prestige, identity and networks affect adoption. Spread need not be uniform or form perfectly circular waves.

questions.prompt: Why might a nearby community resist an innovation that spreads elsewhere?
questions.shortAnswer: Its networks, identities or attitudes may favour different norms.
questions.answer: Its networks, identities or attitudes may favour different norms. Social boundaries can reduce diffusion even when physical distance is small.
keyPoints: Its networks, identities or attitudes may favour different norms. Social boundaries can reduce diffusion even when physical distance is small.

questions.prompt: Explain diglossia briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Diglossia involves a relatively stable functional distribution of varieties or languages within a community.
questions.answer: Diglossia involves a relatively stable functional distribution of varieties or languages within a community. Ferguson's classic account contrasts high and low varieties; later usage extends the concept. The labels refer to social functions and prestige.
keyPoints: Diglossia involves a relatively stable functional distribution of varieties or languages within a community.
Ferguson's classic account contrasts high and low varieties; later usage extends the concept. The labels refer to social functions and prestige.

questions.prompt: How does diglossia differ from an individual's bilingual ability?
questions.shortAnswer: Diglossia concerns the community's functional allocation of codes, while bilingualism concerns use or knowledge of two languages; they can coexist without being identical.
questions.answer: Diglossia concerns the community's functional allocation of codes, while bilingualism concerns use or knowledge of two languages; they can coexist without being identical.
keyPoints: Diglossia concerns the community's functional allocation of codes, while bilingualism concerns use or knowledge of two languages; they can coexist without being identical.

questions.prompt: Explain bilingualism briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Bilingualism is the use or knowledge of two languages by individuals or communities.
questions.answer: Bilingualism is the use or knowledge of two languages by individuals or communities. Competence varies across skills, domains and time. Balanced native-like proficiency in every domain is not necessary.
keyPoints: Bilingualism is the use or knowledge of two languages by individuals or communities.
Competence varies across skills, domains and time. Balanced native-like proficiency in every domain is not necessary.

questions.prompt: Can someone be bilingual while reading better in one language and speaking better in another?
questions.shortAnswer: Yes.
questions.answer: Yes. Language skills and domains of use are often unevenly distributed; bilingualism is not an all-or-nothing equal-proficiency condition.
keyPoints: Yes. Language skills and domains of use are often unevenly distributed; bilingualism is not an all-or-nothing equal-proficiency condition.

questions.prompt: Explain simultaneous and sequential bilingualism briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Simultaneous bilingual development begins with two languages early together; sequential development adds another after initial first-language development.
questions.answer: Simultaneous bilingual development begins with two languages early together; sequential development adds another after initial first-language development. The timing distinction does not predict identical outcomes for all learners. Input, use and social conditions matter.
keyPoints: Simultaneous bilingual development begins with two languages early together; sequential development adds another after initial first-language development.
The timing distinction does not predict identical outcomes for all learners. Input, use and social conditions matter.

questions.prompt: What information would help distinguish simultaneous from sequential bilingual development?
questions.shortAnswer: The child's language-exposure history and timing of meaningful acquisition, rather than just current proficiency in the two languages.
questions.answer: The child's language-exposure history and timing of meaningful acquisition, rather than just current proficiency in the two languages.
keyPoints: The child's language-exposure history and timing of meaningful acquisition, rather than just current proficiency in the two languages.

questions.prompt: Explain multilingualism and domains briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Multilingualism concerns the use or knowledge of multiple languages, at individual or societal levels.
questions.answer: Multilingualism concerns the use or knowledge of multiple languages, at individual or societal levels. A society may distribute languages across home, education, work or worship without every member speaking every language.
keyPoints: Multilingualism concerns the use or knowledge of multiple languages, at individual or societal levels.
A society may distribute languages across home, education, work or worship without every member speaking every language.

questions.prompt: Can a multilingual society contain monolingual individuals?
questions.shortAnswer: Yes.
questions.answer: Yes. Multilingualism may describe the community's repertoire and distribution of languages, even if some individuals use only one.
keyPoints: Yes. Multilingualism may describe the community's repertoire and distribution of languages, even if some individuals use only one.

questions.prompt: Explain code-switching briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Code-switching alternates languages or varieties within an interaction or utterance.
questions.answer: Code-switching alternates languages or varieties within an interaction or utterance. Switching may mark topic, audience, solidarity, stance or clarification. Linguistic competence and social purposes both matter.
keyPoints: Code-switching alternates languages or varieties within an interaction or utterance.
Switching may mark topic, audience, solidarity, stance or clarification. Linguistic competence and social purposes both matter.

questions.prompt: Why might a fluent bilingual deliberately switch language mid-conversation?
questions.shortAnswer: To signal a relationship, quote another voice, mark a topic shift, clarify a point or position an identity; the local interaction determines the interpretation.
questions.answer: To signal a relationship, quote another voice, mark a topic shift, clarify a point or position an identity; the local interaction determines the interpretation.
keyPoints: To signal a relationship, quote another voice, mark a topic shift, clarify a point or position an identity; the local interaction determines the interpretation.

questions.prompt: Explain types of code-switching briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Inter-sentential switching occurs across sentence boundaries; intra-sentential switching occurs within a sentence.
questions.answer: Inter-sentential switching occurs across sentence boundaries; intra-sentential switching occurs within a sentence. Tag-switching inserts a tag or discourse marker. Situational and metaphorical labels concern social motivation rather than sentence position.
keyPoints: Inter-sentential switching occurs across sentence boundaries; intra-sentential switching occurs within a sentence.
Tag-switching inserts a tag or discourse marker. Situational and metaphorical labels concern social motivation rather than sentence position.

questions.prompt: Can the same switch be both intra-sentential and metaphorical?
questions.shortAnswer: Yes.
questions.answer: Yes. Intra-sentential identifies where the switch occurs, while metaphorical concerns a shift in social meaning or stance within the interaction.
keyPoints: Yes. Intra-sentential identifies where the switch occurs, while metaphorical concerns a shift in social meaning or stance within the interaction.

questions.prompt: Explain code-mixing and the matrix language briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Code-mixing commonly refers to combining elements from different languages within an utterance.
questions.answer: Code-mixing commonly refers to combining elements from different languages within an utterance. Terminology overlaps with code-switching across frameworks. Matrix-language approaches ask which language supplies the grammatical frame and which contributes embedded material.
keyPoints: Code-mixing commonly refers to combining elements from different languages within an utterance.
Terminology overlaps with code-switching across frameworks. Matrix-language approaches ask which language supplies the grammatical frame and which contributes embedded material.

questions.prompt: Why should a researcher define code-mixing before counting it in a classroom study?
questions.shortAnswer: Different frameworks classify mixed utterances differently.
questions.answer: Different frameworks classify mixed utterances differently. An explicit definition makes examples, coding and comparisons interpretable and reproducible.
keyPoints: Different frameworks classify mixed utterances differently. An explicit definition makes examples, coding and comparisons interpretable and reproducible.

questions.prompt: Explain insertion, alternation and congruent lexicalization briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: These are analytical patterns for different forms of bilingual combination.
questions.answer: These are analytical patterns for different forms of bilingual combination. Insertion places material within a frame; alternation moves between structures; congruent lexicalization involves shared structural patterns filled by material from both languages.
keyPoints: These are analytical patterns for different forms of bilingual combination.
Insertion places material within a frame; alternation moves between structures; congruent lexicalization involves shared structural patterns filled by material from both languages.

questions.prompt: What makes insertion different from simply switching between two full clauses?
questions.shortAnswer: Insertion integrates material into an existing grammatical frame, whereas full-clause alternation can involve a transition between larger structures associated with different languages.
questions.answer: Insertion integrates material into an existing grammatical frame, whereas full-clause alternation can involve a transition between larger structures associated with different languages.
keyPoints: Insertion integrates material into an existing grammatical frame, whereas full-clause alternation can involve a transition between larger structures associated with different languages.

questions.prompt: Explain borrowing briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Borrowing incorporates linguistic material into another language's conventional repertoire.
questions.answer: Borrowing incorporates linguistic material into another language's conventional repertoire. Loanwords can become socially established and may undergo phonological or morphological adaptation. Speakers need not be bilingual to use established loans.
keyPoints: Borrowing incorporates linguistic material into another language's conventional repertoire.
Loanwords can become socially established and may undergo phonological or morphological adaptation. Speakers need not be bilingual to use established loans.

questions.prompt: How can borrowing differ from a momentary code-switch?
questions.shortAnswer: A borrowing is established in the recipient language's usage, while a code-switch concerns an interactional use of multiple codes; ambiguous cases require contextual and community evidence.
questions.answer: A borrowing is established in the recipient language's usage, while a code-switch concerns an interactional use of multiple codes; ambiguous cases require contextual and community evidence.
keyPoints: A borrowing is established in the recipient language's usage, while a code-switch concerns an interactional use of multiple codes; ambiguous cases require contextual and community evidence.

questions.prompt: Explain loanwords, blends and calques briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: A loanword borrows form; a loan translation or calque translates component meanings; loan-blends combine borrowed and recipient material.
questions.answer: A loanword borrows form; a loan translation or calque translates component meanings; loan-blends combine borrowed and recipient material. Borrowing categories concern the relation between imported and substituted material. Not every newly blended word is a cross-language loan-blend.
keyPoints: A loanword borrows form; a loan translation or calque translates component meanings; loan-blends combine borrowed and recipient material.
Borrowing categories concern the relation between imported and substituted material. Not every newly blended word is a cross-language loan-blend.

questions.prompt: Why is a calque different from importing a foreign word unchanged?
questions.shortAnswer: A calque reproduces an expression's structure or meaning through recipient-language material, rather than importing its complete foreign form.
questions.answer: A calque reproduces an expression's structure or meaning through recipient-language material, rather than importing its complete foreign form.
keyPoints: A calque reproduces an expression's structure or meaning through recipient-language material, rather than importing its complete foreign form.

questions.prompt: Explain language planning briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Language planning is deliberate activity intended to influence language functions, forms or acquisition.
questions.answer: Language planning is deliberate activity intended to influence language functions, forms or acquisition. It can be carried out by states, institutions and local actors. Plans interact with existing practices, resources and attitudes.
keyPoints: Language planning is deliberate activity intended to influence language functions, forms or acquisition.
It can be carried out by states, institutions and local actors. Plans interact with existing practices, resources and attitudes.

questions.prompt: Why might a language plan fail despite an official announcement?
questions.shortAnswer: Implementation depends on resources, teacher preparation, public attitudes, institutional incentives and the fit between the plan and everyday practices.
questions.answer: Implementation depends on resources, teacher preparation, public attitudes, institutional incentives and the fit between the plan and everyday practices.
keyPoints: Implementation depends on resources, teacher preparation, public attitudes, institutional incentives and the fit between the plan and everyday practices.

questions.prompt: Explain status, corpus and acquisition planning briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Status planning concerns functions, corpus planning concerns linguistic forms, and acquisition planning concerns learning and users.
questions.answer: Status planning concerns functions, corpus planning concerns linguistic forms, and acquisition planning concerns learning and users. The categories can work together within a policy. New public functions may require terminology, materials and teaching.
keyPoints: Status planning concerns functions, corpus planning concerns linguistic forms, and acquisition planning concerns learning and users.
The categories can work together within a policy. New public functions may require terminology, materials and teaching.

questions.prompt: Classify creating technical vocabulary and training teachers to teach it.
questions.shortAnswer: Terminology development is corpus planning; increasing teachers' and learners' ability to use it is acquisition planning.
questions.answer: Terminology development is corpus planning; increasing teachers' and learners' ability to use it is acquisition planning. Their classroom role also relates to status planning.
keyPoints: Terminology development is corpus planning; increasing teachers' and learners' ability to use it is acquisition planning. Their classroom role also relates to status planning.

questions.prompt: Explain language policy and ideology briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Language policy includes decisions and practices shaping which codes are used, valued or learned.
questions.answer: Language policy includes decisions and practices shaping which codes are used, valued or learned. Ideologies can frame one language as unity, progress or authenticity while marginalising others. Examine both explicit rules and institutional practice.
keyPoints: Language policy includes decisions and practices shaping which codes are used, valued or learned.
Ideologies can frame one language as unity, progress or authenticity while marginalising others. Examine both explicit rules and institutional practice.

questions.prompt: How can a policy be unequal even if it never explicitly bans a minority language?
questions.shortAnswer: Resource allocation, assessment, employment rules or medium-of-instruction requirements may systematically privilege another language and restrict participation.
questions.answer: Resource allocation, assessment, employment rules or medium-of-instruction requirements may systematically privilege another language and restrict participation.
keyPoints: Resource allocation, assessment, employment rules or medium-of-instruction requirements may systematically privilege another language and restrict participation.

questions.prompt: Explain critical language policy briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Critical language policy examines how policies reproduce or challenge unequal power.
questions.answer: Critical language policy examines how policies reproduce or challenge unequal power. It asks whose interests and rights policies serve, while attending to local agency and negotiation rather than assuming people are passive.
keyPoints: Critical language policy examines how policies reproduce or challenge unequal power.
It asks whose interests and rights policies serve, while attending to local agency and negotiation rather than assuming people are passive.

questions.prompt: What would a critical policy analysis add to checking whether a rule was implemented?
questions.shortAnswer: It would examine who benefits, who bears costs, how inequality is reproduced, and how people negotiate or resist the rule.
questions.answer: It would examine who benefits, who bears costs, how inequality is reproduced, and how people negotiate or resist the rule.
keyPoints: It would examine who benefits, who bears costs, how inequality is reproduced, and how people negotiate or resist the rule.

questions.prompt: Explain analysing a policy case briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: A policy case connects stated aims, implementation practices, resources and social effects.
questions.answer: A policy case connects stated aims, implementation practices, resources and social effects. Identify stakeholders and evidence about access and outcomes. Distinguish the policy text from classroom enactment.
keyPoints: A policy case connects stated aims, implementation practices, resources and social effects.
Identify stakeholders and evidence about access and outcomes. Distinguish the policy text from classroom enactment.

questions.prompt: How would you investigate whether a bilingual school policy supports both languages?
questions.shortAnswer: Analyse policy documents, observe teaching, examine materials and assessment, and interview participants.
questions.answer: Analyse policy documents, observe teaching, examine materials and assessment, and interview participants. Compare actual opportunities and resources for each language.
keyPoints: Analyse policy documents, observe teaching, examine materials and assessment, and interview participants. Compare actual opportunities and resources for each language.

questions.prompt: Explain orderly heterogeneity briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Orderly heterogeneity means linguistic variation is structured rather than random.
questions.answer: Orderly heterogeneity means linguistic variation is structured rather than random. Forms can vary with linguistic environments, speakers, situations and social meanings. A variable pattern can still be rule-governed.
keyPoints: Orderly heterogeneity means linguistic variation is structured rather than random.
Forms can vary with linguistic environments, speakers, situations and social meanings. A variable pattern can still be rule-governed.

questions.prompt: How could two pronunciations of the same suffix both fit a systematic account?
questions.shortAnswer: Their occurrence may be conditioned by phonological environments and social use.
questions.answer: Their occurrence may be conditioned by phonological environments and social use. Analyse distributions and constraints rather than labelling all variation careless.
keyPoints: Their occurrence may be conditioned by phonological environments and social use. Analyse distributions and constraints rather than labelling all variation careless.

questions.prompt: Explain variation and change briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Variation concerns coexisting alternatives; change concerns shifts in their distribution over time.
questions.answer: Variation concerns coexisting alternatives; change concerns shifts in their distribution over time. Not all variation becomes change. Age patterns can reflect ongoing change or age-grading, so stronger claims need appropriate temporal evidence.
keyPoints: Variation concerns coexisting alternatives; change concerns shifts in their distribution over time.
Not all variation becomes change. Age patterns can reflect ongoing change or age-grading, so stronger claims need appropriate temporal evidence.

questions.prompt: Why is real-time evidence useful when interpreting an age difference in speech?
questions.shortAnswer: It helps distinguish an ongoing community change from a recurring life-stage pattern in which speakers alter their behaviour as they age.
questions.answer: It helps distinguish an ongoing community change from a recurring life-stage pattern in which speakers alter their behaviour as they age.
keyPoints: It helps distinguish an ongoing community change from a recurring life-stage pattern in which speakers alter their behaviour as they age.

questions.prompt: Explain levels and mechanisms of change briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Change can affect sounds, word structure, syntax, vocabulary and meaning.
questions.answer: Change can affect sounds, word structure, syntax, vocabulary and meaning. Contact, analogy, internal patterns and social evaluation can interact. Distinguish an example of different languages from evidence of historical change within one language.
keyPoints: Change can affect sounds, word structure, syntax, vocabulary and meaning.
Contact, analogy, internal patterns and social evaluation can interact. Distinguish an example of different languages from evidence of historical change within one language.

questions.prompt: How does regularization illustrate morphological change?
questions.shortAnswer: An exceptional form is remodelled on a more general pattern, changing the distribution of inflectional forms over time.
questions.answer: An exceptional form is remodelled on a more general pattern, changing the distribution of inflectional forms over time.
keyPoints: An exceptional form is remodelled on a more general pattern, changing the distribution of inflectional forms over time.

questions.prompt: Explain prestige and linguistic insecurity briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Overt prestige attaches to publicly approved forms; covert prestige attaches to forms valued within particular groups.
questions.answer: Overt prestige attaches to publicly approved forms; covert prestige attaches to forms valued within particular groups. Speakers may orient to standard norms and local solidarity in different situations. Linguistic insecurity concerns anxiety about one's speech relative to valued norms.
keyPoints: Overt prestige attaches to publicly approved forms; covert prestige attaches to forms valued within particular groups.
Speakers may orient to standard norms and local solidarity in different situations. Linguistic insecurity concerns anxiety about one's speech relative to valued norms.

questions.prompt: Why might someone keep a nonstandard feature despite knowing it is publicly stigmatised?
questions.shortAnswer: It may index solidarity, authenticity or group membership and carry covert prestige within the community.
questions.answer: It may index solidarity, authenticity or group membership and carry covert prestige within the community.
keyPoints: It may index solidarity, authenticity or group membership and carry covert prestige within the community.

questions.prompt: Explain problems in language-change research briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Change research asks about constraints, embedding, transition, evaluation and actuation.
questions.answer: Change research asks about constraints, embedding, transition, evaluation and actuation. These concerns address possible pathways, social and linguistic location, stages, judgments and why a change arises at a particular time.
keyPoints: Change research asks about constraints, embedding, transition, evaluation and actuation.
These concerns address possible pathways, social and linguistic location, stages, judgments and why a change arises at a particular time.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes evaluation from actuation in language-change research?
questions.shortAnswer: Evaluation concerns how speakers judge variants.
questions.answer: Evaluation concerns how speakers judge variants. Actuation asks why a particular change begins in a particular place and time.
keyPoints: Evaluation concerns how speakers judge variants. Actuation asks why a particular change begins in a particular place and time.

questions.prompt: Explain language and culture briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Language expresses, constructs and symbolises cultural meanings.
questions.answer: Language expresses, constructs and symbolises cultural meanings. Shared practices and communicative conventions connect linguistic choices with ways of interpreting experience; cultures also contain diversity and disagreement.
keyPoints: Language expresses, constructs and symbolises cultural meanings.
Shared practices and communicative conventions connect linguistic choices with ways of interpreting experience; cultures also contain diversity and disagreement.

questions.prompt: Why can knowing grammar still leave a learner uncertain about appropriate address?
questions.shortAnswer: Appropriateness also depends on relationships, activity and culturally situated conventions that grammatical knowledge alone does not specify.
questions.answer: Appropriateness also depends on relationships, activity and culturally situated conventions that grammatical knowledge alone does not specify.
keyPoints: Appropriateness also depends on relationships, activity and culturally situated conventions that grammatical knowledge alone does not specify.

questions.prompt: Explain linguistic relativity and determinism briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Linguistic relativity concerns language-related influences on habitual thought; determinism claims stronger constraints on what can be thought.
questions.answer: Linguistic relativity concerns language-related influences on habitual thought; determinism claims stronger constraints on what can be thought. Treat specific effects as empirical questions. The claim that language completely confines thought is much stronger than evidence of an influence under particular conditions.
keyPoints: Linguistic relativity concerns language-related influences on habitual thought; determinism claims stronger constraints on what can be thought.
Treat specific effects as empirical questions. The claim that language completely confines thought is much stronger than evidence of an influence under particular conditions.

questions.prompt: Does a language without a single word for a concept prevent its speakers from thinking it?
questions.shortAnswer: No.
questions.answer: No. Speakers can use descriptions, learn distinctions or coin expressions. Evidence of habitual linguistic influence does not establish absolute conceptual imprisonment.
keyPoints: No. Speakers can use descriptions, learn distinctions or coin expressions. Evidence of habitual linguistic influence does not establish absolute conceptual imprisonment.

questions.prompt: Explain representation and cultural codes briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Hall's representation theory explains meaning production through concepts and signifying systems.
questions.answer: Hall's representation theory explains meaning production through concepts and signifying systems. Shared cultural codes enable signs to communicate; meanings can be contested and historically changed.
keyPoints: Hall's representation theory explains meaning production through concepts and signifying systems.
Shared cultural codes enable signs to communicate; meanings can be contested and historically changed.

questions.prompt: How could one image produce different interpretations across audiences?
questions.shortAnswer: Audiences may bring different cultural codes, histories and contexts, so the image's signs do not carry one entirely self-contained meaning.
questions.answer: Audiences may bring different cultural codes, histories and contexts, so the image's signs do not carry one entirely self-contained meaning.
keyPoints: Audiences may bring different cultural codes, histories and contexts, so the image's signs do not carry one entirely self-contained meaning.

questions.prompt: Explain gender and language practices briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Language and gender are connected through social practices, identities and relations of power.
questions.answer: Language and gender are connected through social practices, identities and relations of power. Investigate local contexts rather than treating all women and men as homogeneous speech groups. Historical claims about hedges or pitch need contextual evidence.
keyPoints: Language and gender are connected through social practices, identities and relations of power.
Investigate local contexts rather than treating all women and men as homogeneous speech groups. Historical claims about hedges or pitch need contextual evidence.

questions.prompt: Why is 'women always hedge because they lack confidence' an inadequate claim?
questions.shortAnswer: It generalises across people and settings and assigns one function to a form with several possible uses.
questions.answer: It generalises across people and settings and assigns one function to a form with several possible uses. Analyse interaction, role and local meanings.
keyPoints: It generalises across people and settings and assigns one function to a form with several possible uses. Analyse interaction, role and local meanings.

questions.prompt: Explain gendered interaction briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Gendered interaction concerns how turn-taking, topics and other practices participate in social relations.
questions.answer: Gendered interaction concerns how turn-taking, topics and other practices participate in social relations. Overlap can be supportive or competitive; roles, status and activity affect its meaning. Counted forms need contextual interpretation.
keyPoints: Gendered interaction concerns how turn-taking, topics and other practices participate in social relations.
Overlap can be supportive or competitive; roles, status and activity affect its meaning. Counted forms need contextual interpretation.

questions.prompt: Why does counting interruptions alone not prove that one group dominates a conversation?
questions.shortAnswer: The analyst must define interruption, examine functions, participation opportunities, roles and context, and distinguish supportive overlap from floor-taking.
questions.answer: The analyst must define interruption, examine functions, participation opportunities, roles and context, and distinguish supportive overlap from floor-taking.
keyPoints: The analyst must define interruption, examine functions, participation opportunities, roles and context, and distinguish supportive overlap from floor-taking.

questions.prompt: Explain sexism and language reform briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Sexist language practices construct or reproduce unequal gender relations.
questions.answer: Sexist language practices construct or reproduce unequal gender relations. Reform can change occupational labels and address conventions while examining continuing stereotypes and institutional practices.
keyPoints: Sexist language practices construct or reproduce unequal gender relations.
Reform can change occupational labels and address conventions while examining continuing stereotypes and institutional practices.

questions.prompt: Why might replacing chairman with chair help but remain insufficient?
questions.shortAnswer: It removes an unnecessarily gendered label, but participation, representation and institutional power also need attention.
questions.answer: It removes an unnecessarily gendered label, but participation, representation and institutional power also need attention.
keyPoints: It removes an unnecessarily gendered label, but participation, representation and institutional power also need attention.

questions.prompt: Explain language and identity briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Language choices can express and actively construct identities and affiliations.
questions.answer: Language choices can express and actively construct identities and affiliations. Accent, code choice, stance and register can position speakers relative to audiences and groups. Identity is negotiated, multiple and context-sensitive.
keyPoints: Language choices can express and actively construct identities and affiliations.
Accent, code choice, stance and register can position speakers relative to audiences and groups. Identity is negotiated, multiple and context-sensitive.

questions.prompt: How can code-switching construct identity rather than merely reflect it?
questions.shortAnswer: A speaker can use the switch to claim solidarity, distance, expertise or another position in the moment, shaping how others understand the relationship.
questions.answer: A speaker can use the switch to claim solidarity, distance, expertise or another position in the moment, shaping how others understand the relationship.
keyPoints: A speaker can use the switch to claim solidarity, distance, expertise or another position in the moment, shaping how others understand the relationship.

questions.prompt: Explain linguistic imperialism briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Linguistic imperialism analyses dominance maintained through unequal linguistic resources, rights and ideologies.
questions.answer: Linguistic imperialism analyses dominance maintained through unequal linguistic resources, rights and ideologies. Phillipson's framework examines structural and ideological advantages for dominant languages and the marginalisation of others.
keyPoints: Linguistic imperialism analyses dominance maintained through unequal linguistic resources, rights and ideologies.
Phillipson's framework examines structural and ideological advantages for dominant languages and the marginalisation of others.

questions.prompt: What evidence is needed beyond the popularity of English to argue linguistic imperialism?
questions.shortAnswer: Examine unequal resources, exclusion, institutional incentives, rights and ideological claims, while also considering local appropriation and resistance.
questions.answer: Examine unequal resources, exclusion, institutional incentives, rights and ideological claims, while also considering local appropriation and resistance.
keyPoints: Examine unequal resources, exclusion, institutional incentives, rights and ideological claims, while also considering local appropriation and resistance.

questions.prompt: Explain linguicism and native-speakerism briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Linguicism legitimises unequal power on linguistic grounds; native-speakerism privileges idealised native speakers in language education.
questions.answer: Linguicism legitimises unequal power on linguistic grounds; native-speakerism privileges idealised native speakers in language education. Language-based gatekeeping can shape employment and access. Teacher quality should be examined through relevant skills rather than birth-based stereotypes.
keyPoints: Linguicism legitimises unequal power on linguistic grounds; native-speakerism privileges idealised native speakers in language education.
Language-based gatekeeping can shape employment and access. Teacher quality should be examined through relevant skills rather than birth-based stereotypes.

questions.prompt: How could a teacher recruitment rule reproduce native-speakerism?
questions.shortAnswer: It may treat origin or first-language status as an automatic guarantee of competence and exclude qualified multilingual teachers without evaluating their actual expertise.
questions.answer: It may treat origin or first-language status as an automatic guarantee of competence and exclude qualified multilingual teachers without evaluating their actual expertise.
keyPoints: It may treat origin or first-language status as an automatic guarantee of competence and exclude qualified multilingual teachers without evaluating their actual expertise.

questions.prompt: Explain english, empowerment and inequality briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: English can provide opportunities while also operating within unequal linguistic systems.
questions.answer: English can provide opportunities while also operating within unequal linguistic systems. A critical ELT approach considers access, local identities and multilingual rights, and treats learners as active users rather than passive recipients.
keyPoints: English can provide opportunities while also operating within unequal linguistic systems.
A critical ELT approach considers access, local identities and multilingual rights, and treats learners as active users rather than passive recipients.

questions.prompt: How might an English course support access without devaluing local languages?
questions.shortAnswer: Use inclusive materials, recognise multilingual resources, avoid native-speaker hierarchies and make English an additional capability rather than a measure of human worth.
questions.answer: Use inclusive materials, recognise multilingual resources, avoid native-speaker hierarchies and make English an additional capability rather than a measure of human worth.
keyPoints: Use inclusive materials, recognise multilingual resources, avoid native-speaker hierarchies and make English an additional capability rather than a measure of human worth.

questions.prompt: Explain world englishes and unequal englishes briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: World Englishes examines diverse English varieties; unequal Englishes highlights hierarchies among their users and forms.
questions.answer: World Englishes examines diverse English varieties; unequal Englishes highlights hierarchies among their users and forms. Recognition of multiple varieties can challenge one-centre norms, while institutional judgments may still distribute prestige unequally.
keyPoints: World Englishes examines diverse English varieties; unequal Englishes highlights hierarchies among their users and forms.
Recognition of multiple varieties can challenge one-centre norms, while institutional judgments may still distribute prestige unequally.

questions.prompt: Why might celebrating World Englishes leave inequality unresolved?
questions.shortAnswer: A variety may gain scholarly recognition while schools, employers and media continue to reward a narrow prestigious norm.
questions.answer: A variety may gain scholarly recognition while schools, employers and media continue to reward a narrow prestigious norm.
keyPoints: A variety may gain scholarly recognition while schools, employers and media continue to reward a narrow prestigious norm.

questions.prompt: Explain fossilization briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Fossilization concerns persistent non-targetlike features in an interlanguage despite opportunities for further development.
questions.answer: Fossilization concerns persistent non-targetlike features in an interlanguage despite opportunities for further development. It can be selective rather than a total stop in learning. Longitudinal evidence is needed to distinguish persistent patterns from temporary performance or a plateau.
keyPoints: Fossilization concerns persistent non-targetlike features in an interlanguage despite opportunities for further development.
It can be selective rather than a total stop in learning. Longitudinal evidence is needed to distinguish persistent patterns from temporary performance or a plateau.

questions.prompt: Why should one avoid declaring fossilization after observing an error once?
questions.shortAnswer: A single occurrence could reflect performance, task conditions or ongoing development.
questions.answer: A single occurrence could reflect performance, task conditions or ongoing development. Fossilization is a claim about persistent patterns over time.
keyPoints: A single occurrence could reflect performance, task conditions or ongoing development. Fossilization is a claim about persistent patterns over time.

questions.prompt: Explain stabilization and fossilization briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Stabilization describes relative persistence; fossilization makes a stronger claim about enduring resistance to development.
questions.answer: Stabilization describes relative persistence; fossilization makes a stronger claim about enduring resistance to development. Input, feedback, processing and social conditions may affect patterns. Motivation alone is not a universal explanation.
keyPoints: Stabilization describes relative persistence; fossilization makes a stronger claim about enduring resistance to development.
Input, feedback, processing and social conditions may affect patterns. Motivation alone is not a universal explanation.

questions.prompt: If a previously persistent form changes after instruction, what does that imply?
questions.shortAnswer: The earlier pattern may have been stabilization rather than demonstrated permanent fossilization.
questions.answer: The earlier pattern may have been stabilization rather than demonstrated permanent fossilization. Avoid treating persistence during a limited observation period as proof that change is impossible.
keyPoints: The earlier pattern may have been stabilization rather than demonstrated permanent fossilization. Avoid treating persistence during a limited observation period as proof that change is impossible.

questions.prompt: Explain meaning and its difficulties briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Linguistic meaning concerns what expressions contribute to interpretation and communication.
questions.answer: Linguistic meaning concerns what expressions contribute to interpretation and communication. Meaning can refer to conventional content, contextual reference or a speaker's intended message. Ambiguity, context and differing analytical goals make one universal definition difficult.
keyPoints: Linguistic meaning concerns what expressions contribute to interpretation and communication.
Meaning is not identical to one person's private association with a word.

questions.prompt: Why is looking up every word insufficient to understand an utterance?
questions.shortAnswer: Dictionary meanings do not determine every referent, context or communicative intention.
questions.answer: Dictionary meanings do not determine every referent, context or communicative intention. A hearer also interprets how the words are being used in the situation.
keyPoints: Dictionary meanings do not determine every referent, context or communicative intention.
A hearer also interprets how the words are being used in the situation.

questions.prompt: What is levels of meaning?
questions.shortAnswer: Expression meaning concerns conventional content, utterance meaning its contextual use, and communicative meaning the message conveyed.
questions.answer: Expression meaning concerns conventional content, utterance meaning its contextual use, and communicative meaning the message conveyed. The levels distinguish a language expression from a particular use and the speaker's intended contribution.
keyPoints: Expression meaning concerns conventional content, utterance meaning its contextual use, and communicative meaning the message conveyed.
These levels interact; they are analytical distinctions rather than three unrelated messages.

questions.prompt: How can 'The door is open' convey more than its literal description?
questions.shortAnswer: In context it may invite entry or request closure.
questions.answer: In context it may invite entry or request closure. The sentence content describes a state, while communicative interpretation adds the relevant intended action.
keyPoints: In context it may invite entry or request closure.
The sentence content describes a state, while communicative interpretation adds the relevant intended action.

questions.prompt: Explain descriptive, social and expressive meaning briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Descriptive meaning represents situations; social meaning indexes social relationships; expressive meaning conveys attitudes or feelings.
questions.answer: Descriptive meaning represents situations; social meaning indexes social relationships; expressive meaning conveys attitudes or feelings. An expression can contribute more than one dimension. The guide supplies this three-part account rather than a complete inventory of every textbook taxonomy.
keyPoints: Descriptive meaning represents situations; social meaning indexes social relationships; expressive meaning conveys attitudes or feelings.
An expression's emotional associations are not automatically part of its descriptive truth conditions.

questions.prompt: How can two expressions refer to the same person but differ in social meaning?
questions.shortAnswer: One may use a formal title and another an intimate nickname.
questions.answer: One may use a formal title and another an intimate nickname. Their reference can coincide while they position the speaker's relationship differently.
keyPoints: One may use a formal title and another an intimate nickname.
Their reference can coincide while they position the speaker's relationship differently.

questions.prompt: What is sense?
questions.shortAnswer: Sense is the semantic content through which an expression is understood, distinct from a particular referent.
questions.answer: Sense is the semantic content through which an expression is understood, distinct from a particular referent. Expressions can share a referent while presenting it differently. The guide gives limited technical coverage of sense.
keyPoints: Sense is the semantic content through which an expression is understood, distinct from a particular referent.
A sense is not simply the object referred to.

questions.prompt: Why can 'morning star' and 'evening star' differ in sense while sharing reference?
questions.shortAnswer: They present the object through different descriptive modes.
questions.answer: They present the object through different descriptive modes. In the relevant astronomical interpretation both refer to Venus, but they do not convey the same descriptive information.
keyPoints: They present the object through different descriptive modes.
In the relevant astronomical interpretation both refer to Venus, but they do not convey the same descriptive information.

questions.prompt: Explain reference and denotation briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Reference identifies an entity in use; denotation concerns what an expression conventionally applies to.
questions.answer: Reference identifies an entity in use; denotation concerns what an expression conventionally applies to. A common noun can denote a category, while a speaker uses a noun phrase to identify a particular member.
keyPoints: Reference identifies an entity in use; denotation concerns what an expression conventionally applies to.
Reference needs not be fixed solely by dictionary meaning.

questions.prompt: What information is needed to identify the referent of 'that book'?
questions.shortAnswer: The expression's meaning provides instructions, but the situation, gesture or previous discourse helps identify which particular book the speaker intends.
questions.answer: The expression's meaning provides instructions, but the situation, gesture or previous discourse helps identify which particular book the speaker intends.
keyPoints: The expression's meaning provides instructions, but the situation, gesture or previous discourse helps identify which particular book the speaker intends.

questions.prompt: Explain propositions briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: A proposition is the content that can be asserted, denied or evaluated for truth.
questions.answer: A proposition is the content that can be asserted, denied or evaluated for truth. Different sentence forms can be related to the same situation content, while questions need not assert it.
keyPoints: A proposition is the content that can be asserted, denied or evaluated for truth.
A proposition is not simply the sequence of words in a sentence.

questions.prompt: Can two differently worded sentences express the same proposition?
questions.shortAnswer: Yes, in an appropriate context they can convey the same truth-evaluable content.
questions.answer: Yes, in an appropriate context they can convey the same truth-evaluable content. Wording, sentence form and propositional content should be distinguished.
keyPoints: Yes, in an appropriate context they can convey the same truth-evaluable content.
Wording, sentence form and propositional content should be distinguished.

questions.prompt: Explain ambiguity, homonymy and polysemy briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Ambiguity allows distinct readings; homonymy involves unrelated lexical meanings, while polysemy involves related meanings.
questions.answer: Ambiguity allows distinct readings; homonymy involves unrelated lexical meanings, while polysemy involves related meanings. Lexical ambiguity can come from homonymy or polysemy; structural ambiguity comes from alternative grammatical organisation.
keyPoints: Ambiguity allows distinct readings; homonymy involves unrelated lexical meanings, while polysemy involves related meanings.
Relatedness is sometimes debatable; contextual variation does not always establish a stored lexical sense.

questions.prompt: How does 'I saw the man with the telescope' differ from bank-type ambiguity?
questions.shortAnswer: Its readings can come from different attachment structures: the observer used the telescope, or the man had it.
questions.answer: Its readings can come from different attachment structures: the observer used the telescope, or the man had it. Bank-type ambiguity is lexical rather than dependent on this phrase attachment.
keyPoints: Its readings can come from different attachment structures: the observer used the telescope, or the man had it.
Bank-type ambiguity is lexical rather than dependent on this phrase attachment.

questions.prompt: Explain vagueness briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Vagueness concerns unclear boundaries within a reading rather than several distinct readings.
questions.answer: Vagueness concerns unclear boundaries within a reading rather than several distinct readings. A vague term can have borderline cases even when its intended sense is understood.
keyPoints: Vagueness concerns unclear boundaries within a reading rather than several distinct readings.
A vague word need not have two separate dictionary senses.

questions.prompt: Why is asking 'How tall must someone be to count as tall?' a question about vagueness?
questions.shortAnswer: The issue is the boundary of one gradable meaning, not choosing between distinct unrelated readings.
questions.answer: The issue is the boundary of one gradable meaning, not choosing between distinct unrelated readings. The relevant standard can vary with context.
keyPoints: The issue is the boundary of one gradable meaning, not choosing between distinct unrelated readings.
The relevant standard can vary with context.

questions.prompt: Explain lexical and grammatical meaning briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Lexical meaning is associated with vocabulary items; grammatical meaning is contributed by forms and constructions.
questions.answer: Lexical meaning is associated with vocabulary items; grammatical meaning is contributed by forms and constructions. Inflections, function words and word order can express number, tense or participant relations.
keyPoints: Lexical meaning is associated with vocabulary items; grammatical meaning is contributed by forms and constructions.
Grammatical meaning is not empty or less meaningful than lexical content.

questions.prompt: What meaning changes between 'the dog chased the cat' and 'the cat chased the dog'?
questions.shortAnswer: The lexical items remain largely the same, but word order changes the participant roles expressed by the construction, producing different situation meanings.
questions.answer: The lexical items remain largely the same, but word order changes the participant roles expressed by the construction, producing different situation meanings.
keyPoints: The lexical items remain largely the same, but word order changes the participant roles expressed by the construction, producing different situation meanings.

questions.prompt: Explain componential analysis briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Componential analysis represents word meanings through combinations of semantic features.
questions.answer: Componential analysis represents word meanings through combinations of semantic features. It is useful for explicit contrasts within a lexical set, but some meanings resist a simple feature checklist.
keyPoints: Componential analysis represents word meanings through combinations of semantic features.
A convenient feature analysis is a model, not proof that all meaning consists of binary features.

questions.prompt: What is a limitation of defining every category by a fixed feature checklist?
questions.shortAnswer: Some categories have vague boundaries, context-sensitive use or typicality effects.
questions.answer: Some categories have vague boundaries, context-sensitive use or typicality effects. A fixed checklist may miss these aspects or rely on disputed features.
keyPoints: Some categories have vague boundaries, context-sensitive use or typicality effects.
A fixed checklist may miss these aspects or rely on disputed features.

questions.prompt: Explain semantic roles briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Semantic roles describe how participants relate to an event, such as agent, theme or patient.
questions.answer: Semantic roles describe how participants relate to an event, such as agent, theme or patient. An agent typically initiates an action; a patient is affected; a theme is involved or moved. Role inventories differ across frameworks.
keyPoints: Semantic roles describe how participants relate to an event, such as agent, theme or patient.
Semantic roles do not equal grammatical functions: a subject need not be an agent.

questions.prompt: In 'The cup was broken by the child', is the subject the agent?
questions.shortAnswer: No.
questions.answer: No. The cup is the grammatical subject but the affected patient. The child remains the agent in the passive construction.
keyPoints: No.
The cup is the grammatical subject but the affected patient.
The child remains the agent in the passive construction.

questions.prompt: Explain synonymy and near-synonymy briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Synonymy concerns sameness or close similarity of meaning between expressions.
questions.answer: Synonymy concerns sameness or close similarity of meaning between expressions. Near synonyms can differ in register, distribution, connotation or collocation, so complete interchangeability is unusual.
keyPoints: Synonymy concerns sameness or close similarity of meaning between expressions.
Sharing a referent does not automatically make two expressions synonyms.

questions.prompt: Why may replacing every word with a dictionary synonym change a text?
questions.shortAnswer: Near synonyms can differ in tone, grammar and typical combinations.
questions.answer: Near synonyms can differ in tone, grammar and typical combinations. Semantic similarity does not guarantee equivalent use in every context.
keyPoints: Near synonyms can differ in tone, grammar and typical combinations.
Semantic similarity does not guarantee equivalent use in every context.

questions.prompt: Explain hyponymy and meronymy briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Hyponymy is a kind-of relation; meronymy is a part-of relation.
questions.answer: Hyponymy is a kind-of relation; meronymy is a part-of relation. These organise vocabulary in different ways and should be identified by the relevant conceptual link.
keyPoints: Hyponymy is a kind-of relation; meronymy is a part-of relation.
A part is not necessarily a subtype of its whole.

questions.prompt: Is wheel a hyponym of car?
questions.shortAnswer: No.
questions.answer: No. A wheel is part of a car, so the relation is meronymy. A hatchback, by contrast, is a kind of car and illustrates hyponymy.
keyPoints: No.
A wheel is part of a car, so the relation is meronymy.
A hatchback, by contrast, is a kind of car and illustrates hyponymy.

questions.prompt: Explain antonymy and complementarity briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Antonymy concerns oppositeness; complementary terms divide a relevant domain into mutually exclusive alternatives.
questions.answer: Antonymy concerns oppositeness; complementary terms divide a relevant domain into mutually exclusive alternatives. Gradable opposites permit degrees and often a middle range. Complementarity depends on the domain and interpretation.
keyPoints: Antonymy concerns oppositeness; complementary terms divide a relevant domain into mutually exclusive alternatives.
Not hot does not normally entail cold.

questions.prompt: Why does 'not hot' fail to entail 'cold'?
questions.shortAnswer: Hot and cold are gradable opposites with an intermediate range.
questions.answer: Hot and cold are gradable opposites with an intermediate range. Something can be warm or neutral, so denying one endpoint does not establish the other.
keyPoints: Hot and cold are gradable opposites with an intermediate range.
Something can be warm or neutral, so denying one endpoint does not establish the other.

questions.prompt: What is structural theories of meaning?
questions.shortAnswer: Structural approaches explain meanings through relations within a language system.
questions.answer: Structural approaches explain meanings through relations within a language system. Contrast and combination help determine a lexical item's place in a semantic network.
keyPoints: Structural approaches explain meanings through relations within a language system.
A word's meaning is not explained only by pointing to an external object.

questions.prompt: How would a structural analysis approach colour vocabulary?
questions.shortAnswer: It would examine contrasts and relations among the terms in that language, including how they divide the semantic field, rather than treating each word in isolation.
questions.answer: It would examine contrasts and relations among the terms in that language, including how they divide the semantic field, rather than treating each word in isolation.
keyPoints: It would examine contrasts and relations among the terms in that language, including how they divide the semantic field, rather than treating each word in isolation.

questions.prompt: What is behaviourist approaches to meaning?
questions.shortAnswer: Behaviourist approaches seek to explain verbal meaning through observable conditions and responses.
questions.answer: Behaviourist approaches seek to explain verbal meaning through observable conditions and responses. Bloomfield connected utterances with the practical situations preceding and following speech. This offers a different explanatory emphasis from mental concepts.
keyPoints: Behaviourist approaches seek to explain verbal meaning through observable conditions and responses.
A stimulus–response sketch does not provide a complete analysis of every abstract or novel meaning.

questions.prompt: Why is one fixed response inadequate as the meaning of 'Close the door'?
questions.shortAnswer: The hearer may comply, refuse or misunderstand.
questions.answer: The hearer may comply, refuse or misunderstand. Meaning cannot be equated with the actual response on every occasion; this is a limitation of a simple response-based account.
keyPoints: The hearer may comply, refuse or misunderstand.
Meaning cannot be equated with the actual response on every occasion; this is a limitation of a simple response-based account.

questions.prompt: Explain cognitive semantics briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Cognitive approaches connect meaning with conceptualisation and categorisation.
questions.answer: Cognitive approaches connect meaning with conceptualisation and categorisation. Concepts, prototypes and background knowledge help explain interpretation, while the guide distinguishes conventional meaning from richer personal knowledge.
keyPoints: Cognitive approaches connect meaning with conceptualisation and categorisation.
Typicality is not identical to membership: a less typical penguin is still fully a bird.

questions.prompt: Does a penguin's low typicality make it partly a bird?
questions.shortAnswer: No.
questions.answer: No. Typicality judgments concern how representative an example seems, not necessarily how fully it belongs to the category.
keyPoints: No.
Typicality judgments concern how representative an example seems, not necessarily how fully it belongs to the category.

questions.prompt: Explain truth-conditional semantics briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: A truth-conditional account asks what must hold for a statement to be true.
questions.answer: A truth-conditional account asks what must hold for a statement to be true. Specify the reading and contextual reference before evaluating its truth. Truth conditions differ from whether we currently know the statement is true.
keyPoints: A truth-conditional account asks what must hold for a statement to be true.
A statement can have clear truth conditions even when its truth is unknown.

questions.prompt: Why does 'The sun was drying the washing' not entail that the washing became dry?
questions.shortAnswer: The progressive describes an ongoing process without guaranteeing completion.
questions.answer: The progressive describes an ongoing process without guaranteeing completion. Truth conditions must preserve that difference from a completed successful drying event.
keyPoints: The progressive describes an ongoing process without guaranteeing completion.
Truth conditions must preserve that difference from a completed successful drying event.

questions.prompt: Explain generative semantics briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Historical generative semantics explored a close derivational relationship between semantic representations and sentence structure.
questions.answer: Historical generative semantics explored a close derivational relationship between semantic representations and sentence structure. It developed within debates about transformational grammar, with scholars including Lakoff, McCawley, Postal and Ross. The syllabus's broad label should be distinguished from other generative approaches.
keyPoints: Historical generative semantics explored a close derivational relationship between semantic representations and sentence structure.
Generative semantics, Chomskyan grammar and the Generative Lexicon are not interchangeable labels.

questions.prompt: Why should a brief mention of the Generative Lexicon not stand in for all generative meaning theory?
questions.shortAnswer: They are distinct research programmes with different histories and proposals.
questions.answer: They are distinct research programmes with different histories and proposals. State which framework you mean rather than treating every theory called generative as the same account.
keyPoints: They are distinct research programmes with different histories and proposals.
State which framework you mean rather than treating every theory called generative as the same account.

questions.prompt: What is metaphor?
questions.shortAnswer: Metaphor uses a source domain to structure or describe a different target domain through selected similarities.
questions.answer: Metaphor uses a source domain to structure or describe a different target domain through selected similarities. The comparison transfers relevant features rather than asserting literal identity.
keyPoints: Metaphor uses a source domain to structure or describe a different target domain through selected similarities.
Nonliteral language is not automatically metaphor; the relation may be metonymic or ironic.

questions.prompt: What does 'the roots of the disagreement' illustrate?
questions.shortAnswer: A conventional metaphor: plant roots supply a pattern for the origin or basis of an abstract disagreement.
questions.answer: A conventional metaphor: plant roots supply a pattern for the origin or basis of an abstract disagreement. It does not imply actual botanical parts.
keyPoints: A conventional metaphor: plant roots supply a pattern for the origin or basis of an abstract disagreement.
It does not imply actual botanical parts.

questions.prompt: Explain irony and hyperbole briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Irony can create a critical contrast between literal wording and intended interpretation; hyperbole exaggerates.
questions.answer: Irony can create a critical contrast between literal wording and intended interpretation; hyperbole exaggerates. Context helps a hearer recognise the mismatch. Exaggeration alone does not establish irony.
keyPoints: Irony can create a critical contrast between literal wording and intended interpretation; hyperbole exaggerates.
Nonliteralness alone does not identify which figure is being used.

questions.prompt: Is 'I waited a thousand years for coffee' necessarily irony?
questions.shortAnswer: No.
questions.answer: No. It is an obvious exaggeration and therefore hyperbole. It may express impatience without the pretended praise or critical contrast typical of many ironic uses.
keyPoints: No.
It is an obvious exaggeration and therefore hyperbole.
It may express impatience without the pretended praise or critical contrast typical of many ironic uses.

questions.prompt: What is metonymy?
questions.shortAnswer: Metonymy uses an expression to refer to something closely connected with what it denotes.
questions.answer: Metonymy uses an expression to refer to something closely connected with what it denotes. Common connections include author–work, place–institution and container–contents, depending on context.
keyPoints: Metonymy uses an expression to refer to something closely connected with what it denotes.
Metonymy relies on association rather than primarily on resemblance across domains.

questions.prompt: Why is 'The White House announced a policy' metonymic?
questions.shortAnswer: The place stands for the relevant administration or officials associated with it.
questions.answer: The place stands for the relevant administration or officials associated with it. The link is institutional association rather than a claim that officials resemble a building.
keyPoints: The place stands for the relevant administration or officials associated with it.
The link is institutional association rather than a claim that officials resemble a building.

questions.prompt: Explain pragmatics briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Pragmatics studies meaning in contextual language use, including inference, action and interaction.
questions.answer: Pragmatics studies meaning in contextual language use, including inference, action and interaction. It examines how speakers communicate more than linguistic form explicitly states and how hearers interpret that contribution.
keyPoints: Pragmatics studies meaning in contextual language use, including inference, action and interaction.
Context-sensitive interpretation does not mean hearers can infer anything without evidence.

questions.prompt: Why might an entirely grammatical answer still be inappropriate in conversation?
questions.shortAnswer: Its relevance, timing, politeness or intended action may not fit the context.
questions.answer: Its relevance, timing, politeness or intended action may not fit the context. Pragmatic appropriateness involves more than sentence grammar.
keyPoints: Its relevance, timing, politeness or intended action may not fit the context.
Pragmatic appropriateness involves more than sentence grammar.

questions.prompt: Explain sentence and utterance briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: A sentence is an abstract linguistic form; an utterance is a particular instance of language use.
questions.answer: A sentence is an abstract linguistic form; an utterance is a particular instance of language use. The same sentence can be uttered by different people at different times with different references or intentions.
keyPoints: A sentence is an abstract linguistic form; an utterance is a particular instance of language use.
An utterance can be a fragment rather than a complete sentence.

questions.prompt: Can 'Coffee?' count as an utterance even though it is not a full sentence?
questions.shortAnswer: Yes.
questions.answer: Yes. It is a situated communicative act and can offer coffee, request it or check a preference depending on context.
keyPoints: Yes.
It is a situated communicative act and can offer coffee, request it or check a preference depending on context.

questions.prompt: What is context?
questions.shortAnswer: Context includes linguistic surroundings, the situation, participants and relevant background assumptions.
questions.answer: Context includes linguistic surroundings, the situation, participants and relevant background assumptions. It helps resolve reference, ambiguity and intended actions. Shared knowledge may be incomplete and open to correction.
keyPoints: Context includes linguistic surroundings, the situation, participants and relevant background assumptions.
Context is not only the preceding sentence.

questions.prompt: What different kinds of context help interpret 'Put it there'?
questions.shortAnswer: The participants, objects, gestures, location and preceding talk can identify it and there.
questions.answer: The participants, objects, gestures, location and preceding talk can identify it and there. The imperative form alone cannot supply those referents.
keyPoints: The participants, objects, gestures, location and preceding talk can identify it and there.
The imperative form alone cannot supply those referents.

questions.prompt: What is entailment?
questions.shortAnswer: Entailment is a relation in which one proposition's truth guarantees another's, under a fixed interpretation.
questions.answer: Entailment is a relation in which one proposition's truth guarantees another's, under a fixed interpretation. It is a semantic consequence rather than merely a likely inference.
keyPoints: Entailment is a relation in which one proposition's truth guarantees another's, under a fixed interpretation.
A plausible consequence is not necessarily an entailment.

questions.prompt: Does 'Amina owns a dog' entail 'Amina owns a poodle'?
questions.shortAnswer: No.
questions.answer: No. Poodle is a subtype of dog, so the inference works from poodle to dog, not from the broader category to that particular subtype.
keyPoints: No.
Poodle is a subtype of dog, so the inference works from poodle to dog, not from the broader category to that particular subtype.

questions.prompt: Explain presupposition and triggers briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: A presupposition is background information treated as already accepted or required for an utterance.
questions.answer: A presupposition is background information treated as already accepted or required for an utterance. Definite expressions, factive verbs and change-of-state expressions can trigger presuppositions. Projection through negation is a useful diagnostic, with contextual qualifications.
keyPoints: A presupposition is background information treated as already accepted or required for an utterance.
Presuppositions can be challenged, accommodated or blocked in context.

questions.prompt: How does 'She did not stop smoking' help distinguish presupposition from entailment?
questions.shortAnswer: The background assumption of previous smoking commonly remains under negation, while the assertion that stopping occurred is denied.
questions.answer: The background assumption of previous smoking commonly remains under negation, while the assertion that stopping occurred is denied. This persistence is a diagnostic, not an exceptionless mechanical test.
keyPoints: The background assumption of previous smoking commonly remains under negation, while the assertion that stopping occurred is denied.
This persistence is a diagnostic, not an exceptionless mechanical test.

questions.prompt: Explain conventional and conversational implicature briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Conventional implicature is tied to particular expressions; conversational implicature is inferred through context and communicative expectations.
questions.answer: Conventional implicature is tied to particular expressions; conversational implicature is inferred through context and communicative expectations. Conversational implicatures can often be cancelled or changed by context. A generalized inference needs less special context than a particularized one.
keyPoints: Conventional implicature is tied to particular expressions; conversational implicature is inferred through context and communicative expectations.
Conversational implicature is not a strict logical entailment.
