questions.prompt: Why can 'Some students passed—in fact, all did' be consistent?
questions.shortAnswer: Some does not semantically exclude all in the relevant logical reading.
questions.answer: Some does not semantically exclude all in the relevant logical reading. The not-all suggestion is normally an implicature that the continuation can cancel.
keyPoints: Some does not semantically exclude all in the relevant logical reading.
The not-all suggestion is normally an implicature that the continuation can cancel.

questions.prompt: Explain cooperation and conversational maxims briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Grice's Cooperative Principle describes an expectation of contributions appropriate to an exchange's purpose.
questions.answer: Grice's Cooperative Principle describes an expectation of contributions appropriate to an exchange's purpose. The maxims concern Quality, Quantity, Relation and Manner: truthfulness, informativeness, relevance and clarity.
keyPoints: Grice's Cooperative Principle describes an expectation of contributions appropriate to an exchange's purpose.
Cooperation is a framework for interpreting conversation, not a rule requiring social agreement.

questions.prompt: Which maxim is relevant if someone knowingly supplies false information?
questions.shortAnswer: Quality, because it concerns truthfulness and adequate evidence.
questions.answer: Quality, because it concerns truthfulness and adequate evidence. The interpretation also depends on whether deception or an openly recognisable nonliteral use is involved.
keyPoints: Quality, because it concerns truthfulness and adequate evidence.
The interpretation also depends on whether deception or an openly recognisable nonliteral use is involved.

questions.prompt: Explain flouting and violating maxims briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Flouting makes a mismatch conspicuous so an implicature can be inferred; violating covertly fails an expectation.
questions.answer: Flouting makes a mismatch conspicuous so an implicature can be inferred; violating covertly fails an expectation. A hearer may infer irony or an indirect message when the apparent mismatch is openly recognisable.
keyPoints: Flouting makes a mismatch conspicuous so an implicature can be inferred; violating covertly fails an expectation.
A maxim departure is not automatically deliberate or interpretable as one fixed message.

questions.prompt: How does an obvious ironic compliment differ from a successful lie in Gricean terms?
questions.shortAnswer: The ironic mismatch is meant to be noticed and can flout Quality.
questions.answer: The ironic mismatch is meant to be noticed and can flout Quality. A lie covertly violates truthfulness while aiming to be accepted as true.
keyPoints: The ironic mismatch is meant to be noticed and can flout Quality.
A lie covertly violates truthfulness while aiming to be accepted as true.

questions.prompt: Explain deixis and the deictic centre briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Deixis links interpretation to an utterance's participants, time, place or related contextual coordinates.
questions.answer: Deixis links interpretation to an utterance's participants, time, place or related contextual coordinates. The ordinary centre is speaker, here and now. Some uses are anaphoric rather than deictic, depending on how a referent is identified.
keyPoints: Deixis links interpretation to an utterance's participants, time, place or related contextual coordinates.
A form such as that can have deictic or anaphoric uses.

questions.prompt: Why can 'I'll be here tomorrow' become unclear when read days later?
questions.shortAnswer: Here and tomorrow depend on the relevant contextual centre.
questions.answer: Here and tomorrow depend on the relevant contextual centre. The reader must recover the intended place and time instead of automatically using their own current coordinates.
keyPoints: Here and tomorrow depend on the relevant contextual centre.
The reader must recover the intended place and time instead of automatically using their own current coordinates.

questions.prompt: What is deictic projection?
questions.shortAnswer: Deictic projection shifts the interpretive centre away from the speaker's immediate here and now.
questions.answer: Deictic projection shifts the interpretive centre away from the speaker's immediate here and now. A narrative or represented viewpoint can organise deictic expressions around another participant, time or location.
keyPoints: Deictic projection shifts the interpretive centre away from the speaker's immediate here and now.
Deictic projection shifts viewpoint; presupposition projection concerns background assumptions in larger constructions.

questions.prompt: How does deictic projection differ from presupposition projection?
questions.shortAnswer: Deictic projection shifts the contextual viewpoint used to interpret expressions such as here or now.
questions.answer: Deictic projection shifts the contextual viewpoint used to interpret expressions such as here or now. Presupposition projection concerns whether an assumption is inherited by a larger sentence.
keyPoints: Deictic projection shifts the contextual viewpoint used to interpret expressions such as here or now.
Presupposition projection concerns whether an assumption is inherited by a larger sentence.

questions.prompt: Explain types of deixis briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Major categories include person, place, time, discourse and social deixis.
questions.answer: Major categories include person, place, time, discourse and social deixis. Person concerns participant roles, place and time locate events, discourse points within communication and social deixis encodes relationships.
keyPoints: Major categories include person, place, time, discourse and social deixis.
A demonstrative's grammatical form alone does not settle which deictic function it performs.

questions.prompt: What kind of deixis appears in 'As explained above'?
questions.shortAnswer: Discourse deixis: above points to a location in the text rather than an ordinary physical place.
questions.answer: Discourse deixis: above points to a location in the text rather than an ordinary physical place. Interpretation depends on the organisation of the discourse.
keyPoints: Discourse deixis: above points to a location in the text rather than an ordinary physical place.
Interpretation depends on the organisation of the discourse.

questions.prompt: Explain honorifics briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Honorifics conventionally encode social relationships such as respect, status or formality.
questions.answer: Honorifics conventionally encode social relationships such as respect, status or formality. They can concern the addressee or a person being referred to; their precise forms and meanings are language-specific.
keyPoints: Honorifics conventionally encode social relationships such as respect, status or formality.
An honorific does not guarantee sincere respect or a polite overall interaction.

questions.prompt: Why are honorifics related to social deixis?
questions.shortAnswer: Their interpretation depends on socially organised relations among participants or referents.
questions.answer: Their interpretation depends on socially organised relations among participants or referents. They can encode status or deference rather than merely describing an object.
keyPoints: Their interpretation depends on socially organised relations among participants or referents.
They can encode status or deference rather than merely describing an object.

questions.prompt: Explain performatives and constatives briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: A performative utterance can enact an action under suitable conditions; a constative is presented as a statement describing a situation.
questions.answer: A performative utterance can enact an action under suitable conditions; a constative is presented as a statement describing a situation. Austin's initial distinction motivated a wider theory in which ordinary assertions are also actions.
keyPoints: A performative utterance can enact an action under suitable conditions; a constative is presented as a statement describing a situation.
The presence of I plus a verb alone does not guarantee successful performance.

questions.prompt: Why does 'I apologise' differ from 'I apologised yesterday'?
questions.shortAnswer: The first can perform an apology in the current interaction.
questions.answer: The first can perform an apology in the current interaction. The second ordinarily reports a past event, though both are utterances performing some communicative action.
keyPoints: The first can perform an apology in the current interaction.
The second ordinarily reports a past event, though both are utterances performing some communicative action.

questions.prompt: Explain felicity conditions briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Felicity conditions are the contextual and procedural requirements for a speech act to be appropriate or successfully performed.
questions.answer: Felicity conditions are the contextual and procedural requirements for a speech act to be appropriate or successfully performed. They may involve authority, circumstances, procedure, sincerity and subsequent conduct. Failures differ in kind.
keyPoints: Felicity conditions are the contextual and procedural requirements for a speech act to be appropriate or successfully performed.
Insincerity and lack of institutional authority are different kinds of failure.

questions.prompt: Why can a random spectator not successfully declare two people married merely by saying the words?
questions.shortAnswer: The required authority and institutional circumstances are absent.
questions.answer: The required authority and institutional circumstances are absent. The formula alone cannot satisfy the felicity conditions for that act.
keyPoints: The required authority and institutional circumstances are absent.
The formula alone cannot satisfy the felicity conditions for that act.

questions.prompt: Explain locution, illocution and perlocution briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Locution concerns producing meaningful words; illocution concerns the act performed; perlocution concerns its effects.
questions.answer: Locution concerns producing meaningful words; illocution concerns the act performed; perlocution concerns its effects. Distinguish the linguistic content, communicative force and actual consequences.
keyPoints: Locution concerns producing meaningful words; illocution concerns the act performed; perlocution concerns its effects.
A speaker's intended effect need not actually occur.

questions.prompt: If a warning is ignored, has it necessarily failed to be a warning?
questions.shortAnswer: No.
questions.answer: No. Its illocutionary force can still be a warning even if it fails to produce the desired perlocutionary effect, such as making the hearer avoid danger.
keyPoints: No.
Its illocutionary force can still be a warning even if it fails to produce the desired perlocutionary effect, such as making the hearer avoid danger.

questions.prompt: Explain searle's speech-act categories briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Searle distinguishes representatives, directives, commissives, expressives and declarations.
questions.answer: Searle distinguishes representatives, directives, commissives, expressives and declarations. These concern commitments to truth, attempts to get action, future commitments, expressed attitudes and institutionally effective changes.
keyPoints: Searle distinguishes representatives, directives, commissives, expressives and declarations.
A declarative grammatical sentence need not perform a declaration.

questions.prompt: Why is 'The room is empty' not automatically a declaration in Searle's sense?
questions.shortAnswer: It normally represents a state of affairs rather than changing an institutional state through authorised utterance.
questions.answer: It normally represents a state of affairs rather than changing an institutional state through authorised utterance. Grammatical declarative form and speech-act category are different classifications.
keyPoints: It normally represents a state of affairs rather than changing an institutional state through authorised utterance.
Grammatical declarative form and speech-act category are different classifications.

questions.prompt: Explain indirect speech acts briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: An indirect speech act performs an action through a form conventionally associated with another action.
questions.answer: An indirect speech act performs an action through a form conventionally associated with another action. Interpretation relies on context and familiar patterns, not only on literal sentence type.
keyPoints: An indirect speech act performs an action through a form conventionally associated with another action.
Indirectness does not automatically mean greater politeness in every context.

questions.prompt: What makes 'Can you open the window?' an indirect request in an ordinary room?
questions.shortAnswer: Its literal form asks about ability, but the context makes a request for action the relevant interpretation.
questions.answer: Its literal form asks about ability, but the context makes a request for action the relevant interpretation. The hearer need not stop at answering yes.
keyPoints: Its literal form asks about ability, but the context makes a request for action the relevant interpretation.
The hearer need not stop at answering yes.

questions.prompt: Explain politeness and context briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Politeness concerns how interaction attends to social relations and participants' expectations.
questions.answer: Politeness concerns how interaction attends to social relations and participants' expectations. Interpretation depends on relationship, activity, wording and context. Face-based theory is one influential account, not the only account.
keyPoints: Politeness concerns how interaction attends to social relations and participants' expectations.
Formality, indirectness and politeness are related but not equivalent.

questions.prompt: Does adding please guarantee that a request is polite?
questions.shortAnswer: No.
questions.answer: No. The relationship, entitlement, tone and wider interaction affect its interpretation. One word does not determine the social effect of the whole act.
keyPoints: No.
The relationship, entitlement, tone and wider interaction affect its interpretation.
One word does not determine the social effect of the whole act.

questions.prompt: Explain positive and negative face briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: In Brown and Levinson's framework, positive face concerns approval and negative face concerns freedom from imposition.
questions.answer: In Brown and Levinson's framework, positive face concerns approval and negative face concerns freedom from imposition. Face wants motivate ways of managing potentially threatening acts.
keyPoints: In Brown and Levinson's framework, positive face concerns approval and negative face concerns freedom from imposition.
Positive and negative do not mean good and bad personalities.

questions.prompt: Why can a friendly request still threaten negative face?
questions.shortAnswer: It can impose on the hearer's time or choices even when it expresses warmth and approval.
questions.answer: It can impose on the hearer's time or choices even when it expresses warmth and approval. The two face dimensions are analytically different.
keyPoints: It can impose on the hearer's time or choices even when it expresses warmth and approval.
The two face dimensions are analytically different.

questions.prompt: Explain positive and negative politeness briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Positive politeness attends to approval or solidarity; negative politeness attends to non-imposition.
questions.answer: Positive politeness attends to approval or solidarity; negative politeness attends to non-imposition. Strategies can include common-ground appeals or respectful mitigation, depending on context.
keyPoints: Positive politeness attends to approval or solidarity; negative politeness attends to non-imposition.
Negative politeness is not rudeness; positive politeness is not simply praise.

questions.prompt: How does offering an easy refusal help manage a request?
questions.shortAnswer: It acknowledges the hearer's autonomy and reduces pressure to comply, which fits negative-politeness concerns in the face-based framework.
questions.answer: It acknowledges the hearer's autonomy and reduces pressure to comply, which fits negative-politeness concerns in the face-based framework.
keyPoints: It acknowledges the hearer's autonomy and reduces pressure to comply, which fits negative-politeness concerns in the face-based framework.

questions.prompt: Explain impoliteness briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Impoliteness involves behaviour interpreted as damaging or attacking social relations or face in context.
questions.answer: Impoliteness involves behaviour interpreted as damaging or attacking social relations or face in context. Insults, exclusion and dismissive wording can contribute, but interpretation depends on the activity and participants.
keyPoints: Impoliteness involves behaviour interpreted as damaging or attacking social relations or face in context.
Directness alone is not proof of impoliteness.

questions.prompt: Why might the same direct command be acceptable in an emergency but offensive in ordinary conversation?
questions.shortAnswer: Urgency and shared activity change expectations and entitlement.
questions.answer: Urgency and shared activity change expectations and entitlement. Its social meaning depends on the situation rather than sentence form alone.
keyPoints: Urgency and shared activity change expectations and entitlement.
Its social meaning depends on the situation rather than sentence form alone.

questions.prompt: What is topic management?
questions.shortAnswer: Conversation participants establish, maintain, shift and negotiate what their talk is about.
questions.answer: Conversation participants establish, maintain, shift and negotiate what their talk is about. Topic conflict can arise when speakers pursue incompatible agendas or resist each other's proposed direction.
keyPoints: Conversation participants establish, maintain, shift and negotiate what their talk is about.
A topic shift can still belong to an orderly conversational sequence.

questions.prompt: Why should a change of subject not automatically be labelled incoherent?
questions.shortAnswer: A shift may be understood as avoidance, a new proposal or part of a sequence.
questions.answer: A shift may be understood as avoidance, a new proposal or part of a sequence. Participants can make sense of it through its interactional position and context.
keyPoints: A shift may be understood as avoidance, a new proposal or part of a sequence.
Participants can make sense of it through its interactional position and context.

questions.prompt: What is repair?
questions.shortAnswer: Repair addresses problems in speaking, hearing or understanding.
questions.answer: Repair addresses problems in speaking, hearing or understanding. Distinguish who initiates repair from who supplies the solution.
keyPoints: Repair addresses problems in speaking, hearing or understanding.
Repair is broader than correcting grammar mistakes.

questions.prompt: In 'A: Tuesday. B: Tuesday? A: Thursday, sorry', who initiates and who repairs?
questions.shortAnswer: B initiates repair by questioning Tuesday, and A supplies the solution.
questions.answer: B initiates repair by questioning Tuesday, and A supplies the solution. It is other-initiated self-repair.
keyPoints: B initiates repair by questioning Tuesday, and A supplies the solution.
It is other-initiated self-repair.

questions.prompt: Explain insertion sequences briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: An insertion sequence occurs between the parts of a base adjacency pair.
questions.answer: An insertion sequence occurs between the parts of a base adjacency pair. The inserted exchange can resolve something needed before the pending response.
keyPoints: An insertion sequence occurs between the parts of a base adjacency pair.
The inserted turns delay, rather than necessarily abandon, the original response.

questions.prompt: Why does asking 'When?' before answering a borrowing request not necessarily change the topic?
questions.shortAnswer: It can be an inserted clarification needed to decide the response.
questions.answer: It can be an inserted clarification needed to decide the response. The original request remains pending until the clarification and subsequent answer.
keyPoints: It can be an inserted clarification needed to decide the response.
The original request remains pending until the clarification and subsequent answer.

questions.prompt: Explain adjacency pairs briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: An adjacency pair links a first action with a relevant responsive action by another speaker.
questions.answer: An adjacency pair links a first action with a relevant responsive action by another speaker. A first pair part makes a limited range of second actions relevant, such as a greeting and return greeting.
keyPoints: An adjacency pair links a first action with a relevant responsive action by another speaker.
Adjacency is an organisational relation, not a claim that the turns must always be physically next to each other.

questions.prompt: Can an adjacency pair remain connected when another exchange intervenes?
questions.shortAnswer: Yes.
questions.answer: Yes. An insertion sequence can occur between its first and second parts while the original response remains conditionally relevant.
keyPoints: Yes.
An insertion sequence can occur between its first and second parts while the original response remains conditionally relevant.

questions.prompt: What is the semantics–pragmatics interface?
questions.shortAnswer: Semantics and pragmatics distinguish conventional linguistic contributions from context-sensitive use and inference, while interacting in interpretation.
questions.answer: Semantics and pragmatics distinguish conventional linguistic contributions from context-sensitive use and inference, while interacting in interpretation. Deictic reference and implied messages show why the boundary is analytically useful but theoretically debated.
keyPoints: Semantics and pragmatics distinguish conventional linguistic contributions from context-sensitive use and inference, while interacting in interpretation.
Semantics is not wholly unrelated to context, and pragmatics is not unrestricted guesswork.

questions.prompt: Why is 'semantics is completely context-free' an oversimplification?
questions.shortAnswer: Expressions such as pronouns and indexicals require contextual values even when their conventional meaning supplies a rule.
questions.answer: Expressions such as pronouns and indexicals require contextual values even when their conventional meaning supplies a rule. Theories differ on where to locate particular contextual contributions.
keyPoints: Expressions such as pronouns and indexicals require contextual values even when their conventional meaning supplies a rule.
Theories differ on where to locate particular contextual contributions.

questions.prompt: What is cohesion?
questions.shortAnswer: Cohesion consists of identifiable linguistic ties connecting parts of a text.
questions.answer: Cohesion consists of identifiable linguistic ties connecting parts of a text. Reference, substitution, ellipsis, lexical relations and conjunction can link clauses or turns.
keyPoints: Cohesion consists of identifiable linguistic ties connecting parts of a text.
Cohesive devices alone do not guarantee a sensible overall message.

questions.prompt: Can a passage contain many connectives yet remain incoherent?
questions.shortAnswer: Yes.
questions.answer: Yes. Explicit ties can link sentences formally while their ideas fail to make sense together. Coherence needs an interpretable relationship, not only markers.
keyPoints: Yes.
Explicit ties can link sentences formally while their ideas fail to make sense together.
Coherence needs an interpretable relationship, not only markers.

questions.prompt: Explain reference ties briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Reference ties connect an expression with an entity interpreted through text or situation.
questions.answer: Reference ties connect an expression with an entity interpreted through text or situation. Anaphora points back; cataphora points forward. Endophoric reference is text-internal, while exophoric reference depends on the situation.
keyPoints: Reference ties connect an expression with an entity interpreted through text or situation.
Exophoric reference may support interpretation without forming a text-internal tie.

questions.prompt: How do anaphora and deixis differ?
questions.shortAnswer: Anaphora retrieves a referent through discourse, while deixis anchors interpretation to contextual coordinates.
questions.answer: Anaphora retrieves a referent through discourse, while deixis anchors interpretation to contextual coordinates. Some expressions can serve either role depending on use.
keyPoints: Anaphora retrieves a referent through discourse, while deixis anchors interpretation to contextual coordinates.
Some expressions can serve either role depending on use.

questions.prompt: Explain substitution and ellipsis briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Substitution replaces material with a grammatical substitute; ellipsis leaves recoverable material unspoken.
questions.answer: Substitution replaces material with a grammatical substitute; ellipsis leaves recoverable material unspoken. They can involve nominal, verbal or clausal material, depending on the construction.
keyPoints: Substitution replaces material with a grammatical substitute; ellipsis leaves recoverable material unspoken.
A pronoun's reference relation is not automatically the same as grammatical substitution.

questions.prompt: What is omitted in 'Has she finished the essay? Yes, she has'?
questions.shortAnswer: The material finished the essay is recoverable from the question.
questions.answer: The material finished the essay is recoverable from the question. The auxiliary remains while the repeated verbal content is elided.
keyPoints: The material finished the essay is recoverable from the question.
The auxiliary remains while the repeated verbal content is elided.

questions.prompt: What is lexical cohesion?
questions.shortAnswer: Lexical cohesion connects a text through vocabulary relations and associations.
questions.answer: Lexical cohesion connects a text through vocabulary relations and associations. Reiteration can use repetition, near synonyms, superordinates or general words. Associated vocabulary can also establish links.
keyPoints: Lexical cohesion connects a text through vocabulary relations and associations.
Related words need not be interchangeable synonyms.

questions.prompt: Why does 'The oven was hot. Its heat warmed the kitchen' show lexical cohesion?
questions.shortAnswer: Hot and heat are related lexical choices that maintain the temperature theme and connect the two descriptions.
questions.answer: Hot and heat are related lexical choices that maintain the temperature theme and connect the two descriptions.
keyPoints: Hot and heat are related lexical choices that maintain the temperature theme and connect the two descriptions.

questions.prompt: What is conjunction in discourse?
questions.shortAnswer: Conjunction marks relations such as addition, contrast, cause or sequence between discourse parts.
questions.answer: Conjunction marks relations such as addition, contrast, cause or sequence between discourse parts. Interpret the connection signalled by and, however, therefore or then in its actual context.
keyPoints: Conjunction marks relations such as addition, contrast, cause or sequence between discourse parts.
A temporal sequence does not by itself establish causation.

questions.prompt: Why do then and therefore suggest different relations?
questions.shortAnswer: Then primarily orders events in time, while therefore presents a consequence or inference.
questions.answer: Then primarily orders events in time, while therefore presents a consequence or inference. A sequence alone need not imply that one event caused the next.
keyPoints: Then primarily orders events in time, while therefore presents a consequence or inference.
A sequence alone need not imply that one event caused the next.

questions.prompt: What is coherence?
questions.shortAnswer: Coherence is the meaningful connectedness that makes discourse interpretable as a whole.
questions.answer: Coherence is the meaningful connectedness that makes discourse interpretable as a whole. Hearers use context, shared knowledge and inference to connect ideas, including brief exchanges with few overt ties.
keyPoints: Coherence is the meaningful connectedness that makes discourse interpretable as a whole.
Coherence is not identical to grammatical correctness or visible cohesion.

questions.prompt: How can 'A walk?'—'My ankle' be coherent without an explicit refusal?
questions.shortAnswer: Shared knowledge of an ankle injury can make the second fragment a relevant reason for declining.
questions.answer: Shared knowledge of an ankle injury can make the second fragment a relevant reason for declining. The hearer supplies the context-supported connection.
keyPoints: Shared knowledge of an ankle injury can make the second fragment a relevant reason for declining.
The hearer supplies the context-supported connection.

questions.prompt: Explain phonetics briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Phonetics studies the production, transmission and perception of speech sounds.
questions.answer: Phonetics studies the production, transmission and perception of speech sounds. It describes physical speech events, including articulatory movements, acoustic properties and auditory processing.
keyPoints: Phonetics studies the production, transmission and perception of speech sounds.
Phonetics is not restricted to spelling or to sounds that distinguish words.

questions.prompt: What would an articulatory phonetician examine when you say pin?
questions.shortAnswer: They would examine how the lips close and release, how the vocal folds behave and how the tongue forms the following vowel.
questions.answer: They would examine how the lips close and release, how the vocal folds behave and how the tongue forms the following vowel.
keyPoints: They would examine how the lips close and release, how the vocal folds behave and how the tongue forms the following vowel.

questions.prompt: What is phonology?
questions.shortAnswer: Phonology studies how sounds are organised and patterned in a language.
questions.answer: Phonology studies how sounds are organised and patterned in a language. It concerns contrasts, distribution, syllable patterns and sound processes. Phonetic evidence helps explain these patterns.
keyPoints: Phonology studies how sounds are organised and patterned in a language.
Phonology also studies non-contrastive patterns such as allophony.

questions.prompt: Why is aspiration in English relevant to phonology even when it does not change a word's meaning?
questions.shortAnswer: Its distribution is patterned: voiceless stops are typically aspirated at the start of stressed syllables but not after /s/ in the same onset.
questions.answer: Its distribution is patterned: voiceless stops are typically aspirated at the start of stressed syllables but not after /s/ in the same onset. Phonology explains that organisation.
keyPoints: Its distribution is patterned: voiceless stops are typically aspirated at the start of stressed syllables but not after /s/ in the same onset.
Phonology explains that organisation.

questions.prompt: Explain branches of phonetics briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: The three main branches are articulatory, acoustic and auditory phonetics.
questions.answer: The three main branches are articulatory, acoustic and auditory phonetics. They study sound production, physical sound signals and sound perception respectively.
keyPoints: The three main branches are articulatory, acoustic and auditory phonetics.
The branches examine related stages of speech rather than unrelated kinds of language.

questions.prompt: Which branch would investigate formants in a recorded vowel?
questions.shortAnswer: Acoustic phonetics, because formants are resonances observable in the sound signal.
questions.answer: Acoustic phonetics, because formants are resonances observable in the sound signal. Their patterns can also inform analysis of articulation and perception.
keyPoints: Acoustic phonetics, because formants are resonances observable in the sound signal.
Their patterns can also inform analysis of articulation and perception.

questions.prompt: Explain phone and phoneme briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: A phone is a speech sound; a phoneme is an abstract contrastive unit in a language.
questions.answer: A phone is a speech sound; a phoneme is an abstract contrastive unit in a language. Phones are conventionally written in brackets and phonemes in slashes. A phoneme can have different phonetic realisations.
keyPoints: A phone is a speech sound; a phoneme is an abstract contrastive unit in a language.
A letter is not a phoneme: spelling and sound units do not correspond one to one.

questions.prompt: Why do we write /p/ but [pʰ]?
questions.shortAnswer: /p/ identifies the phonological category; [pʰ] specifies an aspirated phonetic realisation.
questions.answer: /p/ identifies the phonological category; [pʰ] specifies an aspirated phonetic realisation. The notation indicates the level of analysis.
keyPoints: /p/ identifies the phonological category; [pʰ] specifies an aspirated phonetic realisation.
The notation indicates the level of analysis.

questions.prompt: Explain minimal pairs briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: A minimal pair consists of words differing in one sound in the same position, with different meanings.
questions.answer: A minimal pair consists of words differing in one sound in the same position, with different meanings. It provides evidence that the sound difference is contrastive in the language.
keyPoints: A minimal pair consists of words differing in one sound in the same position, with different meanings.
Two words differing in several sounds do not form a minimal pair.

questions.prompt: Are ship and sheep evidence for two English vowel phonemes?
questions.shortAnswer: Yes.
questions.answer: Yes. Their consonantal frame is the same and the vowel difference distinguishes meaning, supporting a contrast between /ɪ/ and /iː/ in this accent.
keyPoints: Yes.
Their consonantal frame is the same and the vowel difference distinguishes meaning, supporting a contrast between /ɪ/ and /iː/ in this accent.

questions.prompt: Explain allophones briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Allophones are phonetic variants of a phoneme that do not establish a lexical contrast in the relevant language.
questions.answer: Allophones are phonetic variants of a phoneme that do not establish a lexical contrast in the relevant language. Their occurrence may depend on context or vary with speaker and style.
keyPoints: Allophones are phonetic variants of a phoneme that do not establish a lexical contrast in the relevant language.
Sounds that are allophones in one language may contrast in another.

questions.prompt: Why are [pʰ] and [p] usually treated as variants of English /p/?
questions.shortAnswer: Their distribution is largely predictable and does not distinguish English words by itself.
questions.answer: Their distribution is largely predictable and does not distinguish English words by itself. Their shared articulation also supports treating them as related realisations.
keyPoints: Their distribution is largely predictable and does not distinguish English words by itself.
Their shared articulation also supports treating them as related realisations.

questions.prompt: What is complementary distribution?
questions.shortAnswer: Complementary distribution means two sounds occur in non-overlapping environments.
questions.answer: Complementary distribution means two sounds occur in non-overlapping environments. It supports an allophonic analysis when combined with a plausible phonetic relationship and wider evidence.
keyPoints: Complementary distribution means two sounds occur in non-overlapping environments.
Non-overlap alone does not prove two phones belong to the same phoneme.

questions.prompt: If two sounds never occur in the same position, must they be allophones?
questions.shortAnswer: No.
questions.answer: No. Complementary distribution needs to be considered with phonetic similarity and the wider sound system; unrelated phonemes may also have non-overlapping distributions.
keyPoints: No.
Complementary distribution needs to be considered with phonetic similarity and the wider sound system; unrelated phonemes may also have non-overlapping distributions.

questions.prompt: What is free variation?
questions.shortAnswer: Free variation is non-contrastive variation in a comparable environment.
questions.answer: Free variation is non-contrastive variation in a comparable environment. A speaker may produce a final stop with or without an audible release without changing the intended word.
keyPoints: Free variation is non-contrastive variation in a comparable environment.
Variation can still be influenced by style, social factors or phonetic context.

questions.prompt: Does an unreleased final [t̚] necessarily turn cat into a different word?
questions.shortAnswer: No.
questions.answer: No. It may be a phonetic variant of /t/ in that environment. The difference in release does not itself create an English lexical contrast.
keyPoints: No.
It may be a phonetic variant of /t/ in that environment.
The difference in release does not itself create an English lexical contrast.

questions.prompt: Explain trubetzkoy and phonological opposition briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Trubetzkoy helped establish phonology as the study of functional sound oppositions.
questions.answer: Trubetzkoy helped establish phonology as the study of functional sound oppositions. He analysed phonological systems through distinctive contrasts and discussed neutralisation and markedness.
keyPoints: Trubetzkoy helped establish phonology as the study of functional sound oppositions.
A sound's phonological role depends on the system, not only its physical properties.

questions.prompt: What does neutralisation mean in phonology?
questions.shortAnswer: A contrast between phonological categories is not maintained in a particular environment.
questions.answer: A contrast between phonological categories is not maintained in a particular environment. German final devoicing is a standard illustration of a final-position voicing contrast being lost.
keyPoints: A contrast between phonological categories is not maintained in a particular environment.
German final devoicing is a standard illustration of a final-position voicing contrast being lost.

questions.prompt: Explain jakobson and distinctive features briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Jakobson developed analyses of speech sounds using distinctive features.
questions.answer: Jakobson developed analyses of speech sounds using distinctive features. Features capture recurring contrasts and natural classes, allowing generalisations across multiple segments.
keyPoints: Jakobson developed analyses of speech sounds using distinctive features.
Feature systems differ across theories and historical versions.

questions.prompt: Why use features rather than only lists of individual phonemes?
questions.shortAnswer: Features explain shared behaviour.
questions.answer: Features explain shared behaviour. A process affecting a natural class can be stated once instead of repeated independently for each segment.
keyPoints: Features explain shared behaviour.
A process affecting a natural class can be stated once instead of repeated independently for each segment.

questions.prompt: Explain daniel jones briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Daniel Jones contributed to phonetic description, pronunciation teaching and the cardinal vowel system.
questions.answer: Daniel Jones contributed to phonetic description, pronunciation teaching and the cardinal vowel system. Cardinal vowels provide reference points for describing vowel quality; they are not the vowel inventory of one language.
keyPoints: Daniel Jones contributed to phonetic description, pronunciation teaching and the cardinal vowel system.
Cardinal vowels are analytical reference qualities rather than simply English vowel phonemes.

questions.prompt: Are cardinal vowels the same as the English vowels?
questions.shortAnswer: No.
questions.answer: No. They form a reference system for describing vowels across languages. English vowels can be located relative to those reference points.
keyPoints: No.
They form a reference system for describing vowels across languages.
English vowels can be located relative to those reference points.

questions.prompt: What is generative phonology?
questions.shortAnswer: Generative phonology relates underlying representations to surface pronunciations through formal processes.
questions.answer: Generative phonology relates underlying representations to surface pronunciations through formal processes. Chomsky and Halle's The Sound Pattern of English is a major work in this tradition. Feature-based representations support general rules.
keyPoints: Generative phonology relates underlying representations to surface pronunciations through formal processes.
An underlying form is a theoretical representation rather than a directly recorded sound.

questions.prompt: How does a generative account connect an underlying form with pronunciation?
questions.shortAnswer: It proposes phonological rules or processes that map the underlying representation to a surface form, explaining regular alternations and contextual effects.
questions.answer: It proposes phonological rules or processes that map the underlying representation to a surface form, explaining regular alternations and contextual effects.
keyPoints: It proposes phonological rules or processes that map the underlying representation to a surface form, explaining regular alternations and contextual effects.

questions.prompt: What is vowel classification?
questions.shortAnswer: Vowels are produced with a relatively open vocal tract and commonly form syllable nuclei.
questions.answer: Vowels are produced with a relatively open vocal tract and commonly form syllable nuclei. Describe vowel quality using tongue height, frontness or backness and lip rounding; duration is another relevant property.
keyPoints: Vowels are produced with a relatively open vocal tract and commonly form syllable nuclei.
The absence of a complete oral closure does not mean articulators are inactive.

questions.prompt: Which features distinguish /iː/ from /uː/?
questions.shortAnswer: Both are close vowels, but /iː/ is front and unrounded while /uː/ is traditionally back and rounded.
questions.answer: Both are close vowels, but /iː/ is front and unrounded while /uː/ is traditionally back and rounded. Actual positions vary across accents.
keyPoints: Both are close vowels, but /iː/ is front and unrounded while /uː/ is traditionally back and rounded.
Actual positions vary across accents.

questions.prompt: Explain monophthongs briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: A monophthong has a relatively steady vowel quality within a syllable.
questions.answer: A monophthong has a relatively steady vowel quality within a syllable. Traditional RP teaching describes twelve monophthong phonemes, including /ɪ e æ ɒ ʊ ʌ ə/ and /iː ɑː ɔː uː ɜː/.
keyPoints: A monophthong has a relatively steady vowel quality within a syllable.
The inventory and symbol conventions vary across accents and analyses.

questions.prompt: Does the traditional RP count describe every English accent?
questions.shortAnswer: No.
questions.answer: No. It is an accent-specific teaching model. Vowel contrasts and their phonetic realisations differ across English varieties.
keyPoints: No.
It is an accent-specific teaching model.
Vowel contrasts and their phonetic realisations differ across English varieties.

questions.prompt: Explain vowel length and quality briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Traditional long–short vowel pairs commonly differ in quality as well as duration.
questions.answer: Traditional long–short vowel pairs commonly differ in quality as well as duration. The length mark /ː/ belongs to a transcription convention; actual duration also depends on stress and neighbouring sounds.
keyPoints: Traditional long–short vowel pairs commonly differ in quality as well as duration.
Simply stretching /ɪ/ does not reliably produce /iː/.

questions.prompt: Why is 'sheep has a longer ship vowel' an incomplete explanation?
questions.shortAnswer: Because /iː/ and /ɪ/ normally differ in tongue position or vowel quality as well as typical duration.
questions.answer: Because /iː/ and /ɪ/ normally differ in tongue position or vowel quality as well as typical duration. Both features help describe the contrast.
keyPoints: Because /iː/ and /ɪ/ normally differ in tongue position or vowel quality as well as typical duration.
Both features help describe the contrast.

questions.prompt: Explain diphthongs briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: A diphthong involves a change in vowel quality within one syllabic nucleus.
questions.answer: A diphthong involves a change in vowel quality within one syllabic nucleus. Traditional RP descriptions distinguish closing and centring diphthongs.
keyPoints: A diphthong involves a change in vowel quality within one syllabic nucleus.
A diphthong is not identified by the number of written vowel letters.

questions.prompt: Why does say contain one syllable despite its changing vowel quality?
questions.shortAnswer: Its /eɪ/ is a single diphthongal nucleus.
questions.answer: Its /eɪ/ is a single diphthongal nucleus. The internal glide does not automatically create an additional syllable.
keyPoints: Its /eɪ/ is a single diphthongal nucleus.
The internal glide does not automatically create an additional syllable.

questions.prompt: Explain closing and centring diphthongs briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Closing diphthongs move toward a closer quality; centring diphthongs move toward a central quality.
questions.answer: Closing diphthongs move toward a closer quality; centring diphthongs move toward a central quality. The traditional RP inventory lists /eɪ aɪ ɔɪ əʊ aʊ/ and /ɪə eə ʊə/. Contemporary realisations and mergers vary.
keyPoints: Closing diphthongs move toward a closer quality; centring diphthongs move toward a central quality.
Some traditionally centring diphthongs are monophthongal for modern speakers.

questions.prompt: Why should a transcription of tour allow accent variation?
questions.shortAnswer: The traditional /ʊə/ analysis does not fit every speaker.
questions.answer: The traditional /ʊə/ analysis does not fit every speaker. Some merge it with /ɔː/ or use another realisation, so the target accent must be stated.
keyPoints: The traditional /ʊə/ analysis does not fit every speaker.
Some merge it with /ɔː/ or use another realisation, so the target accent must be stated.

questions.prompt: Explain triphthong sequences briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Traditional British descriptions call sequences such as /aɪə/ triphthongs.
questions.answer: Traditional British descriptions call sequences such as /aɪə/ triphthongs. They can be analysed as a closing diphthong followed by schwa. Their syllabification and smoothing vary; they are not five extra vowel phonemes added to the usual inventory.
keyPoints: Traditional British descriptions call sequences such as /aɪə/ triphthongs.
The guide's total of 25 RP vowel phonemes incorrectly adds sequences as separate phonemes.

questions.prompt: Should five triphthongs be added to twelve monophthongs and eight diphthongs as five more RP vowel phonemes?
questions.shortAnswer: No.
questions.answer: No. These are usually analysed as diphthong-plus-schwa sequences. Their phonetic form and syllable structure vary, so they should not simply inflate the phoneme count.
keyPoints: No.
These are usually analysed as diphthong-plus-schwa sequences.
Their phonetic form and syllable structure vary, so they should not simply inflate the phoneme count.

questions.prompt: Explain schwa and vowel reduction briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Schwa /ə/ is a central vowel strongly associated with unstressed syllables in standard British descriptions.
questions.answer: Schwa /ə/ is a central vowel strongly associated with unstressed syllables in standard British descriptions. Reduction helps explain weak forms and unstressed syllables. Not every unstressed vowel is schwa.
keyPoints: Schwa /ə/ is a central vowel strongly associated with unstressed syllables in standard British descriptions.
Schwa is a sound category, not the name for every short or unclear vowel.

questions.prompt: Why might can contain /ə/ in 'I can swim'?
questions.shortAnswer: An unstressed can may take the weak form /kən/.
questions.answer: An unstressed can may take the weak form /kən/. If can is contrastively stressed, the stronger /kæn/ form is more likely.
keyPoints: An unstressed can may take the weak form /kən/.
If can is contrastively stressed, the stronger /kæn/ form is more likely.

questions.prompt: What is consonant classification?
questions.shortAnswer: Consonants are commonly described by voicing, place and manner of articulation.
questions.answer: Consonants are commonly described by voicing, place and manner of articulation. These dimensions identify laryngeal activity, the location of constriction and how airflow is controlled.
keyPoints: Consonants are commonly described by voicing, place and manner of articulation.
A spelling letter does not guarantee one fixed consonant sound.

questions.prompt: Describe /f/ using the three standard dimensions.
questions.shortAnswer: /f/ is a voiceless labiodental fricative: no regular voicing, constriction between lower lip and upper teeth, and turbulent airflow.
questions.answer: /f/ is a voiceless labiodental fricative: no regular voicing, constriction between lower lip and upper teeth, and turbulent airflow.
keyPoints: /f/ is a voiceless labiodental fricative: no regular voicing, constriction between lower lip and upper teeth, and turbulent airflow.

questions.prompt: What is places of articulation?
questions.shortAnswer: Place of articulation identifies where the principal constriction is formed.
questions.answer: Place of articulation identifies where the principal constriction is formed. English descriptions include bilabial, labiodental, dental, alveolar, postalveolar, palatal, velar and glottal places.
keyPoints: Place of articulation identifies where the principal constriction is formed.
English /r/ is commonly a postalveolar approximant; its exact articulation varies.

questions.prompt: How do /n/ and /ŋ/ differ if both are nasals?
questions.shortAnswer: They differ in place: /n/ is alveolar and /ŋ/ is velar.
questions.answer: They differ in place: /n/ is alveolar and /ŋ/ is velar. Both allow airflow through the nose during oral closure.
keyPoints: They differ in place: /n/ is alveolar and /ŋ/ is velar.
Both allow airflow through the nose during oral closure.

questions.prompt: Explain stops and fricatives briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Stops involve a complete closure; fricatives involve a narrow constriction producing friction.
questions.answer: Stops involve a complete closure; fricatives involve a narrow constriction producing friction. The difference concerns airflow control, not simply loudness or duration.
keyPoints: Stops involve a complete closure; fricatives involve a narrow constriction producing friction.
A stop can lack an audible release in a particular environment.

questions.prompt: How would you distinguish /p/ from /f/ articulatorily?
questions.shortAnswer: /p/ uses complete bilabial closure, while /f/ uses a narrow labiodental constriction producing friction.
questions.answer: /p/ uses complete bilabial closure, while /f/ uses a narrow labiodental constriction producing friction. Their place and manner differ.
keyPoints: /p/ uses complete bilabial closure, while /f/ uses a narrow labiodental constriction producing friction.
Their place and manner differ.

questions.prompt: Explain affricates briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: An affricate combines a stop closure with a closely coordinated fricative release.
questions.answer: An affricate combines a stop closure with a closely coordinated fricative release. English /tʃ/ and /dʒ/ are commonly analysed as single consonant phonemes.
keyPoints: An affricate combines a stop closure with a closely coordinated fricative release.
Two IPA letters can represent one affricate phoneme.

questions.prompt: Why is /tʃ/ not simply the same sound as /ʃ/?
questions.shortAnswer: /tʃ/ starts with a complete stop closure and releases into friction, whereas /ʃ/ has sustained frication without that initial stop phase.
questions.answer: /tʃ/ starts with a complete stop closure and releases into friction, whereas /ʃ/ has sustained frication without that initial stop phase.
keyPoints: /tʃ/ starts with a complete stop closure and releases into friction, whereas /ʃ/ has sustained frication without that initial stop phase.

questions.prompt: Explain nasals, laterals and approximants briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Nasals route airflow through the nose; laterals allow side airflow; approximants have relatively open constriction.
questions.answer: Nasals route airflow through the nose; laterals allow side airflow; approximants have relatively open constriction. English has /m n ŋ/, lateral /l/ and approximants conventionally transcribed /r j w/.
keyPoints: Nasals route airflow through the nose; laterals allow side airflow; approximants have relatively open constriction.
Calling /w/ bilabial alone omits its velar component.

questions.prompt: Why is /w/ described as labial-velar?
questions.shortAnswer: Its articulation combines rounded lips and a raised tongue back toward the velum.
questions.answer: Its articulation combines rounded lips and a raised tongue back toward the velum. Both constrictions contribute to the sound.
keyPoints: Its articulation combines rounded lips and a raised tongue back toward the velum.
Both constrictions contribute to the sound.

questions.prompt: Explain voicing contrasts briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Voicing involves vocal-fold vibration and helps distinguish consonant categories.
questions.answer: Voicing involves vocal-fold vibration and helps distinguish consonant categories. English contrasts include /f–v/, /s–z/ and /t–d/. The full phonetic distinction may involve duration and aspiration as well.
keyPoints: Voicing involves vocal-fold vibration and helps distinguish consonant categories.
A phonologically voiced stop need not show continuous voicing throughout every token.

questions.prompt: How do /θ/ and /ð/ differ?
questions.shortAnswer: Both are dental fricatives, but /θ/ belongs to the voiceless category and /ð/ to the voiced category.
questions.answer: Both are dental fricatives, but /θ/ belongs to the voiceless category and /ð/ to the voiced category. They contrast in English rather than being spelling variants.
keyPoints: Both are dental fricatives, but /θ/ belongs to the voiceless category and /ð/ to the voiced category.
They contrast in English rather than being spelling variants.

questions.prompt: Explain phonetic and phonological syllables briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Phonetically, syllables relate to sonority patterns; phonologically, they organise positions and sound sequences.
questions.answer: Phonetically, syllables relate to sonority patterns; phonologically, they organise positions and sound sequences. A simple sonority peak model is useful but does not resolve every syllable-boundary question.
keyPoints: Phonetically, syllables relate to sonority patterns; phonologically, they organise positions and sound sequences.
Sonority is not simply identical to physical loudness.

questions.prompt: Why might a physical 'beat' description of syllables be insufficient?
questions.shortAnswer: It does not fully explain language-specific permissible sequences or structural positions.
questions.answer: It does not fully explain language-specific permissible sequences or structural positions. Phonological syllable models capture these organisational restrictions.
keyPoints: It does not fully explain language-specific permissible sequences or structural positions.
Phonological syllable models capture these organisational restrictions.

questions.prompt: Explain onset, nucleus, coda and rhyme briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: The onset precedes the nucleus; the coda follows it; the rhyme contains nucleus and coda.
questions.answer: The onset precedes the nucleus; the coda follows it; the rhyme contains nucleus and coda. Onsets and codas can be absent. A nucleus is required in the usual syllable model.
keyPoints: The onset precedes the nucleus; the coda follows it; the rhyme contains nucleus and coda.
A rhyme is not the whole syllable: it excludes the onset.

questions.prompt: Analyse the syllable structure of string.
questions.shortAnswer: In /strɪŋ/, /str/ is the onset, /ɪ/ the nucleus and /ŋ/ the coda.
questions.answer: In /strɪŋ/, /str/ is the onset, /ɪ/ the nucleus and /ŋ/ the coda. The rhyme is /ɪŋ/.
keyPoints: In /strɪŋ/, /str/ is the onset, /ɪ/ the nucleus and /ŋ/ the coda.
The rhyme is /ɪŋ/.

questions.prompt: Explain open, closed and syllabic consonants briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: An open syllable has no coda; a closed syllable has one; a syllabic consonant can form a nucleus.
questions.answer: An open syllable has no coda; a closed syllable has one; a syllabic consonant can form a nucleus. Syllable analysis concerns sounds rather than written vowels.
keyPoints: An open syllable has no coda; a closed syllable has one; a syllabic consonant can form a nucleus.
A written vowel letter is not necessary for every spoken syllable.

questions.prompt: How can button have two syllables when the second has no pronounced vowel in some accents?
questions.shortAnswer: The consonant [n̩] can function as the second nucleus.
questions.answer: The consonant [n̩] can function as the second nucleus. A syllabic consonant carries the syllable rather than merely forming a coda.
keyPoints: The consonant [n̩] can function as the second nucleus.
A syllabic consonant carries the syllable rather than merely forming a coda.

questions.prompt: Explain phonotactics briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Phonotactics concerns language-specific restrictions on sound sequences and syllable positions.
questions.answer: Phonotactics concerns language-specific restrictions on sound sequences and syllable positions. English permits complex clusters such as /str/ initially, while native lexical onsets normally exclude /ŋ/.
keyPoints: Phonotactics concerns language-specific restrictions on sound sequences and syllable positions.
A sequence possible in one language need not be possible in another.

questions.prompt: Why may an English speaker insert a vowel into an unfamiliar consonant cluster?
questions.shortAnswer: The cluster may conflict with the speaker's learned phonotactic patterns.
questions.answer: The cluster may conflict with the speaker's learned phonotactic patterns. Insertion can adapt it to a more familiar syllable structure.
keyPoints: The cluster may conflict with the speaker's learned phonotactic patterns.
Insertion can adapt it to a more familiar syllable structure.

questions.prompt: Explain strong and weak forms briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Many English function words alternate between full strong forms and reduced weak forms.
questions.answer: Many English function words alternate between full strong forms and reduced weak forms. Stress, contrast, position, accent and speaking style influence which form is appropriate.
keyPoints: Many English function words alternate between full strong forms and reduced weak forms.
Weak forms are not compulsory in every connected utterance.

questions.prompt: Why would to be stronger in 'I said TO London, not FROM London'?
questions.shortAnswer: The preposition is contrastively focused, so a strong form is appropriate.
questions.answer: The preposition is contrastively focused, so a strong form is appropriate. Function words can receive stress when the intended contrast requires it.
keyPoints: The preposition is contrastively focused, so a strong form is appropriate.
Function words can receive stress when the intended contrast requires it.

questions.prompt: Explain contractions briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: A contraction is a conventional shortened form of a word or combination of words.
questions.answer: A contraction is a conventional shortened form of a word or combination of words. Forms such as I'm, don't and I'd occur in speech and have conventional written representations.
keyPoints: A contraction is a conventional shortened form of a word or combination of words.
Contraction and weak-form reduction are related phenomena but are not identical.

questions.prompt: How would you determine whether I'd means I had or I would?
questions.shortAnswer: Use the following verb construction: I'd finished normally means I had finished; I'd finish normally means I would finish.
questions.answer: Use the following verb construction: I'd finished normally means I had finished; I'd finish normally means I would finish.
keyPoints: Use the following verb construction: I'd finished normally means I had finished; I'd finish normally means I would finish.

questions.prompt: What is elision?
questions.shortAnswer: Elision is the absence of a sound that may occur in a fuller pronunciation.
questions.answer: Elision is the absence of a sound that may occur in a fuller pronunciation. It often affects consonant clusters or unstressed material and varies with style and context.
keyPoints: Elision is the absence of a sound that may occur in a fuller pronunciation.
Elision removes a segment; assimilation changes its properties.

questions.prompt: What process can explain /neks deɪ/ for next day?
questions.shortAnswer: Elision of /t/ from the consonant cluster.
questions.answer: Elision of /t/ from the consonant cluster. It is a possible connected-speech realisation, not a rule requiring every speaker to delete it.
keyPoints: Elision of /t/ from the consonant cluster.
It is a possible connected-speech realisation, not a rule requiring every speaker to delete it.

questions.prompt: What is regressive assimilation?
questions.shortAnswer: Regressive assimilation occurs when a following sound influences an earlier one.
questions.answer: Regressive assimilation occurs when a following sound influences an earlier one. The earlier segment may adopt a place feature of the following segment.
keyPoints: Regressive assimilation occurs when a following sound influences an earlier one.
The resulting pronunciation depends on context and style; it is not a spelling change.

questions.prompt: Why can ten boys sound like tem boys?
questions.shortAnswer: The alveolar nasal can anticipate the bilabial closure of /b/ and become [m].
questions.answer: The alveolar nasal can anticipate the bilabial closure of /b/ and become [m]. This is regressive place assimilation.
keyPoints: The alveolar nasal can anticipate the bilabial closure of /b/ and become [m].
This is regressive place assimilation.

questions.prompt: Explain progressive and coalescent assimilation briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Progressive assimilation reflects an earlier sound's influence; coalescence combines neighbouring segments into a new outcome.
questions.answer: Progressive assimilation reflects an earlier sound's influence; coalescence combines neighbouring segments into a new outcome. Plural voicing patterns illustrate left-to-right conditioning; /t+j/ can coalesce as [tʃ] in connected speech.
keyPoints: Progressive assimilation reflects an earlier sound's influence; coalescence combines neighbouring segments into a new outcome.
Not every sequence of /t/ and /j/ must coalesce.

questions.prompt: How does assimilation in don't you differ from assimilation in ten boys?
questions.shortAnswer: Don't you can involve coalescence of /t/ and /j/ into [tʃ].
questions.answer: Don't you can involve coalescence of /t/ and /j/ into [tʃ]. Ten boys involves an earlier nasal adopting the following consonant's place.
keyPoints: Don't you can involve coalescence of /t/ and /j/ into [tʃ].
Ten boys involves an earlier nasal adopting the following consonant's place.

questions.prompt: Explain stress and prominence briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Stress is the relative prominence of a syllable within a word or larger utterance.
questions.answer: Stress is the relative prominence of a syllable within a word or larger utterance. Prominence can involve pitch, duration, intensity and vowel quality, with their relative contribution varying.
keyPoints: Stress is the relative prominence of a syllable within a word or larger utterance.
Stress is relative prominence, not merely shouting louder.

questions.prompt: Why can a stressed syllable remain perceptually prominent without being the loudest one?
questions.shortAnswer: Pitch movement, duration and vowel quality can also signal prominence.
questions.answer: Pitch movement, duration and vowel quality can also signal prominence. Stress is realised through a combination of cues rather than intensity alone.
keyPoints: Pitch movement, duration and vowel quality can also signal prominence.
Stress is realised through a combination of cues rather than intensity alone.

questions.prompt: Explain primary, secondary and word stress briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Primary stress is the strongest word-level prominence; secondary stress is a weaker prominence in longer words.
questions.answer: Primary stress is the strongest word-level prominence; secondary stress is a weaker prominence in longer words. IPA uses /ˈ/ for primary and /ˌ/ for secondary stress before the relevant syllable.
keyPoints: Primary stress is the strongest word-level prominence; secondary stress is a weaker prominence in longer words.
The stress mark precedes a syllable rather than marking a vowel as a separate unit.

questions.prompt: Where should the IPA primary-stress mark be placed?
questions.shortAnswer: Immediately before the stressed syllable.
questions.answer: Immediately before the stressed syllable. It indicates that syllable's relative prominence in the word.
keyPoints: Immediately before the stressed syllable.
It indicates that syllable's relative prominence in the word.

questions.prompt: Explain stress placement and suffixes briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: English word stress is influenced by syllable structure, word class, morphology and lexical history.
questions.answer: English word stress is influenced by syllable structure, word class, morphology and lexical history. Some suffixes attract or condition stress, while others preserve it. Generalisations are tendencies with exceptions and accent differences.
keyPoints: English word stress is influenced by syllable structure, word class, morphology and lexical history.
A single suffix rule cannot predict every English word's stress.

questions.prompt: Why is 'all two-syllable verbs have final stress' unsafe?
questions.shortAnswer: Many verbs follow that pattern, but exceptions exist.
questions.answer: Many verbs follow that pattern, but exceptions exist. Word class is one influence among several, so lexical and morphological evidence must also be considered.
keyPoints: Many verbs follow that pattern, but exceptions exist.
Word class is one influence among several, so lexical and morphological evidence must also be considered.

questions.prompt: Explain compound and contrastive stress briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Stress can distinguish some compounds from phrases and can highlight a contrast in discourse.
questions.answer: Stress can distinguish some compounds from phrases and can highlight a contrast in discourse. Compound stress patterns are useful tendencies, not absolute tests. Sentence focus can move prominence to the contrasted element.
keyPoints: Stress can distinguish some compounds from phrases and can highlight a contrast in discourse.
Content words are not always stressed and function words are not always unstressed.

questions.prompt: What does stressing I in 'I didn't borrow your book' suggest?
questions.shortAnswer: It can contrast the speaker with another possible borrower.
questions.answer: It can contrast the speaker with another possible borrower. The exact inference depends on context; stress highlights the alternative being considered.
keyPoints: It can contrast the speaker with another possible borrower.
The exact inference depends on context; stress highlights the alternative being considered.

questions.prompt: What is chunking speech?
questions.shortAnswer: Chunking divides speech into meaningful intonation units.
questions.answer: Chunking divides speech into meaningful intonation units. Grammar, information structure, planning and speaking style help determine boundaries. Units need not match written punctuation exactly.
keyPoints: Chunking divides speech into meaningful intonation units.
A pause after every word does not produce useful meaning-based chunking.

questions.prompt: Why can punctuation alone not determine spoken chunk boundaries?
questions.shortAnswer: Speakers organise information and interaction dynamically.
questions.answer: Speakers organise information and interaction dynamically. A written sentence may be spoken in several units, while a short clause may form one unit without a pause.
keyPoints: Speakers organise information and interaction dynamically.
A written sentence may be spoken in several units, while a short clause may form one unit without a pause.

questions.prompt: What is tone-unit structure?
questions.shortAnswer: A tone unit is a stretch of speech organised around a main pitch-bearing nucleus.
questions.answer: A tone unit is a stretch of speech organised around a main pitch-bearing nucleus. A traditional model may distinguish pre-head, head, nucleus and tail, with the nucleus as the essential element.
keyPoints: A tone unit is a stretch of speech organised around a main pitch-bearing nucleus.
The nucleus need not be the last word or the loudest syllable.

questions.prompt: Why might the nucleus move to SHE in 'SHE is coming tomorrow'?
questions.shortAnswer: The speaker is contrasting who is coming.
questions.answer: The speaker is contrasting who is coming. Nuclear placement helps express information focus and alternatives.
keyPoints: The speaker is contrasting who is coming.
Nuclear placement helps express information focus and alternatives.

questions.prompt: What is types of tone?
questions.shortAnswer: Common pedagogical tones include fall, rise, fall–rise, rise–fall and level.
questions.answer: Common pedagogical tones include fall, rise, fall–rise, rise–fall and level. Pitch contours contribute to interactional interpretation, but no contour has one invariant meaning across all contexts.
keyPoints: Common pedagogical tones include fall, rise, fall–rise, rise–fall and level.
Tone is a pitch pattern; its interpretation depends on discourse and accent.

questions.prompt: Does a rising tone always identify a yes–no question?
questions.shortAnswer: No.
questions.answer: No. A rise can signal continuation, uncertainty or other interactional meanings, and yes–no questions can have other contours depending on context.
keyPoints: No.
A rise can signal continuation, uncertainty or other interactional meanings, and yes–no questions can have other contours depending on context.

questions.prompt: Explain intonation and its functions briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Intonation is the organisation of pitch patterns across speech.
questions.answer: Intonation is the organisation of pitch patterns across speech. It can signal focus, attitude, grammatical interpretation, discourse organisation and turn management.
keyPoints: Intonation is the organisation of pitch patterns across speech.
Pitch pattern does not mechanically determine the speaker's private attitude.

questions.prompt: How can the same words perform different conversational work through intonation?
questions.shortAnswer: Changes in pitch contour and nuclear placement can signal a statement, confirmation request, contrast or reservation.
questions.answer: Changes in pitch contour and nuclear placement can signal a statement, confirmation request, contrast or reservation. Context remains necessary for interpretation.
keyPoints: Changes in pitch contour and nuclear placement can signal a statement, confirmation request, contrast or reservation.
Context remains necessary for interpretation.

questions.prompt: Explain tag questions and interpretation briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Tag-question intonation can contribute to whether a speaker seeks information or invites agreement.
questions.answer: Tag-question intonation can contribute to whether a speaker seeks information or invites agreement. A rising tag often seeks confirmation, while a falling tag often displays a stronger expectation of agreement; these are tendencies.
keyPoints: Tag-question intonation can contribute to whether a speaker seeks information or invites agreement.
A contour is a cue rather than conclusive evidence of certainty.

questions.prompt: Why should we avoid teaching rising tag equals uncertainty as an exceptionless rule?
questions.shortAnswer: Intonation interacts with context, stance and conversational purpose.
questions.answer: Intonation interacts with context, stance and conversational purpose. The rise is informative but does not uniquely reveal a mental state.
keyPoints: Intonation interacts with context, stance and conversational purpose.
The rise is informative but does not uniquely reveal a mental state.

questions.prompt: Explain ipa and transcription levels briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: The IPA represents speech sounds; broad transcription abstracts categories while narrow transcription adds phonetic detail.
questions.answer: The IPA represents speech sounds; broad transcription abstracts categories while narrow transcription adds phonetic detail. Slashes conventionally mark phonemic analysis, while brackets permit more detailed phonetic description.
keyPoints: The IPA represents speech sounds; broad transcription abstracts categories while narrow transcription adds phonetic detail.
IPA transcription represents sounds rather than converting each written letter into a symbol.

questions.prompt: Why would an aspiration study need more detail than a pronunciation dictionary?
questions.shortAnswer: The study compares phonetic realisations such as aspiration, which ordinary broad phonemic notation may omit.
questions.answer: The study compares phonetic realisations such as aspiration, which ordinary broad phonemic notation may omit. Narrower transcription or measurement better fits that purpose.
keyPoints: The study compares phonetic realisations such as aspiration, which ordinary broad phonemic notation may omit.
Narrower transcription or measurement better fits that purpose.

questions.prompt: What is connected-speech transcription?
questions.shortAnswer: Connected-speech transcription represents sounds in a continuous utterance rather than isolated dictionary forms.
questions.answer: Connected-speech transcription represents sounds in a continuous utterance rather than isolated dictionary forms. Account for weak forms, possible assimilation or elision, linking and prominence. State the accent and level of detail.
keyPoints: Connected-speech transcription represents sounds in a continuous utterance rather than isolated dictionary forms.
A written sentence can have several legitimate spoken realisations.

questions.prompt: Why is there no single obligatory connected-speech transcription of a sentence without a recording?
questions.shortAnswer: Accent, focus, speed and style affect pronunciation.
questions.answer: Accent, focus, speed and style affect pronunciation. A proposed transcription should identify its assumptions or represent a particular recorded performance.
keyPoints: Accent, focus, speed and style affect pronunciation.
A proposed transcription should identify its assumptions or represent a particular recorded performance.

questions.prompt: Explain linking and intrusive r briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: In non-rhotic accents, linking /r/ appears before a following vowel where historical or spelling r supports it.
questions.answer: In non-rhotic accents, linking /r/ appears before a following vowel where historical or spelling r supports it. Intrusive /r/ occurs in comparable vowel-linking contexts without a written r. Both vary across speakers and styles.
keyPoints: In non-rhotic accents, linking /r/ appears before a following vowel where historical or spelling r supports it.
These descriptions do not apply identically to rhotic accents.

questions.prompt: How do far away and law and order illustrate different r-linking labels?
questions.shortAnswer: Far away can have linking r associated with the word far.
questions.answer: Far away can have linking r associated with the word far. Law and order can contain intrusive r despite no r in law's spelling, in some non-rhotic accents.
keyPoints: Far away can have linking r associated with the word far.
Law and order can contain intrusive r despite no r in law's spelling, in some non-rhotic accents.

questions.prompt: What is morphology?
questions.shortAnswer: Morphology studies the internal structure of words and how their forms relate to meaning and grammar.
questions.answer: Morphology studies the internal structure of words and how their forms relate to meaning and grammar. It identifies recurring meaningful units and the rules or patterns that combine or alter them.
keyPoints: Morphology studies the internal structure of words and how their forms relate to meaning and grammar.

questions.prompt: Why is teachers a useful example of morphology?
questions.shortAnswer: It combines a root with derivational -er and inflectional -s.
questions.answer: It combines a root with derivational -er and inflectional -s. Their order and contribution show how word structure expresses both lexical and grammatical information.
keyPoints: It combines a root with derivational -er and inflectional -s.
Their order and contribution show how word structure expresses both lexical and grammatical information.

questions.prompt: Explain inflection and derivation briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Inflection expresses grammatical forms of a lexeme; derivation typically creates a new lexeme.
questions.answer: Inflection expresses grammatical forms of a lexeme; derivation typically creates a new lexeme. Derivation can change word class or meaning; inflection normally supplies contrasts such as number or tense within a paradigm.
keyPoints: Inflection expresses grammatical forms of a lexeme; derivation typically creates a new lexeme.

questions.prompt: Does unhappy show derivation although happy and unhappy are both adjectives?
questions.shortAnswer: Yes.
questions.answer: Yes. Derivation can change lexical meaning without changing word class. Unhappy is a distinct adjective lexeme, while happier is normally an inflected comparative form.
keyPoints: Yes.
Derivation can change lexical meaning without changing word class.
Unhappy is a distinct adjective lexeme, while happier is normally an inflected comparative form.
